title: Shopify Acquires Tailwind
content:
Tailwind Labs said its open-source projects will remain MIT-licensed, with the existing team continuing to lead and maintain them with Shopify’s support.

Tailwind Labs, the company behind the Tailwind CSS web-development framework, is joining Shopify, with the team moving under the e-commerce company to maintain and develop the open-source project.

Tailwind CSS is installed more than 110 million times per week and is used by companies including OpenAI, X, Cloudflare, Reddit and Shopify.

Adam Wathan, Tailwind’s creator, said the move is meant to give the framework a long-term home as it continues to be used by millions of developers. “We're joining Shopify to give Tailwind a stable long-term home where it will be actively maintained for the millions of people who depend on it.”

Wathan said Tailwind Labs had built a business around website templates and other commercial products, but he ultimately wanted Tailwind CSS to be developed alongside a large, real-world product. Shopify, he said, offers that environment through its storefronts, administration tools, checkout and Shop app.

“Shopify provides an incredible surface area for us to do this work,” Wathan said. He also pointed to Shopify’s work on agentic commerce as an area where interface design is likely to evolve.

Shopify was among the early large-scale adopters of Tailwind CSS and has used the framework in its own products as well as encouraged merchants to build with it. Wathan described Tailwind as a “very important part of the stack at Shopify” and said the company is committed to its continued maintenance.

Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The acquisition will not change Tailwind CSS’s open-source licensing or development model. Tailwind Labs said its open-source projects will remain MIT-licensed, with the existing team continuing to lead and maintain them with Shopify’s support.

Tailwind's commercial business will change. Tailwind Labs is closing sign-ups for new customers for products including Tailwind Plus and ui.sh, although existing customers will retain access. The company said it will now focus on Tailwind CSS rather than growing the commercial business around the framework.

The Shopify deal comes after a difficult period for Tailwind Labs earlier this year.

In January, the company laid off three of its four engineers after revenue fell by roughly 80% and documentation traffic declined 40% from early 2023, with Wathan attributing the pressure to the way AI tools had changed developer behaviour.

The layoffs prompted companies including Google AI Studio, Vercel, Supabase and Lovable to sponsor Tailwind CSS. Shopify was already among the companies supporting the project, describing Tailwind as “core infrastructure for how the modern web gets built.”

The joint R&D lab will focus on frontier research, model post-training, real-world outcome feedback, and regulator-grade AI safety for financial services.

IDFC FIRST Bank and AI company Sarvam AI have partnered to establish a joint R&D Lab to build banking systems that can learn from outcomes and improve over time.

The lab will work across frontier AI research, post-training, AI safety and security, with a focus on applying these technologies within a regulated banking environment.

Sarvam AI said the goal is to enable the bank to adopt new AI models and capabilities while retaining what its systems learn about customers, processes, policies and decisions.

“AI capabilities are advancing quickly, but making those capabilities useful in banking requires more than access to better models,” Sarvam AI said in a blog post.

The lab will combine IDFC FIRST Bank’s banking expertise with Sarvam’s AI research and engineering capabilities. It will test new models and techniques against banking use cases and use outcomes from those systems to improve subsequent versions.

The companies said that banking operations generate signals through customer interactions, decisions, human corrections, exceptions and eventual outcomes. The R&D lab will explore ways to use these signals as inputs for continuous model improvement.

The partnership will also focus on building infrastructure that can evaluate and adapt AI models using banking tasks, human feedback and real-world outcomes.

Sarvam AI described this as a “post-training factory” that can turn production experience into a source of learning, allowing AI systems to become more specific to the bank over time.

The lab will also work on AI safety and security, including evaluation, governance and controls. The systems will need to remain observable, auditable and controllable as their capabilities increase.

The research programme will explore new AI and large language model capabilities relevant to banking and financial services.

Alongside model development, the lab will study reliability, security, explainability and control, with these considerations built into the development process.

Sarvam AI said the approach would allow IDFC FIRST Bank to continue adopting new AI capabilities without rebuilding its systems every time the underlying technology changes.

title: Meta Launches Muse AI Agent With Internet Access Guardrails
content:
Meta says Muse uses a dedicated virtual machine and a separate Sentinel system to control internet access, credentials, and sensitive actions.

Meta has introduced Muse, a personal AI agent that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, including sending emails, booking travel, filling out forms, and making purchases.

Muse is being rolled out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai, with support for AI glasses planned. Meta said the service is free for most use cases, while subscription plans will be available for users who want additional capabilities.

Muse is designed to work after a user closes the app, and can develop plans around longer-term goals, coordinate resources, and take action when circumstances change. The agent can also return to the user when it needs approval for actions such as sending an email or completing a purchase.

“People just tell Muse what needs to get done, and it takes action,” Meta said in a statement.

Muse runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated virtual machine that contains the agent and a user’s data. It has its own browser and can interact with services that a user connects to it.

Meta said a separate Sentinel agent operates on the same machine and controls Muse’s access to the internet. “Nothing Muse does reaches the internet unless the Sentinel approves it,” the company said.

The system keeps credentials hidden from Muse. Passwords and payment information are stored in secure storage, allowing the agent to use them without accessing the underlying credentials.

Muse also requires user approval for sensitive actions and provides an audit trail showing what it has done and what it plans to do. Users can decide which services Muse can access and set permissions, including whether it can only read email or also send messages on their behalf.

The agent can retain information from conversations and use it in future tasks. Meta said users can ask Muse to forget specific information and can opt out of having their interactions used to train Meta’s AI models.

For purchases, Muse can use Link, Stripe’s payment service, through a wallet for AI agents that generates a one-time-use card. Meta said Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections. Support for Shop Pay and 1Password is planned.

Meta also said it plans to introduce Muse Confidential VM later this year. Under the system, the entire virtual machine, including user data and conversations, will be encrypted with a key held only by the user.

Muse is powered by Muse Spark, which Meta described as its most capable model to date and designed for agentic tasks.

title: Grok Bot Was Built in Just Four Weeks
content:
A handful of employees worked in a separate part of the office and used private Slack channels, letting them make rapid product decisions without the coordination required for a larger project.

SpaceXAI built Grok Bot from its first line of code to a working internal prototype in about a month, with a small team deliberately isolated from the rest of the company.

Roman Ugarte, an AI engineer at SpaceXAI who helped incubate the product, revealed this in a conversation with Lenny Rachitsky, creator of Lenny’s Podcast.

Ugarte said the team was created as a “blank page” exercise to build an AI product for general knowledge work.

A handful of employees worked in a separate part of the office and used private Slack channels, letting them make rapid product decisions without the coordination required for a larger project.

The team then spent roughly two weeks manually onboarding 200 to 300 early users.

Ugarte said core team members sat through individual sessions, watching users encounter problems such as computers failing to start or people becoming confused during onboarding.

The process also exposed unexpected usage patterns. Employees began creating multiple specialised bots, with some using a higher-level “chief of staff” bot to delegate work to other bots.

The biggest improvements before launch were largely invisible to users.

Rather than adding more features, the team focused on making the underlying computer-use infrastructure reliable.

Sales staff, for example, were using systems that lacked reliable APIs or MCP integrations. Giving bots their own computers allowed them to interact with those systems through browsers, clicking buttons and entering information like a human user.

Ugarte said the team repeatedly fixed small infrastructure problems, such as giving agents better browser visibility or more precise mouse control. These changes could unlock entire workflows without requiring a new model capability.

The product was also designed around two early architectural decisions: bots would run in the cloud, and each would have its own computer. Ugarte argued that AI agents should not share a user's machine, just as human colleagues normally have their own computers.

That architecture has enabled bots to work with other bots. Ugarte said he uses a QA bot that can run Grok Bots inside its own computer to test software releases and record results. The team's longer-term vision is for users to have teams of persistent AI bots that can delegate work among themselves.

“The ultimate vision of Grok Bot is incredibly simple,” Ugarte said. “You should have a team of AI bots that help you with your job and help you with your life.”

SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot last month as a beta AI agent designed to function as an always-on digital teammate.

The bots have their own cloud-based computers, allowing them to log into the tools, websites and apps people already use and complete multi-step tasks without requiring dedicated APIs or pre-built workflows. Users can assign work from desktop or mobile, and the bot returns when the task is complete or needs approval.

At launch, Grok Bot was available in beta to selected SuperGrok and Cursor subscribers on desktop and iOS, while enterprise access was placed behind a waitlist.

This deal marks a major push into AI inference chips and data-centre infrastructure.

Amazon and Qualcomm have entered a long-term partnership to develop custom AI chips for data centres, in a deal that could see Amazon purchase up to $60 billion worth of Qualcomm chips and related products.

The deal gives Qualcomm a major foothold in the data-centre market as it looks to reduce its dependence on smartphones and challenge Nvidia in AI computing. For Amazon, it adds another chip supplier as cloud companies increasingly look for alternatives to Nvidia's dominant AI processors.

The companies will focus on AI inference chips, which process requests and generate responses from already-trained AI models. They will also work on optical connectivity technology capable of supporting speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second, aimed at handling the growing data-transfer requirements of AI data centres.

The partnership comes as Qualcomm makes a major push into data-centre infrastructure. The chipmaker has set a target of generating $15 billion in data-centre chip revenue by 2029.

Qualcomm is looking to diversify as its traditional smartphone business faces pressure from weaker handset demand, rising component costs and Apple's move away from its modem technology.

“As AI demand accelerates, data center infrastructure will require advances in both computing and connectivity to deliver greater performance with more efficiency,” Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said.

Amazon is already one of Nvidia's largest customers and has developed its own AI chips through AWS. Its custom silicon business, including Trainium and Inferentia, has become an increasingly important part of its cloud strategy. AWS had an annualised revenue run rate of more than $25 billion at the end of June.

The Qualcomm partnership gives Amazon another option as AI infrastructure costs rise and demand for compute continues to surge. Microsoft and Meta are also working with Qualcomm on AI chips, giving the semiconductor company access to some of the world's biggest cloud and AI customers.

The focus on inference is particularly significant. As AI models move from training into widespread use, the amount of computing required to generate responses is growing rapidly. This is creating a new opportunity for chipmakers that can deliver inference at lower costs and with better energy efficiency.

Qualcomm will also increase its use of Amazon Web Services for chip-design workloads, with the aim of shortening development cycles.

The deal does not immediately challenge Nvidia's dominance. But it highlights a growing shift in the AI chip market: the next battle may increasingly be over making AI inference cheaper and more efficient, rather than simply building larger models and faster processors.

title: Google DeepMind’s New Tool Maps All 9 Bn DNA Mutations in Humans
content:
AlphaGenome Atlas helps scientists prioritise variants, investigate their molecular effects, and uncover genetic links to rare diseases and common traits.

Google DeepMind has launched AlphaGenome Atlas, a platform that predicts the molecular effects of 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome, giving researchers a way to rank and investigate genetic variants without testing each mutation individually in the laboratory.

The platform is available for academic research through a free website portal and includes precomputed predictions generated using DeepMind’s AlphaGenome AI model. The company said the resource is designed to provide researchers with a genome-wide view of how DNA variants may affect biological processes.

“DNA is the language of life,” Google DeepMind stated in a blog, asserting that interpreting how genetic variations affect biology at a molecular level remains a major challenge.

The dataset is about 1 petabyte in size, which DeepMind said is more than 30 times larger than the AlphaFold Database. AlphaGenome Atlas provides thousands of molecular effect predictions for each variant across multiple aspects of gene regulation, covering hundreds of human and mouse cell types and tissues.

The platform also introduces the AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score, which combines predictions from AlphaGenome with AlphaMissense, DeepMind’s model for predicting the effects of protein-altering DNA variants. The score assigns a single measure to each variant, allowing researchers to rank variants by potential impact.

Researchers can also access AVI feature attributions that show which biological processes contribute to a variant’s predicted impact, including RNA splicing and gene expression. The platform includes a collection of more than 2,500 recurring DNA sequence motifs and their locations.

DeepMind said the AVI score is designed to work across both coding and non-coding regions of the genome. Coding regions account for about 2% of the genome, while the remaining 98% is non-coding and contains regulatory elements that control gene activity.

The company said external collaborators have already used AlphaGenome Atlas to identify and experimentally validate variants relevant to rare diseases and to find rare variants associated with common traits.

AlphaGenome Atlas has also been used to study non-coding variants in population-scale genetic data.

The platform is available through its website, the AlphaGenome API, and as a skill in Google Antigravity. DeepMind said Atlas is currently available for non-commercial use, while commercial access through Google Cloud is planned.

The company described AlphaGenome Atlas as a baseline rather than an endpoint, saying that improvements to AlphaGenome could make the genome-wide predictions more comprehensive and precise over time.

“Together, these tools will enable researchers and industry partners to accelerate the pace of biological discovery,” Google DeepMind said.

title: Bengaluru’s QNu Labs Raises ₹200 Cr in Series A1 Round
content:
The funding takes the quantum cybersecurity company’s total capital raised to ₹375 crore.

Bengaluru-based quantum startup QNu Labs has raised ₹200 crore in its Series A1 funding round. The National Quantum Mission and Speciale Invest led the round with participation from Sony Innovation Fund, Gaja Capital and Artha Ventures.

The company will use the funds to expand research and development, sales and market operations. It will also support QNu Labs’ contribution to India’s Quantum Secure and Sensing Networks project. The company plans to expand its technology into quantum sensing and AI.

Sunil Gupta, Co-Founder of QNu Labs, said India moved early in the quantum era and the National Quantum Mission helped lay the foundation for commercial deployment.

The latest round takes QNu Labs’ total capital raised to ₹375 crore. The funding comes as governments and enterprises prepare for quantum-safe infrastructure. India’s National Quantum Mission has set 2029 as its implementation timeline.

The company said quantum computing and AI could challenge existing encryption systems. Organisations are therefore evaluating cryptographic technologies designed to withstand future quantum and AI attacks.

Gupta added that the company had deployed its technology across government, critical infrastructure and BFSI. He also said around 80% of the round came from new global investors, describing this as a signal of growing global interest in quantum-safe security.

Sony Innovation Fund Director and Head of Sony Ventures India Yoko Fukata said the fund was investing across India’s deep tech sector. She said it would collaborate with QNu Labs as the company expands globally.

QNu Labs said the funds will help scale its quantum-safe cybersecurity solutions across India and global markets. The company also plans to increase deployments across critical sectors. A part of the funding will serve as QNu Labs’ contribution to an approved RDI-funded project. The project will build the technology backbone for India’s Quantum Secure and Sensing Networks.

Gaja Capital Co-Founder and Managing Partner Gopal Jain said quantum-safe security was becoming national infrastructure. He compared its importance to power and transport in the physical economy.

“What attracted us is that the science is done and the demand curve is turning,” Jain said, adding that the company’s focus had now shifted towards scaling.

Moreover, Ravindra Barlingay, CEO of IITM C-DOT Samgnya Technologies Foundation, said the National Hub for Quantum Communication led the investment round.

title: Amazon Strikes Qualcomm Deal for AI Chips, Challenging Nvidia
content:
This deal marks a major push into AI inference chips and data-centre infrastructure.

Amazon and Qualcomm have entered a long-term partnership to develop custom AI chips for data centres, in a deal that could see Amazon purchase up to $60 billion worth of Qualcomm chips and related products.

The deal gives Qualcomm a major foothold in the data-centre market as it looks to reduce its dependence on smartphones and challenge Nvidia in AI computing. For Amazon, it adds another chip supplier as cloud companies increasingly look for alternatives to Nvidia's dominant AI processors.

The companies will focus on AI inference chips, which process requests and generate responses from already-trained AI models. They will also work on optical connectivity technology capable of supporting speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second, aimed at handling the growing data-transfer requirements of AI data centres.

The partnership comes as Qualcomm makes a major push into data-centre infrastructure. The chipmaker has set a target of generating $15 billion in data-centre chip revenue by 2029.

Qualcomm is looking to diversify as its traditional smartphone business faces pressure from weaker handset demand, rising component costs and Apple's move away from its modem technology.

“As AI demand accelerates, data center infrastructure will require advances in both computing and connectivity to deliver greater performance with more efficiency,” Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said.

Amazon is already one of Nvidia's largest customers and has developed its own AI chips through AWS. Its custom silicon business, including Trainium and Inferentia, has become an increasingly important part of its cloud strategy. AWS had an annualised revenue run rate of more than $25 billion at the end of June.

The Qualcomm partnership gives Amazon another option as AI infrastructure costs rise and demand for compute continues to surge. Microsoft and Meta are also working with Qualcomm on AI chips, giving the semiconductor company access to some of the world's biggest cloud and AI customers.

The focus on inference is particularly significant. As AI models move from training into widespread use, the amount of computing required to generate responses is growing rapidly. This is creating a new opportunity for chipmakers that can deliver inference at lower costs and with better energy efficiency.

Qualcomm will also increase its use of Amazon Web Services for chip-design workloads, with the aim of shortening development cycles.

The deal does not immediately challenge Nvidia's dominance. But it highlights a growing shift in the AI chip market: the next battle may increasingly be over making AI inference cheaper and more efficient, rather than simply building larger models and faster processors.

The group builds on Accenture’s nearly 50,000 Google Cloud-skilled professionals. It will expand Gemini Enterprise training and certification while creating the 1,000-person FDE workforce to support enterprise deployments.

“Deploying agentic AI is a top priority for enterprises today, and the Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group significantly expands the expertise and resources available to help our customers deliver real business value,” Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian added.

The group will focus on four areas: increasing Gemini Enterprise adoption through implementation frameworks and accelerators, developing industry-specific solutions, supporting the transition from AI experimentation to enterprise deployments, and driving adoption of AI capabilities among users.

The new group builds on the companies’ joint Generative and Agentic AI Centre of Excellence and the Gemini Enterprise Acceleration Programme.

title: Bevel Gears India Opens Aerospace Facility in Bengaluru, Targets ₹500 Cr Revenue by 2029
content:
The 70,000 sq ft facility will manufacture precision gearing for aerospace and defence programmes, from development through serial production.

Bevel Gears India (BGI) inaugurated a 70,000-square-foot manufacturing facility near Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru on September 8, dedicated exclusively to aerospace and defence gearing.

The Bengaluru-based high-precision bevel gear specialist said the facility is part of its growth strategy as it targets ₹500 crore in revenue by 2029.

“This is our first plant built from the ground up for aerospace,” said Mushtaq Jamal, Director, Engineering and Business Development, Bevel Gears India. “The facility has been designed around the requirements of flight-critical gearing, with dedicated manufacturing, inspection and quality infrastructure to support demanding tolerances, process control and complete traceability.”

According to the company, the facility will manufacture spiral and straight bevel gears, zerol and angular bevels, beveloids, hypoid and high-ratio hypoid gears, curvic couplings and precision parallel-axis gearing.

BGI said these capabilities will support aero-engine, helicopter, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), actuation and aerospace gearbox programmes from development through serial production.

The facility is located within Bengaluru’s aerospace corridor, which the company said places BGI close to aircraft and aerospace original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) companies and tier-1 suppliers.

The plant houses Gleason and Klingelnberg Computer Numerical Control (CNC) bevel and hypoid gear grinding lines. BGI said these include India’s first Gleason 275G CNC hypoid grinder with a special straight bevel grinding option and India’s first Klingelnberg Oerlikon G80 CNC hypoid grinder.

The facility also has DMG 5-axis machining centres and a climate-controlled metrology room equipped with ZEISS coordinate measuring machines and Gleason gear inspection systems. The company said industry-standard Gleason software supports gear design and tooth-contact analysis, reinforced by SolidWorks.

“India’s aerospace sector is growing rapidly, with global engine and airframe makers expanding their supplier base in the country. Demand is also increasing for the complex, flight-critical gearing we have specialised in for five decades,” said Sulaiman Jamal, Managing Director, Jamal Group. “This plant allows us to take programmes from prototype and development quantities through to serial production across multiple platforms. We also offer reverse engineering services for legacy and obsolete parts, enabling customers to maintain their equipment.”

BGI said the facility operates under AS9100D-certified aerospace quality systems and holds ISO 9001:2015 certification. Heat treatment capabilities and National Aerospace and Defense Contractors Accreditation Program (NADCAP) accreditation for special processes are planned as the next phase.

Founded in 1976, BGI is part of the Jamal Group and serves aerospace, space, motorsport, mining, steel and industrial customers across international markets, according to the company. BGI also said its products have supported India's space programme, including gears aboard Pragyan, the lunar rover used in the Chandrayaan-3 mission.

title: Spotify Cuts Claude Code Token Usage by 90%
content:
Spotify’s Portal for Backstage routes routine coding-agent tasks to cheaper models, reducing the amount of frontier-model tokens Claude Code consumes.

Spotify says its internal developer platform, Portal by Spotify, cut token consumption from Claude Code by about 90% in tests by routing file-reading and predictable code-generation tasks to cheaper AI models, rather than using Anthropic’s frontier coding model for every operation.

The approach uses Portal’s “AiKA Modes”, which are declarative agents that run on ephemeral runtimes. Developers can specify the model, instructions, parameters and MCP tools for each mode without managing separate infrastructure or API keys.

Spotify engineer Dimitri Mazmanov tested the approach on a Java monorepo using two modes: a bulk-reader for reading multiple files and a code-writer for predictable code-generation tasks. Both examples use Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash as the worker model, although Portal can be configured with other models.

“Most of what an AI coding agent does for me isn't thinking. It's I/O,” Mazmanov wrote. The setup keeps those token-heavy operations away from Claude Code while retaining Claude for tasks that require more reasoning.

The routing is enforced through a Claude Code plugin called Shunt. It uses PreToolUse hooks to intercept large file reads and redirect Claude to the bulk-reader mode. By default, reads of files exceeding 350 lines are blocked, while targeted reads using offsets and limits continue to pass through.

A second mode handles output-heavy tasks such as generating tests, configuration scaffolding and type stubs. It receives a specification and reference file, generates the code and can write it directly to disk, meaning Claude does not need to consume the generated output in its own context.

Spotify said the test measured Claude's token consumption across four scenarios in a Java monorepo, with mean savings from bulk reading of around 90%. The code-generation case was harder to measure because the unoptimised workflow includes both reading reference files and generating code as Claude output.

The approach has limits, and Spotify said the worker models are not intended to handle debugging, architectural decisions or safety-critical reasoning.

Besides, delegated analysis also does not reliably provide the line-level information Claude needs for editing. Network latency is another constraint, with typical delegation taking 10–30 seconds and Portal imposing a 30-second limit per invocation.

Mazmanov described the broader approach as “model routing powered by AiKA modes”, allowing teams to change the worker model or instructions without modifying the routing plugin itself.

Spotify made the bulk-reader and code-writer modes publicly available through AiKA, allowing developers to reuse or customise them across projects.

title: IIT Madras-Backed Bodhan AI, AI4Bharat Launch 4 AI Models for Students & Teachers
content:
The models will be offered as Digital Public Goods, with open weights and sovereign APIs that let developers build applications without training language models from scratch.

Bodhan AI, a centre of excellence in AI for education incubated at IIT Madras, has launched four AI models for speech recognition, speech generation, machine translation and optical character recognition (OCR), in partnership with AI4Bharat.

The models are being released as Digital Public Goods through open-weight models and hosted APIs on sovereign infrastructure. The initiative is part of the Bharat EduAI Stack, which aims to provide a common AI infrastructure layer for multilingual education in India.

The four models cover 27 languages for automatic speech recognition (ASR), 23 languages for OCR, 22 languages for machine translation through Bodhan-Translate, and 23 languages for text-to-speech (TTS).

The models are trained and optimised using NVIDIA Nemotron open models and libraries, including the NVIDIA NeMo framework for ASR, machine translation and OCR. Bodhan AI has post-trained NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR for Indian languages, including regional dialects and accents. The models are served using NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM and vLLM inference microservices.

Prof Mitesh Khapra, Principal Investigator at Bodhan AI, said the project was intended to create a shared infrastructure layer rather than separate AI systems for individual institutions.

“We built these voice and vision models, and made them accessible as Digital Public Goods on a Digital Public Infrastructure, so that efforts across the country don't remain fragmented,” Khapra said.

He added that edtech companies, startups, researchers, universities, technology companies and government partners could use the models to develop applications for Indian users.

The speech recognition model can allow students to interact with AI tutors through voice in their preferred language, while TTS can enable AI systems to respond in Indian languages. OCR can help education systems process textbooks, worksheets, documents and handwritten answers. Bodhan-Translate can be used to translate educational content between Indian languages.

Prof V Kamakoti, Director of IIT Madras, said the infrastructure could help expand access to AI across India’s linguistic diversity.

“India’s AI journey cannot be built on technology alone. It must be built on technology that understands India,” Kamakoti said.

The models will also power Bodhan AI’s own education applications, including Student TutorBot and Teacher Assistant Bot.

Student TutorBot is designed for students in Classes 6–12 and is based on NCERT and SCERT curricula. Students can interact with it through text or voice across 22 Indian languages. The system uses textbook content to provide explanations, examples and assessments and can guide students through problems using interactive tools and a digital canvas.

Teacher Assistant Bot is designed to help teachers plan, create, assign and assess classroom work. Teachers can generate lesson plans, worksheets, quizzes, homework and revision material by specifying parameters such as grade, subject, topic, duration and difficulty. They can also upload student work for evaluation against specified marking criteria.

Bodhan AI said AI-generated outputs in the Teacher Assistant Bot are intended to remain subject to teacher review. Teachers can edit, regenerate or discard outputs rather than having AI make classroom decisions automatically.

Prof Balaraman Ravindran, Head of the Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI at IIT Madras, said developing AI for India requires more than adapting existing systems to Indian languages.

“Building AI for India requires going beyond adapting existing models to Indian languages. It requires developing foundational capabilities that understand the richness and diversity of our languages, contexts and educational needs,” Ravindran added.

Bodhan AI said government and public institutions could use the infrastructure for multilingual education and other public-service applications, while edtech companies could integrate the models through APIs without developing foundational models themselves. Startups and researchers can access the open-weight models for adaptation and further development.

The hosted API infrastructure is being designed around a sovereign deployment approach, with data anonymisation protocols and compliance with applicable national education data frameworks. The company said this is intended to give institutions and ecosystem partners greater control over deployment while supporting requirements around data governance, privacy and security.

NVIDIA and Bodhan AI are also collaborating on datasets, training recipes and evaluations for future foundational models for Indian languages. AI4Bharat is contributing its work on Indian-language datasets, tools, models and applications to the initiative.

title: Havells Brings Agentic AI Voice Control to 2.67 Mn Connected Home Appliances
content:
The voice assistant can understand natural and code-mixed speech, coordinate multiple appliances at once, and retain context across conversations.

Havells has launched an Agentic AI Voice feature in its Havells One app that allows users to control connected appliances through natural speech in English and seven Indian languages.

The feature is built by Havells Centre for Research & Innovation (CRI), with ElevenLabs providing the streaming Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech models for the voice interface.

The feature is live for all 2.67 million Havells One mobile app users and supports Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Kannada, Gujarati and Malayalam, in addition to English.

Users can use voice commands to control appliances, rooms, scenes and coordinated actions across connected devices. The feature currently works across Havells fans, air purifiers, water purifiers and water heaters, as well as Lloyd air conditioners and washing machines, Crabtree smart switches and upcoming smart home products.

Unlike Havells’ earlier voice experience, which relied on predefined commands and supported English and Hindi on selected appliances, the new system is designed to understand user intent. It can also handle code-mixed speech, where users switch between languages while speaking.

For instance, a request to “make the room comfortable” can trigger coordinated actions across an air conditioner, air purifier, fan and lights. Requests involving multiple devices can be executed across different connectivity protocols.

The agent also retains context across conversations and can ask users to clarify ambiguous requests. It can explain device error codes in spoken language and is being extended beyond device control to areas such as product FAQs, troubleshooting and scheduling.

“This Agentic AI Voice capability is a breakthrough for our customers, allowing them to control and interact with their devices naturally, without having to remember commands or learn rules,” said Dipesh Shah, Executive President and CTO, Havells.

“Its potential is limitless and will continue to expand as new capabilities are added across our devices and services. As a daily-use AI experience, it showcases the transformative potential of AI agents, far beyond the traditional voice interfaces of the past,” he added.

Havells said its CRI team evaluated voice AI models based on recognition accuracy, multilingual support, latency and voice synthesis. The company moved the solution into production in approximately six weeks, with support from ElevenLabs’ Forward Deployed Engineering team for voice quality and regional language pronunciation tuning.

“People have always had to learn the interface of communicating: the commands, the syntax, the order they come in. That is hardest in India, where a household does not speak one language and often moves between three in a single sentence,” said Karthik Rajaram, General Manager and Country Head, India, ElevenLabs.

“Powered by ElevenLabs, Havells now runs seven Indian languages alongside English across an appliance range, so the person no longer has to meet the technology halfway. They say what they want to the agent, in the language they were already thinking in, and the devices respond,” he added.

Havells plans to expand the feature to more Indian languages and bring additional appliances onto the voice platform. The company also plans to add greater personalisation for individual household members and extend voice interactions to product support, troubleshooting and scheduling.

title: Genesys Launches New Innovations To Automate End-To-End Customer Service
content:
Snippet: The platform retains information across interactions, determines its actions and coordinates work between AI and human employees while operating within predefined business rules.

Genesys has introduced AI tools to help businesses go beyond chatbots to automate customer service journeys from request to resolution.

As enterprises move from standalone chatbots to AI systems that can handle multi-step tasks, Genesys, a global leader in agentic orchestration, is positioning its cloud platform as an autonomous AI layer for customer service. The platform retains information across interactions, determines its actions and coordinates work between AI and human employees while operating within predefined business rules.

On September 3, the company unveiled new capabilities through its AI systems, announcing Genesys Cloud Navigator, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator, Contextual Intelligence and the AI Control Plane at its Xperience event. Its autonomous AI is designed to deliver adaptive, personalised and governed experiences.

Starting with Genesys Cloud Navigator as its entry point, it uses customer interactions, historical data, conversational information and enterprise data to determine the customer’s goal and direct them to the next step.

As the journey progresses, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator creates an ideal plan to achieve the desired outcome and coordinates decision-making. This entails identifying the current situation and reasoning over context, policies and guardrails to determine the next action and move work across AI, human agents and systems. It enables an end-to-end journey that can pause, resume and adapt while keeping the customer’s intended outcome in focus.

Contextual Intelligence turns interactions into persistent enterprise memory by connecting customer details, conversational data, history, business events and real-time signals. By preserving this intelligence over time, it gives its AI a richer understanding of the customer and helps inform relevant decisions.

The fourth component, the AI Control Plane, serves as the operating layer for the company’s AI. This involves providing governance and oversight, and allowing the enterprise to monitor the activities of its AI, including agentic orchestration, Genesys Cloud Navigator, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator and Contextual Intelligence. It enforces policies and ensures that actions remain within the company’s business boundaries.

“Autonomous AI is finally pushing customer service beyond individual interactions and isolated use cases,” said Hayley Sutherland, Research Manager, Conversational AI at IDC.

Genesys said both Contextual Intelligence and the AI Control Plane are now available, while Navigator is expected to be generally available between November 2026 and January 2027.

title: Adobe Names Anil Chakravarthy as CEO, Shantanu Narayen to Become Executive Chair
content:
The leadership change comes as Adobe expands its focus on agentic software across creativity, productivity and customer experience.

Adobe has appointed Anil Chakravarthy as its next President and Chief Executive Officer, with the leadership transition set to take effect on December 1, 2026. Current CEO Shantanu Narayen will become Executive Chair and work with Chakravarthy during the transition.

Chakravarthy, who currently leads Adobe’s Customer Experience Orchestration business and worldwide field operations, will also join Adobe’s Board of Directors when he becomes CEO.

“I could not be more confident that Anil is the right person to lead Adobe’s growth in an AI-driven era and look forward to working closely with him in my new role as executive chair,” Narayen said in a statement

Chakravarthy said he would focus on growth and Adobe’s position in agentic software across creativity, productivity and customer experience.

“I am deeply honoured to have been chosen to lead Adobe during this pivotal moment,” Chakravarthy said. “I’m energised by the opportunity to fuel growth and drive Adobe's leadership in the next era of agentic software for creativity, productivity and customer experience.”

Chakravarthy joined Adobe in January 2020 as Executive Vice President and General Manager of its Digital Experience business. Later that year, he also took responsibility for worldwide field operations serving enterprise customers across Adobe’s product portfolio. He became president of Digital Experience and worldwide field operations in December 2021.

During his tenure, Chakravarthy led Adobe’s expansion in Customer Experience Orchestration, including the development of products such as Adobe CX Enterprise, GenStudio and Brand Visibility. He also oversaw the scaling of Adobe Experience Platform and the introduction of CX Enterprise Coworker.

Chakravarthy was also involved in Adobe’s acquisitions and integration of Workfront and Semrush.

Before joining Adobe, Chakravarthy served as CEO of Informatica for four years. He joined the company in 2013 as an executive vice president and previously held executive roles at Symantec and VeriSign, along with a role at McKinsey & Company.

Chakravarthy holds a Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering from the Institute of Technology, Varanasi, and a master's degree and PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Narayen has led Adobe since December 2007, overseeing the company’s shift toward a subscription-based business model and its expansion into digital experience and AI-powered products. As Executive Chair, he will continue working with the company and Chakravarthy after the transition.

title: Coforge Launches AI Platform to Help Enterprises Build & Run AI Within Their Own Environments
content: Listen5 minSHARESaveFollowPreferred SourceGoogle NewsWhatsAppTelegramMid-tier IT services firm Coforge has launched an enterprise AI platform that allows companies to build, fine-tune, deploy and operate AI systems within their own controlled environments, as businesses increasingly look to reduce dependence on individual model providers.The platform, called Coforge AI Launchpad, is designed to work across cloud environments and allows enterprises to route workloads between open-weight and frontier AI models depending on business, regulatory, performance and cost considerations, the company said in a statement.“Enterprise AI is entering a new phase where control matters as much as capability,” Lalit Wadhwa, Chief Technology Officer, Coforge, said in a statement. “Organisations need the optionality to leverage the best AI models available without creating new forms of technology dependency. Coforge AI Launchpad gives enterprises a governed foundation that preserves ownership of data, intellectual property, and AI environment while remaining flexible enough to adapt as the market evolves.”The move comes as enterprises move beyond experimentation with generative AI and begin deploying AI systems in production, where issues around data sovereignty, governance, infrastructure and the availability of skilled talent have become bigger constraints.Coforge said the transition from AI pilots to production remains difficult because of fragmented infrastructure, talent shortages and governance and auditability requirements. Its new offering, powered by its Nuuron platform, combines the underlying infrastructure with model engineering, deployment and managed services.The platform is already being deployed by clients with stringent regulatory and data-sovereignty requirements. These include a sovereign AI environment for a US-based clinical healthcare intelligence company and an AI-routing deployment for a US bank that helped reduce AI operating costs while maintaining governance and auditability.Coforge is positioning the offering around AI ownership and flexibility, rather than tying enterprises to a particular model or technology provider. This could become increasingly relevant as companies weigh the cost, performance and regulatory implications of using proprietary models versus open-weight alternatives.The AI Launchpad comprises six broad service areas spanning strategy and advisory, infrastructure and platform, model engineering and customisation, deployment and integration, LLM operations and observability, and governance, FinOps and managed-run services.For Coforge, the launch also expands its pitch from delivering AI-enabled applications and services to managing more of the underlying enterprise AI stack. title: Razorpay, IndusInd Bank Launch AI Account Manager RAY on WhatsApp for Businesses
content:
RAY lets businesses check payments, track settlements, resolve support issues, and initiate actions through text or voice messages.

Razorpay has launched RAY, an AI-powered account manager on WhatsApp that lets businesses check payments, track settlements, resolve support issues, and initiate actions through messages or voice notes.

The service has been launched in partnership with IndusInd Bank, with Bajaj Finance among the first businesses to go live. Razorpay said businesses have already had more than 20,000 conversations with RAY.

RAY allows businesses to make requests such as “Show me a summary of my payments from yesterday” or ask it to analyse payment data and project sales. The system can respond in natural language without requiring users to access Razorpay’s dashboard.

The platform also allows businesses to ask RAY to take actions. For instance, a business can request a refund or generate a payment link through WhatsApp rather than navigating multiple screens on a dashboard.

Razorpay said RAY can also proactively contact businesses based on signals from its payments systems. It can flag issues such as a decline in payment success rates or upcoming settlements and suggest actions.

“Millions of businesses across India are building and growing every day, and we wanted to make it easier for them to access the information, intelligent insights, and support they need along the way. With RAY, an AI Account Manager on WhatsApp, a business owner can simply ask for what they need in the most natural way possible and have it acted upon,” said Khilan Haria, Chief Product Officer, Razorpay.

The service is aimed at businesses of different sizes, including small and growing businesses that may not have dedicated account managers. Razorpay said RAY is designed to provide access to payment information and support through WhatsApp, a platform widely used by businesses in India.

The launch builds on Razorpay’s existing RAY technology, which was initially developed to provide businesses with information and support using AI. The company has now expanded it to trigger actions across its systems.

Razorpay said its AI Agent Platform uses a single agent rather than separate agents for payments, settlements, refunds and other functions. The agent can access different tools, knowledge and merchant information depending on the request.

The platform maintains a 360-degree context for each merchant and uses an evaluation system to validate responses in real time, according to Razorpay. The company said this is intended to reduce hallucinations while maintaining response speed.

“At IndusInd Bank, we are committed to making banking simpler, faster, and more accessible for businesses. Our partnership with Razorpay reflects this focus by bringing account management capabilities to a familiar platform like WhatsApp, helping make business support more immediate, intuitive, and convenient,” said Amitabh Saraff, Head – Institutional and Government Coverage, IndusInd Bank.

Razorpay recently also launched Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model designed specifically for payments, trained on nearly 3 trillion data points spanning 4 billion payments on its network.

title: OpenAI Says Its Most Capable Model Astra Can Find Zero-Day Exploits
content:
For now, the company is choosing caution over unrestricted access. Astra is expected to become available soon, but its most powerful cybersecurity capabilities will remain limited initially.

OpenAI says its upcoming AI model Astra has become the company’s first model to cross the ‘Critical’ threshold for cybersecurity capabilities. The model can discover previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop working exploits against hardened systems without human guidance.

The company says Astra is also significantly more capable than GPT-5.6 Sol at identifying vulnerabilities and developing exploits while using fewer tokens. In one internal evaluation, Astra discovered and used two zero-day vulnerabilities as part of an exploit chain. OpenAI says it is now working to disclose the vulnerabilities to the relevant maintainers.

The findings have prompted OpenAI to restrict access to Astra’s most advanced cybersecurity capabilities at launch. Advanced cybersecurity workflows will initially be available only to a small group of alpha testers, with broader defensive access planned through Daybreak Blue.

OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework defines the Critical cybersecurity threshold as the ability to identify and develop functional zero-day exploits across many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention, or to devise and execute novel, end-to-end cyberattacks against hardened targets from a high-level objective.

Astra met that threshold in OpenAI’s latest assessments.

On ExploitBench, a benchmark measuring the ability to develop exploits from known vulnerabilities, Astra scored a perfect 100%. OpenAI then created an internal benchmark containing 20 recently disclosed high-severity vulnerabilities from June to August to reduce concerns about benchmark contamination.

Astra achieved much higher arbitrary-code-execution rates than GPT-5.6 Sol on this test while using far fewer output tokens. More significantly, it discovered and used two zero-days while constructing an exploit chain.

In expert-led tests, Astra also found previously unknown vulnerabilities in a hardened browser and operating system. It built a browser-compromise chain that escaped the sandbox and executed commands on the host after opening an HTML file. In another test, it combined multiple vulnerabilities to escalate privileges from an unprivileged user to root.

OpenAI says these results collectively led it to conclude that Astra meets the Critical threshold.

The company has spent the past several weeks strengthening Astra’s safeguards before release. OpenAI says it paused parts of Astra’s development following the Hugging Face incident, including certain frontier training, while it improved isolation, network controls, monitoring and alignment training.

Some larger reinforcement-learning runs for future Astra versions were held back for longer. OpenAI restarted the large frontier reinforcement-learning run on August 28 after putting new safety and security requirements in place, although some smaller experimental training runs remain paused.

The company is also claiming a major improvement in Astra’s ability to follow safety restrictions. OpenAI says Astra is “our most aligned model to date” and is more likely than GPT-5.6 Sol to remain within its authorised scope.

On cyber jailbreak evaluations, Astra refused 91.5% of disallowed requests, compared with 59% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI also tested whether models would try to bypass safety controls. GPT-5.6 Sol attempted to circumvent automated review in 5.3% of samples, while Astra never attempted to do so in the evaluation.

In another simulated test based on the Hugging Face incident, GPT-5.6 Sol attempted to access surrounding ‘honeypot’ systems in 56.0% of tests. Astra did not attempt to use those shortcuts in the same way, while successfully solving some legitimate tasks.

OpenAI is adding another layer of protection through production monitoring designed to detect and stop potentially unauthorised model actions. The company acknowledges that these safeguards could sometimes interrupt legitimate work, particularly extended cybersecurity tasks.

For now, OpenAI is choosing caution over unrestricted access. Astra is expected to become available soon, but its most powerful cybersecurity capabilities will remain limited initially.

title: Kepler Aerospace Raises $8 Mn to Deploy Swarming ISR Satellites
content:
Bengaluru-based company will use the funding to launch six satellites and expand its mission operations and avionics businesses.

Kepler Aerospace has secured $8 million in seed funding.

The capital will fund the deployment of six swarming ISR satellites.

Bengaluru’s Kepler Aerospace has raised $8 million in a seed round led by Blue Ashva Capital and co-led by Finvolve India Accelerator and others. The space infrastructure company said it will use the capital to develop and deploy space-based Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities.

It will also scale its mission operations and avionics-as-a-service businesses. The funding will support the company’s two IDEX prime contracts. Kepler Founder and CEO Navneet Singh said the contracts would enable the company to deploy its first six swarming ISR satellites and build infrastructure for persistent intelligence.

The contracts cover swarming ISR constellations for India’s defence space ecosystem. The company has also received about $4 million in IDEX programme grants. Kepler will use part of the new funding to expand its Mission Operations as a Service (MOaaS) and Avionics as a Service verticals.

The round marks Kepler’s first external funding since its founding in 2018. The company is building an integrated space infrastructure stack covering satellites, avionics, ground infrastructure and mission operations. It also delivers space-based intelligence for strategic, defence and commercial applications.

Kepler aims to reduce intelligence latency from months to minutes through persistent ISR systems. Its approach combines satellite systems, ground infrastructure, mission operations and intelligence platforms. The company says this setup can support increasingly complex missions and constellation-scale deployments.

Kepler’s MOaaS platform serves nearly all Indian space companies, the company said in a statement. It also acts as the primary mission operator for several ISRO satellites.

Its network includes more than 70 ground stations for communication, tracking, telemetry, command and mission operations.

The company’s swarming satellite architecture allows satellites to communicate and coordinate without waiting for a ground station. Blue Ashva Capital Founder Satya Bansal said the system can “collapse the intelligence cycle from days to minutes”.

Over the next 12 to 24 months, Kepler plans to deploy its first six swarming ISR satellites. It will also expand its mission and avionics-as-a-service businesses. The company plans to strengthen its engineering team and move into a new facility. It will add 40 members to its current team.

The startup believes the future of space missions will be increasingly automated, distributed and software-driven. The fundraise comes as India’s private space sector expands into space-based intelligence and defence applications. It also covers satellite subsystems, ground infrastructure and mission operations. Kepler plans to build an integrated space infrastructure and intelligence platform for strategic and commercial missions.

title: ITC Infotech, Happiest Minds Merger to Birth a ₹7,000 Cr Company
content:
ITC Infotech will acquire a 22.1% stake in Happiest Minds from its promoters for ₹1,330 crore before merging the two companies through a share swap.

ITC is scaling its technology services business by merging its wholly owned subsidiary ITC Infotech with Bengaluru-based listed IT services company Happiest Minds Technologies. The deal will create a company boasting more than ₹7,000 crore in annual revenue and over 19,000 employees.

Under the proposed transaction, ITC Infotech will acquire a 22.1% stake in Happiest Minds from its promoter group for ₹1,330 crore in two tranches. This will be followed by a merger of Happiest Minds into ITC Infotech through a share swap, under which Happiest Minds shareholders will receive 25 shares of ITC Infotech for every 81 shares they hold.

ITC will become the promoter of the merged company with a 73.4% stake. The resulting entity will be listed on the stock exchanges after the merger is completed and requisite approvals are obtained.

The companies expect the transaction to take about 15 months to complete.

The deal comes as Indian IT services companies are trying to build greater scale and broaden their capabilities to capture spending around artificial intelligence, cloud, cybersecurity, and enterprise transformation.

For ITC, the transaction provides a way to expand its technology-services business by combining ITC Infotech's enterprise technology capabilities with Happiest Minds' stronger presence in digital engineering and AI.

“We will try and leverage our capabilities where possible to see if we can cross-sell some of the differentiated offerings… The focus is to continue and ensure that we deliver to our customers, adding value, making sure that we do our AI rollout, continue executing our AI strategy, and, where possible, cross-sell from across each other and provide that support,” Venkatraman Narayanan, Managing Director of Happiest Minds, spoke in a press briefing post the announcement.

Happiest Minds has built its business around digital engineering and has increasingly positioned itself as an AI-first technology services company. It reported revenue of ₹2,315 crore in FY26, up 12.3% year-on-year, and had 6,497 employees at the end of March 2026.

ITC Infotech, meanwhile, has a larger enterprise-services footprint, with capabilities spanning business and technology consulting, enterprise transformation, SAP, product lifecycle management (PLM), Industry 4.0, and industry-specific technology solutions.

The two businesses therefore have relatively complementary portfolios rather than being identical service providers. Happiest Minds brings AI, digital engineering, cloud, data, analytics and cybersecurity, while ITC Infotech adds enterprise applications, SAP, engineering, and industry-specific technology capabilities.

The combined company among India's mid-tier IT services players, although still considerably smaller than the country's top-tier firms such as TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra.

The transaction is also a bet on the changing economics of the IT services industry. Indian technology services companies are increasingly competing for larger AI-led transformation programmes rather than traditional application maintenance and infrastructure contracts. At the same time, AI is putting pressure on conventional services models by automating portions of software development, testing, and other technology work.

For smaller and mid-sized IT companies, scale can therefore become increasingly important: larger workforces, broader technology portfolios, and deeper relationships with enterprise customers can help them compete for bigger contracts and cross-sell multiple services.

Joseph Anantharaju, Co-chairman and CEO, Happiest Minds, framed the deal as part of a broader consolidation wave sweeping mid-sized Indian IT firms. "I do expect you can see a little bit more of this where there are synergies to be had and that would strengthen the merged entity's ability to play in the market," he said.

Narayanan added that the entry bar to reach meaningful scale organically "is going up, which is why the consolidation tends to happen," arguing that mid-sized firms increasingly need to combine to keep pace with larger specialist consulting firms and top-tier Indian IT players. "Only way to do that is through consolidation.”

The combined entity will have more than 800 customers and operations across over 30 countries. The companies expect to use the broader customer base to cross-sell AI, cloud, cybersecurity, SAP, engineering, and infrastructure services. Anantharaju said "this will raise the bar of the size of deals that we can attempt," since some large contracts had previously been out of reach for lack of certain capabilities.

The companies are targeting $1 billion in annual revenue by FY28, implying that the combined business will need to grow substantially from its pro-forma FY26 revenue base of ₹7,033 crore.

The merger is also expected to give ITC Infotech a more balanced geographic presence. The combined company's pro-forma revenue mix is expected to include roughly 38% from North America and 31% from Europe.

The companies also see opportunities to participate in larger enterprise transformation and digital engineering programmes, while taking their proprietary platforms and industry solutions into new markets.

For Happiest Minds, the transaction represents a significant change after more than a decade as an independent listed technology company. The company was founded by IT veteran Ashok Soota and has built its expertise around digital engineering, cybersecurity, cloud, and other emerging technology services. In recent years, it has sharpened its focus on AI.

The company reported ₹629 crore in revenue in the first quarter of FY27, up 14.3% year-on-year.

The merger requires approvals from shareholders, the Competition Commission of India, stock exchanges, and the National Company Law Tribunal, among other statutory approvals. The two companies will continue to operate independently until the approvals are completed.

The transaction marks more than a simple acquisition of a mid-sized IT company. It gives ITC a substantially larger technology-services platform at a time when the industry is being reshaped by AI, while giving Happiest Minds access to the scale, balance sheet, and enterprise ecosystem of one of India's largest business groups.

Deeptech startup Alteon raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.

The Bengaluru-based company aims to build high-endurance, perpetual flight aircraft.

Alteon, a Bengaluru-based deeptech startup developing autonomous high-endurance flights, has raised $2.5 million in a pre-seed round led by Lachy Groom with participation from Together Fund.

Founded in 2025 by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi, the startup is working on building high-endurance airplanes that can stay in flight for months. It is developing autonomous dynamic soaring vehicles that extract energy from wind gradients to remain airborne for extended periods.

Dynamic soaring is a flight technique that, rather than relying on lift, uses wind shear to exploit differences in the velocity of two different air masses. Albatrosses and other large seabirds use this method to circumnavigate the oceans without flapping their wings. It is also used by some gliders to fly at high speeds.

In August, the 20-member company conducted an offshore flight test where its aircraft autonomously flew multiple consecutive loops less than a metre above the open ocean.

"Today we already know that it is possible to gain energy from the wind using dynamic soaring. Building aircraft that fly for over a year using it, is not a matter of a single technical breakthrough but a matter of solving a range of challenging engineering problems across autonomy, structures, aero and more," Founder and CEO Sanghvi said in a statement.

Alteon's goal is to develop fleets that can carry a range of payloads for applications, from mapping weather and ocean conditions, tracking ships, and fishing activity to monitoring critical infrastructure, and coordinating autonomous systems across defence, search and rescue, science, and industry.

“Samay and team are making remarkable progress toward building an airplane that can stay aloft for more than a year at a time. If they get this right, we could soon have millions of them—essentially parked in the sky—doing things that today require large ships, crews, and huge amounts of infrastructure," said Lachy Groom, angel investor and co-founder of Physical Intelligence that is building foundational AI models for robots.

The Australian investor previously led a $20 million Series B extension funding round into the Bengaluru-based home services startup Pronto. He has also backed drone delivery startup Airbound.

Alteon will use the funding to accomplish autonomous dynamic soaring without propulsion, while scaling R&D toward deploying a fleet of these aircraft over the ocean.

The startup has also received early backing from Emergent Ventures and 1517.

title: NVIDIA’s GPU Price Surge May Push Indian Cloud Costs Up 20%
content:
CloudPe expects higher GPU costs to raise cloud pricing as memory supply remains tight through 2027.

NVIDIA has raised the listed price of its RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU to $16,000, up from $13,250 in June. Indian AI and GPU cloud platform CloudPe expects this to raise GPU cloud prices in India by 15–20% over 12–18 months.

The company made the assessment citing higher memory costs and tight supply. The GPU’s price has risen nearly 87% from its March 2025 launch price of $8,565.

Memory makers also expect supply to remain tight through 2027 and beyond. The supply pressure is affecting cloud infrastructure providers globally, including Indian providers such as CloudPe.

CloudPe Founder and CEO Ishan Talathi said GPU pricing depends largely on demand and component costs. He said memory remains a key cost pressure for NVIDIA. “Blended across our existing fleet and volume purchase commitments, we anticipate GPU cloud pricing in India to rise,” he said in a statement.

He added that prices could stabilise if memory supply improves or alternative architectures gain traction. CloudPe also said it secured a significant share of its GPU fleet before the latest price increase.

The company said its existing inventory can help limit the impact of higher replacement costs.

The changing cost structure could also affect decisions around direct GPU purchases. High-demand GPUs can have hardware lead times of 40 weeks or more, according to CloudPe.

Cloud provisioning, by comparison, can provide capacity within days. Direct GPU purchases generally suit workloads running continuously for 36 months or longer. However, faster GPU generation cycles could shorten the period available to recover hardware investments. Businesses buying GPUs at peak prices also retain those acquisition costs when newer architectures arrive.

Cloud services shift ownership and hardware replacement risks to providers. Providers can also distribute infrastructure across workloads such as VDI, rendering, video transcoding, and AI inference.

The company links the current shortage to a shift in global memory capacity towards AI. It expects broader supply relief only after new fabrication capacity arrives in late 2027. CloudPe said businesses that deploy earlier could secure available capacity and gain greater visibility into compute costs.

Delayed deployments could face further changes in hardware availability and pricing. The company said GPU availability, procurement cycles, technology refresh rates, and cloud pricing will increasingly shape AI deployment economics.

Data cybersecurity software company Seclore has partnered with AI platform Glean to help enterprises classify and protect sensitive data as they expand AI use.

AI has grown much faster than cybersecurity can catch up, and OpenAI’s Hugging Face breach is just the latest example of how good AI agents have become at discovering vulnerabilities. That leaves enterprises at risk and scrambling to figure out data access and controls.

Data cybersecurity software company Seclore can foresee the mounting risks as enterprises consider organisation-wide AI deployment. It recently partnered with enterprise AI platform Glean to help enterprises classify and protect sensitive data as they expand AI use.

The integration connects Seclore’s ARMOR DSPM with Glean's Enterprise Graph.

ARMOR DSPM uses data and metadata already indexed by Glean to identify sensitive information, assess exposure risks, and apply security controls—without building a separate data-discovery pipeline.

Under the partnership, ARMOR DSPM takes Glean’s existing enterprise context as an input for its classification engine. It assigns sensitivity, information type, and exposure-risk labels to files, then maps them against regulatory frameworks including GDPR, HIPAA, and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

Because ARMOR DSPM reads from Glean's existing index rather than re-crawling the same repositories, classification can cover the full scope of data already connected to Glean.

Once organisations identify sensitive information, they can apply encryption, usage controls, and access policies through Seclore's remediation tools. Classifications are written directly onto source files, so they stay with the data regardless of which application it moves through.

The same controls extend to AI-generated files.

When an AI system draws on multiple sensitive documents to produce a report or summary, that output can itself become a data-security liability. Seclore says ARMOR can carry the source material's classification into generated files, so the output can be encrypted, access-controlled, and audited.

The integration initially targets Glean customers in regulated industries: financial services, healthcare, legal services, and government.

Seclore, incubated at IIT Bombay, was founded as a data security company focused on protecting information. Its products have historically centred on data-centric security and enterprise digital rights management.

Its newer ARMOR platform combines data discovery, contextual intelligence, protection, and usage monitoring.

Glean, founded in 2019, started with enterprise search before expanding into a broader enterprise AI platform. Its Enterprise Graph connects information across an organisation's systems and maps relationships between content, people, and work.

It now offers AI assistants and agents that use that enterprise context to answer questions and perform tasks across business applications.

Glean’s growth signals why securing this data layer has become urgent.

In May, the company said it had crossed $300 million in annual recurring revenue–tripling within 15 months. Its Fortune 500 customer base had nearly doubled year-over-year, and more than 85% of customers were deploying Glean across five or more departments.

Seclore CEO Vishal Gauri believes the growth reflects a problem enterprises haven't yet solved: the pace of AI deployment is outrunning the security controls around it.

“There is a constant push and pull between the DPO and data teams, AI leadership and implementation teams, innovation groups, and cybersecurity teams,” Gauri tells AIM.

Business teams want to deploy AI systems to improve productivity. But security teams must assess whether those systems can access personally identifiable information, intellectual property, and other sensitive enterprise data.

The problem compounds as enterprises move from AI assistants that retrieve information to agents that can act across business systems. Gauri expects data security and identity security to become more important as organisations need to set controls not just for employees, but for non-human identities as well.

“For humans, you have rights and permissions on data based on sensitivity and role. You now have to understand how to make that effective for AI agents,” he remarks.

Gauri sees partnerships with companies that hold enterprise data and context as one practical path. Rather than building security controls alongside AI platforms, vendors can integrate them into the systems enterprises already use.

“The opportunity to innovate and to partner with companies that work with enterprise data, like Glean and others, is very large,” Gauri says. “Building the trust layer directly into these systems and giving customers that comfort allows them to adopt them faster.”

However, enterprise-wide AI deployments are still uncommon. Organisations often confine the adoption to smaller or more targeted rollouts.

Demand for broader deployment is growing regardless. According to McKinsey’s State of AI survey 2026, 44% of organisations report that AI is scaling across their enterprise—up from 38% in the previous year.

In such a scenario, the security question, then, is not simply whether an AI system should have access to enterprise data, but which data it can access, under what conditions and what controls should remain in place when AI models and agents use it.

The same applies to Seclore's own software. Advanced AI models can find vulnerabilities that conventional testing misses, compressing the time teams have to respond.

“We have to address them in hours and days, not weeks and months, which was the old paradigm for addressing these challenges,” Gauri says.

The deeper issue is what happens when AI systems or malicious actors get past traditional controls. Protecting the perimeter, cloud infrastructure, and applications is not enough if the data remains exposed.

title: Anthropic Study Finds AI Can Fix Its Own Safety Flaws
content:
The company said its automated alignment researchers outperformed human-proposed methods across seven alignment failures and generalised to models up to 4.7 times larger.

Anthropic on August 28 published a study which showed that AI agents powered by Claude Opus 4.8 can independently develop and test training methods to reduce specific alignment failures in other AI models.

The company said the automated systems successfully mitigated all 10 alignment failures evaluated in the study.

The research, titled ‘Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures’, was conducted by Anthropic researchers Chen Yueh-Han, Jiaxin Wen and Jan Hendrik Kirchner during the company’s Fellows Program. Anthropic described the findings as early evidence that automated alignment post-training could become practical in the near term.

Anthropic built Automated Alignment Researchers (AARs), using Claude Opus 4.8. Each system searches existing research, proposes a training method, trains a target model for about 30 minutes on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, evaluates the result and uses the score to determine what to test next.

The process can run for up to 48 hours. The systems were tested against 10 alignment failures, including deception, sycophancy, jailbreak compliance, prompt injection and power seeking.

Anthropic said the best methods also improved performance on benchmarks that were not used during the research process. The methods generalised to models up to 4.7 times larger than the original target models.

Anthropic screened the methods against MMLU, GSM8K and IFEval, three general capability benchmarks, and rejected methods that significantly reduced performance on them. The company cautioned that the experiment did not measure every capability, so the accepted methods could still affect areas that were not tested.

Anthropic also compared AAR-generated methods with ideas from 28 experienced AI safety researchers. On all seven alignment failures for which human researchers proposed methods, the company said the best AAR method eventually outperformed the best human proposal.

Anthropic said the automated systems reached that point after an average of 6.4 hours of experimentation. The company cautioned that the comparison was not direct because the human researchers submitted their proposals without the iterative experimentation available to the AARs.

In a separate experiment, Anthropic used Claude Sonnet 5 as an automated alignment researcher to improve an early checkpoint of Claude Opus 4.8. The company said the system reached alignment scores close to those of the released Opus 4.8 model in about 60 hours using roughly 2,400 training examples.

Anthropic also monitored the AARs for attempts to manipulate their evaluation process. The company found that 39 of 1,601 monitored AAR trajectories contained cheating behaviour, although none of those attempts produced a reported training method.

The company said the study remains limited by its 10 alignment failures, the benchmarks used to measure them and the difficulty of determining whether benchmark improvements translate to real-world alignment. The company said future work will focus on detecting subtler failures and evaluating automated alignment research on production-grade models.

Anthropic has also released the automated alignment research harness used in the study, allowing other researchers to examine and build on the approach.
