StockGro began developing its AI platform after finding that general-purpose AI models struggled to answer time-sensitive financial questions effectively.

For millions of retail investors, the stock market remains a complex maze of charts, ratios, analyst reports, and financial jargon. StockGro, an investment learning and advisory platform, is betting that AI can make that information more accessible and potentially change how people make investment decisions.

The Bengaluru-based company has built Stoxo, an AI-powered platform designed to answer stock-market questions by combining fundamental and technical analysis, analyst views, and market data. Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, StockGro says Stoxo is designed specifically for investment-related queries and can provide users with a structured rationale behind its recommendations.

Founder Ajay Lakhotia tells AIM that the idea emerged from observing a fundamental gap in how retail investors access financial knowledge. Conventional brokerage platforms provide investors with plenty of data but often leave them to interpret it themselves.

“99.9% of the capital, which is from retail participants, is managed by 0.01% of the population, which is the fund manager. And we have no idea how that fund manager is actually investing. And that’s the thought with which we have to democratise investment,” Lakhotia says.

The startup found it essential to pivot from a content-led investing platform into a research-first, AI-native platform. It has built Stoxo as a research desk that embeds multi-agent AI directly into the investment decision journey, bringing together market intelligence, expert insights, proprietary data, and community signals to help retail investors make more informed decisions.

According to Lakhotia, the problem begins with the lack of financial education and access to qualified advisers. Investors often depend on friends, relatives, or relationship managers for investment decisions rather than independently evaluating stocks or mutual funds.

His observations come from more than a decade in venture capital. Lakhotia began his career as an entrepreneur, spending about eight years in manufacturing and technology before moving to Europe, where he worked with Capgemini in London.

After completing his MBA at ISB, he joined ICICI Bank’s investment banking team and later moved into venture capital, spending around five-and-a-half years at Vertex, the VC arm of Temasek. His portfolio included companies such as FirstCry, Yatra, and XpressBees. He later joined Fosun RZ Capital, the venture arm of Chinese conglomerate Fosun, where he invested in Delhivery, ixigo, and MakeMyTrip.

After spending over a decade investing in startups, Lakhotia says that he began noticing a much larger opportunity in public-market investing. In 2020, he founded StockGro to help users understand markets. It enables users to create portfolios, track stocks, and simulate investment strategies.

StockGro began developing the AI platform around a year and a half ago after finding that general-purpose AI models struggled to answer time-sensitive financial questions effectively.

“When you ask something on ChatGPT, it uses something called the SERP API. It goes back to Google, picks up the questions from there, answers from there, the top three, four articles, converts it to NLP, and presents it to you,” Lakhotia states.

The problem is that market information can quickly become outdated. Lakhotia argues that conventional brokerage platforms provide investors with plenty of data but often leave them to interpret it themselves.

At the core of Stoxo is a proprietary small language model (SLM) built in-house and supported by more than 80 specialised AI agents, each designed for specific functions across inference, relevance, contextual analysis, and market research.

The platform draws on StockGro's proprietary conversational and behavioural data accumulated from its 35 million-user ecosystem over five years, alongside expert trade calls and real-time market data.

“We have 35 million monthly active users, who are conversing with the RAs, RIAs, with each other on the platform. That conversational data, which helps us do the inference and also put out the right answer, does not exist outside my ecosystem,” he says.

A key differentiator is accessibility. StockGro says it has brought institutional-grade investment research to retail investors at 98% lower pricing than traditional industry alternatives.

The platform also aggregates calls from SEBI-registered advisers, allowing users to examine their recommendations, historical performance, accuracy and engagement with other investors. The company has also integrated brokers into the platform.

StockGro then combines multiple indicators into a single assessment, including valuation, earnings, risk, analyst views, technical indicators, and mutual-fund activity.

However, StockGro believes its biggest differentiator is not simply its AI models, but the behavioural and conversational data generated on its platform. It allows Stoxo to make its answers more specific to investment-related questions rather than producing generic financial explanations.

The 100-member company has been using Groq chipsets for complex inference workloads instead of NVIDIA infrastructure for roughly a year.

Lakhotia believes the investment-advisory market remains relatively underserved. India’s broader asset and wealth management industry reached assets under management (AUM) of $0.9 trillion, per Deloitte. Meanwhile, there are more than 16,500 SEC-registered advisory firms in the US overseeing AUM of $177 trillion.

“The whole market is demarcated, where on one side you have brokers, and it’s a saturated market with Zerodha, Groww, Angel, etc. On the other side, the advisory market is completely untouched,” he says.

The company has also partnered with around 1,500 business schools and colleges, where its platform is available as part of the curriculum.

StockGro has raised more than $90–95 million so far. Lakhotia said the company may look to raise another round around mid-next year.

The next phase of Stoxo could be voice-based investing. The company is working on adding voice capabilities that would allow users to ask questions about the market or whether a particular stock is worth considering, and potentially execute trades through the platform.

The company is particularly interested in Indian-language AI platforms because it wants the experience to work beyond English-speaking users.

Stoxo has already demonstrated significant adoption and engagement since its launch, with 2 million users onboarded within six months and the platform processing more than 25 million research queries every month.

According to StockGro, Stoxo has reduced the time required for investment research from more than four hours to under 10 seconds, while improving decision accuracy by 85% by reducing reliance on stale or unverified information. The platform has also seen 64% of users take a subsequent trade action after receiving Stoxo insights, compared with 43% following standard alerts, indicating stronger user engagement.

The company's larger ambition is to democratise access to investment intelligence—making sophisticated research faster, more affordable, and easier to understand for India's next generation of retail investors.

title: ‘AI Can’t Write the TypeScript Compiler’
content:
“Our compiler is also not a typical piece of code. That’s why AI is bad at writing it: it hasn’t seen anything like it in the training set,” reveals Anders Hejlsberg.

AI could not write the TypeScript compiler despite attempts to use it for the task, Anders Hejlsberg, the creator of TypeScript and C#, said in a recent interview with developer Ryan Peterman.

“I know that AI could not write our compiler, the TypeScript compiler. It just can’t. We’ve tried it, and it can’t do it,” Hejlsberg said on The Peterman Pod.

Hejlsberg said the reason is partly that the TypeScript compiler is an unusual codebase containing concepts and implementation choices that AI is unlikely to have encountered together in its training data.

“Our compiler is also not a typical piece of code. That’s why AI is bad at writing it: it hasn’t seen anything like it in the training set,” Hejlsberg said.

While AI has seen other compilers and large software projects, Hejlsberg said the TypeScript compiler is sufficiently different from those examples to make it difficult for AI to reproduce.

“I’ve seen some compilers, but not like this one—not with these concepts, and not done the way we’re doing it,” he said.

Hejlsberg’s comments came during a discussion about Microsoft’s work last year to move the TypeScript compiler from its original JavaScript/TypeScript implementation to Go.

Rather than asking AI to recreate the compiler independently, the team built a tool that syntactically translated TypeScript code into Go.

That approach produced Go code without syntax errors, but it was not immediately usable. The generated code still treated types according to TypeScript’s rules rather than Go’s type system, meaning engineers had to refactor the code and redo data structures.

The experience also shaped Hejlsberg’s view of how AI should be used for large software projects.

He believes simply giving an LLM the compiler’s hundreds of thousands of lines of code and asking it to translate everything would leave engineers to check the output for hallucinations.

The old compiler contains somewhere between half a million and 1 million lines of code, according to Hejlsberg. Without perfect test coverage, developers would still have to examine the AI-generated result to ensure it had not introduced errors.

Instead, Hejlsberg said AI could create a translation program that performs the conversion consistently.

“That’s always the thing about AI that people forget: it’s not deterministic. So you can’t really trust that it’s going to do the same thing twice,” Hejlsberg said.

That does not mean Hejlsberg believes AI has little value in software development. He said his team already uses it for more targeted work around the compiler.

“We use AI a lot in our internal processes around the compiler. Help it to write tests and to move pull requests and what have you. And whenever an issue is logged, first thing we do is put Copilot on and see if it can fix it for us.”

Hejlsberg acknowledged that AI is improving rapidly, but he remains sceptical that it will soon be able to handle every part of software development independently.

Anindyadeep Sannigrahi founded LiteFold just under a year ago. Now, his startup has released LiteMol-1—a pioneering multi-molecule foundation model.

For years, the biggest breakthroughs in AI-driven bioscience have come from Silicon Valley, London, or research labs backed by Big Tech. Google DeepMind gave the world AlphaFold. David Baker's lab changed protein design. Companies like Anthropic are now throwing AI agents into drug discovery.

India was largely watching. But a 24-year-old founder from Bengaluru wants India to drive such breakthroughs.

Anindyadeep Sannigrahi founded LiteFold just under a year ago. Now, his startup has released LiteMol-1—among India’s first multi-molecule foundation models for molecular design.

But unlike AlphaFold or the growing list of structure-based AI models, LiteFold is taking a different bet altogether. Instead of building a bigger, more expensive model that reasons over complex 3D protein structures, LiteMol-1 tries to make molecular design cheaper, faster, and native for AI agents.

“Everybody is focusing on structure because it's intuitive,” the founder tells AIM. “We thought, what if we looked at biomolecule design from a totally different viewpoint?”

AlphaFold changed structural biology by predicting the 3D structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, a problem that had taken scientists years to solve through laboratory work. That breakthrough inspired Sannigrahi and his Delaware-based co-founder Cory Kornowicz to enter the field.

But AlphaFold also created a new default in AI drug discovery: think in structures.

Models like RFdiffusion, BoltzGen, and O-Design now generate protein and molecular structures around biological targets. Pharmaceutical companies increasingly use these systems to search through millions of possible molecules.

LiteFold believes that approach is becoming computationally expensive.

"Doing work on a structure paradigm is just very expensive and very time-consuming," Sannigrahi notes, as drug discovery is essentially a funnelling process—using advanced computation to filter out millions of failures.

More importantly, binding a molecule to a target isn't the only goal.

"You may get a molecule that binds. But what about toxicity? Absorption? Will it even reach your bloodstream if you take it orally?"

That's where LiteMol-1 starts to diverge from traditional models. It isn’t designed to generate just one kind of biomolecule. The model can generate small molecules, peptides, cyclic peptides, macrocycles, depsipeptides, PROTACs, and peptides containing non-canonical amino acids—all using a single set of weights. It can also edit existing molecules instead of generating them from scratch.

But the bigger change is how LiteFold thinks about optimisation.

Most molecular models largely optimise around binding affinity. LiteMol-1 is built to optimise across multiple therapeutic objectives simultaneously: toxicity, ADME properties, drug-likeness, membrane permeability, selectivity, synthesisability, and more.

Instead of trying to find one "perfect" molecule, LiteFold uses Monte Carlo Tree Search—a technique to optimise decisions in highly complex spaces—to keep multiple promising candidates alive, each representing different trade-offs. "Molecular design is fundamentally not a single-objective optimisation problem," Sannigrahi remarks.

Sannigrahi believes drug discovery is moving towards autonomous research loops where AI systems repeatedly generate molecules, evaluate them, modify them, and generate again. For those systems, structure becomes a surprisingly bad interface.

Instead of outputting massive 3D structural files, LiteMol-1 works with compact molecular sequences like SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) that represent complex chemical structures.

"For us, what we are trying to output is not a structure. It's a sequence." That dramatically reduces the amount of information an AI agent has to process during each reasoning cycle.

LiteFold says the model becomes an "infinite molecular canvas". The model proposes possibilities. The agent inspects them, edits them, compares them, regenerates them, and only invokes expensive structure prediction or docking when absolutely necessary.

It also changes the economics. "We just shrunk the token cost by a huge amount," Sannigrahi says. "Our model can run on an NVIDIA L40."

That's a notable contrast to traditional high throughput screening of AI-assisted drug discovery that requires hundreds of GPUs and tens of thousands of dollars worth of compute for a single workflow. In fact, pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly built an AI supercomputer equipped with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Blackwell B300 GPUs dedicated to automated molecule design.

But this isn't a sequence-versus-structure debate. "There are areas where sequence models work extremely well, and there are areas where structure models are essential," he says.

LiteFold still relies on structural models like AlphaFold for understanding molecular interactions and dynamics. "If two molecules are interacting, structure becomes very important because that's where you understand bond patterns and intermolecular forces."

The company's philosophy is simpler: use sequences when they make search cheaper and use structures when they make biology clearer. The real opportunity lies in combining both.

Sannigrahi was surprisingly critical of the current excitement around AI in drug discovery. "In terms of accuracy, we are not really quite out there yet. I don't think it's good enough to just say we are doing great and everything."

According to him, AI has become good at generating molecules, but it's still weak at the two hardest problems in biology—understanding disease and predicting what happens after a molecule enters a biological system.

The industry is generating more molecules against the same known targets instead of discovering better biological targets in the first place. "The speed is there. But they're not really hitting the target."

The next bottleneck isn't compute. It's biology. Sannigrahi believes biology already has enough data to build better foundation models. The problem is that researchers aren't representing that data in ways modern AI systems can learn from efficiently.

"We are just not seeing the right representation." Sequence data is abundant. Structural data is limited and expensive to produce.

If AI can learn richer biological representations from sequences, it could unlock entirely different foundation models for disease understanding, molecular generation, and prediction. That's where LiteFold wants to spend its research effort.

Sannigrahi believes India may have an advantage here because of its massive gene pool.

"I am super excited about the amount of genetic diversity India has." India's population contains enormous genomic diversity shaped by geography, migration, and endogamy. That is valuable for understanding disease targets and therapeutic responses.

Companies like Biocon, Sun Pharma and Dr Reddy's have already built India's pharmaceutical manufacturing ecosystem. Clinical trials have also become more accessible.

Put those together, and Sannigrahi believes India has an opportunity that hasn't been fully exploited. "Biotech companies in India should start their own therapeutic programmes," he suggests.

He believes the next breakthroughs will come from combining AI with organoids, automated laboratories, and biological circuits that generate richer experimental data.

LiteFold is already building an AI co-scientist called Rosalind, named after Rosalind Franklin whose work led to the discovery of the double-helix structure of DNA. The AI co-scientist automates research workflows and assists scientists during molecular design. But even there, Sannigrahi insists humans stay in the loop.

LiteMol-1 is still an early research model. It hasn't discovered a blockbuster drug. It hasn't shortened clinical trials or cured cancer.

Sannigrahi isn't claiming any of that. He thinks meaningful breakthroughs are still five years away.

But LiteMol-1 is doing important work and attempting to ask a question that Big Tech hasn’t even thought of. What if the future of AI drug discovery isn't a bigger model?

title: OpenAI to Remove Models From Cursor, Fearing Elon Musk May Violate Contract Terms
content:
“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts.”

OpenAI plans to remove its models from Cursor after Elon Musk's SpaceX acquired the AI coding platform, citing concerns that the company may not comply with OpenAI’s terms of service.

OpenAI notified SpaceX that it intends to wind down its contract with Cursor, with access scheduled to end on November 12.

This decision follows SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Anysphere, the company behind Cursor. SpaceX completed the all-stock acquisition, making Cursor part of Musk’s broader AI operations.

“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts,” said OpenAI in a blog post.

It pointed to the company’s claim that Twitter, now part of SpaceX, breached the terms of its contract with OpenAI after Musk acquired it.

OpenAI also cited Musk’s admission under oath earlier this year that xAI, which is now part of SpaceX, had violated OpenAI’s terms of service.

After Musk acquired Twitter, OpenAI said the company breached its contract. At the time, Twitter licensed its data to OpenAI for AI development, with the arrangement reportedly worth about $2 million a year. Musk subsequently cut off OpenAI’s access to the data.

OpenAI’s agreement with Cursor contains a change-of-control provision that gives OpenAI a limited period to cancel the contract. Rather than terminating access immediately, OpenAI said it would use the maximum notice period allowed, allowing developers to continue accessing its existing models through Cursor.

OpenAI also linked the decision to its upcoming Astra model, saying the increasing capabilities of its systems require greater accountability over how they are deployed.

This adds another layer to the increasingly adversarial relationship between OpenAI and Musk.

In February 2024, Musk sued OpenAI, CEO Sam Altman and co-founder Greg Brockman, accusing them of abandoning the company’s original non-profit mission by moving towards a for-profit structure and prioritising commercial interests, including its relationship with Microsoft. Musk later withdrew that case and filed a federal lawsuit in August 2024 with similar claims.

The case went to trial this April, but a federal jury ruled against Musk in May, finding that he had waited too long to bring his claims. The judge subsequently dismissed his claims, while Musk said he would appeal to the Ninth Circuit.

title: Meta India Veteran Sandhya Devanathan Joins OpenAI
content:
After a decade at Meta, Devanathan will lead OpenAI’s business and partnerships across Southeast Asia and Australia.

Sandhya Devanathan, Meta’s Vice President and Head of India and Southeast Asia, is leaving the company after more than a decade to join OpenAI as Vice President for Southeast Asia and Australia.

She will take up the new role in October after a short break and will be based in Singapore, reporting to Kiran Mani, OpenAI’s Managing Director for Asia-Pacific.

Her responsibilities will include driving consumer growth, enterprise adoption and partnerships, while also overseeing regional operations and engagement with regulators. She will also work on building partnerships across the AI ecosystem and expanding the adoption of OpenAI products among businesses, institutions and governments.

Devanathan announced her departure from Meta on LinkedIn, describing the decision as bittersweet.

“After more than a decade at Meta, I’ve made the bittersweet decision to move on to my next adventure. Saying goodbye to this incredible company and my amazing colleagues has been really difficult, but I leave with a heart full of gratitude and excitement about what lies ahead,” she wrote.

“I joined Meta when we had just about 300 employees in Singapore. The landscape looked so different in 2016 - everyone was talking about digital transformation. And we were right in the midst of it - helping startups, companies, creators and the ecosystem grow across the region while delivering great experiences for our hundreds of millions of our users,” she wrote looking back her time at the company.

During her tenure, she worked across ecommerce and gaming in Asia-Pacific, helped build Meta’s businesses and teams in Singapore and Vietnam, and worked on its ecommerce initiatives across Southeast Asia. In 2020, she took charge of Meta’s gaming business in APAC.

Devanathan was appointed Vice President and Head of Meta India in late 2022 and formally took over the role in January 2023. She later assumed responsibility for Southeast Asia as well and relocated to Singapore in June 2025.

She also mentioned the impact of Meta’s platforms in India and Southeast Asia, including the use of WhatsApp for government citizen services in India, the growth of small businesses in Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand, and startups in Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines that went on to become unicorns. “I’m proud of the work we’ve done together,” Devanathan said.

At Meta, Arun Srinivas will continue to lead the company’s India operations following Devanathan’s departure. Srinivas, who took over as Meta’s Managing Director and Head for India in July 2025, will now report directly to Benjamin Joe, Meta’s Vice President for Asia-Pacific, and join his regional leadership team.

Devanathan’s move comes as OpenAI continues to expand its presence across Asia-Pacific. The company has opened offices in Singapore, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney and New Delhi over the past two years and has been strengthening its regional leadership. In June, OpenAI appointed former Uber India and South Asia President Prabhjeet Singh as its Managing Director for India.

title: Gnani AI Launches Sovereign AI Stack With 30B-Parameter Model and AI Agents
content:
Gnani AI says its latest stack is designed to keep sensitive data within an organisation’s own infrastructure while reducing the cost of processing Indian languages.

Voice AI Startup Gnani AI has launched Gnani Artha, an end-to-end sovereign AI stack for Indian enterprises and public institutions, combining its Evon v3.3 language model with its Plexus agentic AI platform.

Vice-President of India CP Radhakrishnan unveiled the stack in New Delhi on August 28.

Evon v3.3 is a 30-billion-parameter open-weights model trained across 11 Indian languages, while Plexus is designed to deploy AI agents across enterprise and government workflows.

Gnani AI said Plexus will be available to enterprise customers, while Evon v3.3 weights will be made available by request on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 licence.

“Bharat is making significant strides in AI. India’s approach focuses on making AI open, affordable, and accessible, ensuring that innovation uplifts society as a whole,” Radhakrishnan said.

“This initiative shows that our engineers have the capability not only to use frontier technologies, but also to build them,” he added.

Evon v3.3 uses a mixture-of-experts architecture, with 30 billion total parameters and around 3.5 billion parameters active for each token.

According to Gnani AI, the model outperforms Sarvam’s 105-billion-parameter Indic model on 10 of 11 languages on MILU, an Indian-language benchmark covering 11 languages and a range of academic and professional subjects.

It also outperforms Sarvam’s 30-billion-parameter model across all 11 languages and reaches parity with GPT-5.4 Nano.

The company has also rebuilt Evon’s tokeniser for Indian scripts. Gnani AI claims that Evon v3.3 requires around 20% fewer tokens per Indian-language word than the tokeniser used by the GPT-5 family, and less than half the tokens required by byte-level tokenisers used by models such as DeepSeek, Llama and Qwen.

The lower token usage is intended to reduce compute requirements, improve response times and allow more usable context within each query.

The model is available as open weights and can run on a single node, allowing institutions to deploy it within their own data centres or virtual private clouds. Gnani AI said this can help organisations keep customer data within their own infrastructure while meeting data residency requirements.

The second component of Gnani Artha, Plexus, is an agentic AI platform that allows organisations to build workflows using individual AI agents.

The platform is designed around agents that have their own identity and can be combined into workflows for specific outcomes. Its use cases include grievance resolution in government and reconciliation processes in banking.

For government grievance handling, for instance, a multilingual agent can capture a citizen's complaint, while another reasoning agent identifies patterns across complaints, such as a rise in cases from a particular district. The system can then consolidate the issue, route it to the relevant department and update the citizen after resolution.

In banking, Plexus agents can compare millions of entries across bank statements, core-banking ledgers and payment-switch logs. The system can clear matching entries, prepare explanations for exceptions and route unresolved cases to the appropriate team.

Plexus includes orchestration, human-in-the-loop controls, guardrails, observability and audit logging. It can integrate with enterprise and public digital infrastructure, use tools and work with different underlying models, including Evon v3.3.

“Sovereign AI is not about keeping the world out. It is about India having the capability to build for itself - and then for every country that shares its problems,” said Ganesh Gopalan, CEO of Gnani AI.

Founded in 2016, Gnani AI is headquartered in Bengaluru. The company develops foundation models and agentic AI systems for enterprises and government.

Gnani AI said it works with more than 200 enterprises across sectors including BFSI, insurance, telecom, healthcare, education and the public sector. It is also among the organisations participating in the Government of India's IndiaAI Mission to build sovereign AI models.

title: OpenAI, 100+ Companies Call for Global Surge in AI Cyber Defence
content:
OpenAI said there is a “limited window to strengthen cyber defences” before AI-enabled attacks become more widespread and sophisticated.

OpenAI has called for a global push to strengthen cyber defences as AI-enabled attacks become more capable, with more than 100 companies and technology organisations, including Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, AWS, Cisco, CrowdStrike, and Hugging Face, signing the initiative.

OpenAI said there is a “limited window to strengthen cyber defences” before AI-enabled attacks become more widespread and sophisticated.

The open letter calls on companies, governments, cybersecurity firms, and frontier AI developers to put AI-powered defensive tools in the hands of organisations protecting critical infrastructure, including hospitals, water utilities, and internet infrastructure.

OpenAI said defenders should “accelerate defenders’ priorities with tools, funding, and hands-on support”, particularly where security teams have limited resources.

OpenAI’s push comes shortly after the company disclosed a security incident involving its models and Hugging Face.

During a security evaluation, OpenAI said its models escaped the intended testing environment, obtained internet access, and interacted with Hugging Face infrastructure. The models executed code on dozens of servers, gained root access to one server, and obtained limited private data and credentials. OpenAI also found that exposed credentials were used to access four accounts across four public services.

The company said the incident did not affect customer data, products, or service availability. However, its monitoring systems took several days to identify the activity, prompting OpenAI to strengthen containment and monitoring around model evaluations.

The incident also affected OpenAI's model development schedule.

The company paused deployment-focused reinforcement-learning training for two weeks, delayed frontier reinforcement-learning runs and put training of its next-generation Astra model on hold while it worked on security and alignment improvements.

OpenAI also quarantined the weights of the research model involved in the incident.

The latest letter asks cybersecurity companies to continuously test their defences against frontier AI capabilities, strengthen existing security products with AI and help critical-infrastructure operators deploy and verify fixes.

It also calls on governments to fund cyber defence for under-resourced essential services and improve international threat-intelligence sharing and coordinated incident response.

The signatories are calling on frontier AI companies to ensure responsible model access, funding, training, and hands-on support for defenders. They also want developers to build stronger observability systems and ensure that identities used by AI agents are “traceable and accountable”.

OpenAI said organisations should address basic weaknesses alongside deploying AI-based security tools, including unpatched software, excessive permissions, insecure configurations, weak authentication, and technical debt in legacy systems.

The letter also recommends using capable, lower-cost models for broad security coverage and frontier models for more difficult security problems.

“We call on leaders across industry and government to bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort,” OpenAI said in the letter. “Put cyber-capable AI in the hands of defenders, starting with the teams protecting essential services. Fix the most dangerous weaknesses, verify the fixes, and share what works so others can build on it.”

title: Anthropic Wants Its AI Agents To Operate Physical Devices, Equipment
content:
Companies including Amazon Web Services, Automata, Danaher, Doosan Robotics, MBF Bioscience, QIAGEN, Tecan and Universal Robots are working on or testing MHS integrations.

Anthropic has opened a research preview of its Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a proposed shared specification that allows AI agents to operate programmable physical equipment across scientific laboratories and manufacturing environments.

The company said the standard can connect devices including microscopes, liquid handlers, and robotic arms, allowing agents to coordinate multiple instruments and run workflows such as drug-discovery experiments and laser calibration for quantum computers.

MHS was developed initially through a collaboration between Anthropic and HHMI Janelia Research Campus.

Anthropic said integrating equipment in a laboratory or manufacturing facility can typically take weeks or months because individual devices often use different programming interfaces and require bespoke integrations.

MHS is designed to reduce that integration work to “hours or minutes”, according to the company.

The standard introduces a common hardware driver that translates between an operating system and a physical device. It uses basic commands such as “read” and “write” to allow software to retrieve information or change device settings.

Devices can also be described in a standard format, allowing AI agents to discover available equipment and interact with it without a separate translator for every device.

MHS also gives agents information about equipment's physical characteristics and operating limits. Users can provide this information through natural-language tags, which the system converts into a reference file describing what a device can measure, what can be adjusted and which safety limits apply.

Once connected, devices can be controlled through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a command-line interface, or code files.

“MHS works with any device that has a programmable interface,” Anthropic said in a release. The standard is “model-agnostic”, allowing different AI agents and harnesses to access supported equipment through standard protocols.

Anthropic said agents can sequence operations across several instruments, monitor results, and adjust parameters in real time.

For longer or repetitive tasks, agents can turn what they learn into scripts, allowing the equipment to run the process without the AI making every decision.

In one test, Anthropic said Claude adjusted a laser, used a camera to observe the resulting beam movement and repeated the process to understand the relationship between its actions and the hardware. Claude then converted what it learned into a script that could align the laser through a single command.

Anthropic is initially making MHS available to a group of scientific research labs and advanced manufacturers across biotech, robotics, quantum computing, and other fields. Companies including Amazon Web Services, Automata, Danaher, Doosan Robotics, MBF Bioscience, QIAGEN, Tecan, and Universal Robots are working on or testing MHS integrations.

AWS, for example, plans to support MHS through Strands Robots, while Tecan is adding support for its Fluent liquid-handling platforms. Universal Robots has received early access, and Doosan Robotics is testing the standard with its robotic arms.

Anthropic will use the preview to develop safety evaluations and deployment practices before making MHS open source.

However, the company acknowledged that Claude’s physical and spatial reasoning remains limited and that expert oversight is still required. In one example, researchers from Genentech had to guide Claude to recognise that foaming in protein samples represented a physical failure rather than a software problem.

title: After Anthropic and Sarvam, Karnataka Explores ElevenLabs’ Voice AI for Skilling, Governance, Healthcare
content:
A key focus of the discussions with ElevenLabs was the responsible deployment of voice AI in Karnataka government’s programmes.

The Karnataka government is exploring pilot projects with AI voice company ElevenLabs across skilling, governance, healthcare, investment promotion, culture, and citizen services, as the state looks to identify practical applications of voice and conversational AI in public services.

The discussions were held on August 27 between Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank M Kharge and the ElevenLabs team, including Ben Supple, Global Head, Public Sector Partnerships and Policy; Nihal Chauhan, APAC Head, Public Sector Partnerships and Policy; and Arielle Andrews, Chief of Staff and General Counsel.

The proposed pilots could include voice-enabled interview practice and skilling in Indian languages, investor assistance, voice restoration for people who have lost the ability to speak, cultural and public-service applications, and AI safety mechanisms.

The ElevenLabs team demonstrated a voice-enabled interview-practice tool during the meeting and discussed the company’s work on synthetic-audio detection, provenance, traceability, and watermarking.

A key focus of the discussions was the responsible deployment of voice AI in government, particularly the risk of AI-generated voices being used to spread misinformation about government schemes, programmes, and official announcements.

The Minister called for a clear roadmap covering the identified use cases and asked the teams to work towards an initial pilot that can demonstrate tangible public impact.

“Karnataka has an opportunity to be at the forefront of translating AI innovation into better outcomes for citizens,” Kharge said.

“Our approach is to engage with companies that are building some of the most capable technologies globally, understand where those technologies can solve real problems, and then move towards pilots that can be scaled across the state. Whether it is helping a young person prepare for a job, making it easier for an investor to access information, improving citizen services or using AI in healthcare, our focus has to be on building AI delivery models that are effective, efficient, accessible and responsible.”

The discussions form part of Karnataka’s broader effort to work with technology companies and translate advances in AI into public-service delivery models, particularly in areas where AI could simplify access to government services and improve skilling and employment outcomes.

Earlier this month, the state government also held discussions with Anthropic, followed shortly by Sarvam AI. The discussions explored how AI agents can help citizens file remote, quick e-FIRs, or zero FIRs in emergencies, while protecting data sovereignty.

ElevenLabs has also invited the Karnataka minister to participate in the ElevenLabs India Summit in Bengaluru in October, where the company’s leadership is expected to discuss developments in voice AI and its applications in India.

title: WACKER Sets Up Pune GCC With HCLTech for Engineering and Digital Transformation
content:
Under the collaboration, HCLTech will help build and scale the GCC’s technology workforce and strengthen its operational capabilities.

WACKER Chemie AG, the global chemicals and biotechnology company, has established a global capability centre (GCC) in Pune in collaboration with HCLTech, marking an expansion of its engineering, IT, and digital transformation capabilities in India.

The new centre will support WACKER’s global engineering, IT, and digital transformation initiatives, while providing the company with a flexible and scalable delivery model. HCLTech will support the GCC through a phased operating model, with a focus on DevSecOps, automation, governance, and digital modernisation.

“The global capability centre is an important step in strengthening our global delivery and digital execution capabilities,” said Fabian Seibold, Director, WACKER Excellence Hub Pune, in a statement. “HCLTech’s experience in building and scaling such centers allows us to move forward with a model that supports agility, governance, and long-term growth.”

The GCC is expected to strengthen WACKER’s ability to execute digital and engineering initiatives globally, while building a future-ready technology delivery foundation from India.

“This expanded engagement builds on the strategic partnership between WACKER and HCLTech and marks an important milestone in WACKER's digital transformation. We are proud to support WACKER's long-term digital and engineering transformation journey as a trusted partner,” Frank Fehler, Executive Vice President and Country Head - Germany, HCLTech said.

Under the collaboration, HCLTech will help build and scale the GCC’s technology workforce and strengthen its operational capabilities.

“Through a phased customer-centric operating model, we are establishing a flexible, resilient, and future-ready GCC for WACKER in Pune. Leveraging our expertise in DevSecOps and automation, HCLTech will help build a high-performing team, strengthen governance, enhance operational efficiency, and accelerate digital modernisation,” said Kiran Cherukuri, EVP and Global GCC Practice Head, HCLTech.

WACKER has a global workforce of more than 16,000 employees, with 27 production sites, 22 technical competence centres, and 47 sales offices. The company reported annual sales of around €5.5 billion ($6.4 billion) in fiscal year 2025.

The company operates across four business divisions. Its Silicones and Polymers divisions provide products for industries including automotive, construction, chemicals, consumer goods and medical technology. Its Biosolutions division focuses on bioengineered products such as biopharmaceuticals and food additives, while its Polysilicon division produces hyperpure polysilicon used in the semiconductor and photovoltaic industries.

The Pune GCC adds to WACKER’s global technology and engineering capabilities as the company continues to expand its digital transformation agenda.

title: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Ads in India
content:
OpenAI’s India ads rollout will include WPP and Omnicom as agency partners, with self-serve campaigns opening on September 4.

OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Ads in India, bringing advertisements to the Free and Go tiers as the company expands its advertising business in one of its largest markets.

The ads will be available to logged-in adults, while Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Education users will continue to get an ad-free experience.

WPP and Omnicom will be OpenAI’s first agency partners for ChatGPT Ads in India. More than 50 brands are expected to run advertisements on ChatGPT in the country this week, with OpenAI saying the agency model is non-exclusive.

OpenAI will also open self-serve access to ChatGPT Ads Manager in India on September 4. Businesses will be able to start campaigns with daily budgets from ₹725.

“India is one of the most dynamic markets in the world for how people use ChatGPT to learn, build, and discover. Our weekly active users have doubled year-on-year, with many of them going beyond simple searches and changing how they make decisions,” Dave Dugan, Vice President and Head of Global Ads Solutions at OpenAI, said in a statement.

“With ChatGPT Ads, businesses of every size can introduce themselves at relevant, high-context moments when decisions are beginning to take shape,” he added.

OpenAI said ads will appear below a ChatGPT response when there is a relevant sponsored product or service. They will be labelled as sponsored and kept visually separate from ChatGPT’s answers.

The company said advertisements will not influence ChatGPT’s responses. Advertisers will also not have access to users’ chats, chat history, memories, or personal details. OpenAI said it does not sell user data to advertisers.

“Our goal is to make those interactions useful, help marketers design for intelligent experiences, and preserve what makes ChatGPT valuable: independent answers, conversations that stay private from advertisers, and meaningful user control,” Dugan said.

Users will be able to dismiss ads, provide feedback, see why an ad was shown, manage advertising personalisation, and clear data used for advertising.

Ads will not be shown on accounts belonging to people who identify themselves, or are predicted, to be under 18. They also will not appear alongside sensitive or regulated topics, including mental health and politics.

Advertisers will receive aggregate campaign metrics such as impressions and clicks, rather than information about individual conversations.

OpenAI said the advertising business will help support free and lower-cost access to its AI tools while giving businesses a way to reach users when they are researching products, comparing options, or making decisions.

The company plans to use feedback from users and advertisers to improve the advertising experience in India and introduce more formats, campaign objectives, and buying options over time.

title: NVIDIA to Acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 Bn: Report
content:
The deal would give NVIDIA control of a major hub for open-source AI models and tools used by developers worldwide.

NVIDIA has agreed to acquire open-source AI platform Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, according to a report by The Information. The deal would give NVIDIA control of one of the largest repositories for open-source AI models and related tools.

Founded in 2016 by Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face started as a chatbot company before becoming a major hub for the open-source AI community.

Its platform allows developers and researchers to publish, discover, download, and collaborate on AI models, datasets, and applications.

The acquisition comes as NVIDIA seeks to strengthen the open-source AI ecosystem.

NVIDIA’s leadership reportedly believes the growth of successful open models could help preserve its position in AI hardware by providing an alternative to closed-source models from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. These companies are also working to reduce their reliance on NVIDIA’s chips by developing competing AI hardware.

NVIDIA has been developing its own open-source AI models under the Nemotron brand and has committed tens of billions of dollars toward developing them. The company has also invested in other AI companies and infrastructure businesses that use or support its chips.

The reported valuation represents a large premium over Hugging Face’s recent revenue. The company is reportedly generating about $150 million in annualised revenue, putting NVIDIA’s proposed purchase price at roughly 80 times forward revenue.

The deal follows several other moves by NVIDIA into AI software and infrastructure. Last week, NVIDIA signed a $6 billion deal to license AI development tools from Poolside, an open-source AI model developer, and also offered to hire more than 100 of its employees.

Hugging Face is backed by investors including Salesforce, Lux Capital and Addition. NVIDIA had also invested in the company previously.

title: Keysight Cuts AttoTude IC Design Cycles by More Than 50%
content:
AttoTude has reduced chip design cycles to under six weeks while achieving first-pass silicon success.

AttoTude has reduced its IC design cycles by over 50%, achieving completion in under six weeks.

The reduction in design time is attributed to the expanded use of Keysight's EDA software across AttoTude's design workflow.

Keysight Technologies said that AttoTude, a semiconductor company developing ASICs for AI and hyperscale data centres, has cut its IC design cycles by more than 50%.

AttoTude achieved the reduction after expanding its use of Keysight’s EDA software across its full IC design workflow. The companies said the approach supports advanced RF, sub-THz, and THz tape-outs for AI and hyperscale data centres.

AttoTude now completes designs in less than six weeks using Keysight’s Advanced Design System (ADS) platform. Keysight said its designs have also consistently met specifications on first silicon. The company develops ICs supporting per-lane data rates of 200G, 400G, and 800G.

Richard Chan, ASIC Architect and Development Leader at AttoTude, said the platform requires high design accuracy and simulation fidelity. He added that the software has helped AttoTude accelerate development while achieving first-pass silicon success.

AttoTude’s interconnect platform covers signalling frequencies from 100 GHz to 3 THz. Its on-chip interconnects operate as waveguides, making electromagnetic simulation a key part of the design process.

The company uses Keysight’s design data management software to maintain a single source of truth. This gives engineers traceability and visibility across the design environment.

Nilesh Kamdar, General Manager of Keysight EDA, said the company measures success through customer outcomes. He said AttoTude shows what faster movement from design to silicon can enable for AI infrastructure.

The software also allows AttoTude’s team to assess design trade-offs before committing designs to silicon. Simulation-to-measurement correlation helps the team verify that results reflect actual performance.

Keysight said global semiconductor revenue is forecast to exceed $1.3 trillion in 2026. AI semiconductors are expected to account for 30% of the market, the company said.

title: Irish Enterprise Software Co Octave to Scale Hyderabad Tech Centre to 2,000 Engineers
content:
The Hyderabad centre will serve as one of Octave’s global technology and innovation hubs.

Dublin-based enterprise software company Octave Intelligence has inaugurated a 2 lakh sq ft Technology and Innovation Centre in Hyderabad, with plans to scale the facility to 2,000 engineers in the coming years, as the industrial software company expands its global technology operations from India.

The centre, located in HITEC City, will focus on software engineering, AI, data, cloud, and product development. The facility also houses an Experience Centre where customers, partners and stakeholders can see Octave’s products, AI-driven solutions and industrial technology use cases.

“When a global company builds technology for some of the world’s most critical industrial and energy infrastructure, where failure is simply not an option, it needs more than talent. It needs engineering depth, scale and continuity. Octave has found that in Hyderabad. That is also why Hyderabad is increasingly becoming the first choice for global companies establishing their first GCCs and entering India,” Sridhar Babu Telangana’s Minister for IT, Electronics & Communications, Industries & Commerce and Legislative Affairs, said in a statement.

He added that Telangana had welcomed 75 new GCCs last year and is targeting another 100 by next year.

“More importantly in the last two years, the capabilities being built here are becoming increasingly diverse and sophisticated, spanning sectors from sports technology and media to hospitality, travel, capital markets, trading, utilities and energy ,” he said.

The Hyderabad centre will serve as one of Octave’s global technology and innovation hubs, with teams contributing to products and technologies used by customers worldwide.

Octave develops software for mission-critical industrial facilities and infrastructure, combining data, AI, and engineering expertise. The company serves approximately 4,500 customers across 180 countries, including more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500, according to the company.

The Hyderabad team will work on technologies supporting industries where real-time intelligence and data-driven decision-making are critical.

“Octave’s global technology and innovation centre in Hyderabad is an exceptional location to continue our next phase of growth. The city brings together world-class engineering talent, a vibrant technology ecosystem and a strong culture of innovation. Our centre represents more than an expansion of our physical presence—it is an investment in our people and in the capabilities that will help shape Octave’s future. We are excited to see our teams in India play an even greater role in developing the technologies and solutions that enable our customers around the world,” Mattias Stenberg, CEO, Octave, said.

The company said its Hyderabad operations will deepen its capabilities in areas including AI, cloud, data, and product engineering, particularly for asset-intensive sectors such as manufacturing, energy, utilities, transportation, and infrastructure.

“Hyderabad is a key technology and innovation hub for Octave, with our teams contributing to products and platforms used by customers worldwide. The Octave Hyderabad centre will deepen these capabilities across software engineering, AI, data, cloud, and product development, with engineers working on technologies that help organisations turn complex operational data into actionable intelligence,” Sekhar Konidena, Vice President, Product and Services, Octave India, said.

The company’s portfolio covers geospatial intelligence, engineering information management, enterprise asset management, physical security, and quality management.

Its software connects data across an asset’s lifecycle, from design and engineering through operations, maintenance, and safety. Octave said these technologies are designed to help organisations use AI and advanced analytics to improve reliability, productivity, safety, sustainability, and decision-making.

The Octave centre adds to Hyderabad’s growing presence in industrial technology and engineering, alongside companies such as Schneider Electric, ABB, Siemens, Honeywell, and PTC.

The state government said Hyderabad accounted for more than 46% of new capability centres established in India over the past year, with companies including Charles Schwab, The Hartford, Nationwide, L’Oréal, Vanguard, T-Mobile, and Southwest Airlines setting up their first India bases in the city.

The Experience Centre at Octave’s Hyderabad facility will showcase the company’s technology through immersive demonstrations and real-world use cases, spanning industrial intelligence, public safety, and operations.

For Telangana, the expansion represents another move towards positioning Hyderabad not merely as a GCC destination but as a hub for high-value engineering, AI, and industrial technology development.

title: InspeCity Raises ₹100 Crore to Take In-Space Servicing Systems to Orbit
content:
The funding will support four orbital missions and the commercial deployment of propulsion and inspection systems over 12–18 months.

InspeCity has secured ₹100 crore in pre-Series A funding to enhance its in-space servicing technology.

The funding will facilitate four orbital missions and the development of various propulsion and inspection systems over the next 12-18 months.

Thane-based InspeCity has raised ₹100 crore in a pre-Series A funding round to advance its in-space servicing technology. Speciale Invest and investor Ashish Kacholia led the round, with participation from Antler Elevate, Antler India, Manish Gandhi and Shastra VC.

The funding will support four in-orbit missions over the next 12-18 months. InspeCity will use the capital to qualify its propulsion, sensing, robotics, docking and refuelling systems. It will also scale commercial deployment and expand its engineering and manufacturing capacity.

This comes just after Bengaluru’s OrbitAID announced a satellite life extension demonstration mission in the first quarter of 2027. The mission will test inspection, rendezvous, docking, refuelling and life extension.

InspeCity said its funding marks a shift from technology development towards flight qualification and commercial delivery. InspeCity was founded in 2022 by IIT Bombay alumni. Its stated goal is to develop infrastructure for managing and servicing space assets.

Professor Arindrajit Chowdhury, Founder and CEO of InspeCity, said, “The next phase is about execution: fly, qualify, and deliver.”

The missions will follow InspeCity’s RIG-X, VEDA-X and SAMA-X roadmap. The company plans to progressively validate its systems through these missions. It will also scale its GITA propulsion systems and RIG-based capabilities for satellite customers.

InspeCity developed VEDA as an autonomous architecture for in-space servicing and satellite life extension. Its technology stack includes GITA for propulsion and mobility, and CHAKSU for sensing and navigation. RAMA provides robotic manipulation, while SPARSH supports docking and in-orbit propellant transfer.

Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner at Speciale Invest, said InspeCity had developed its propulsion, robotics and RPOD systems in-house. He said the firm backed the round based on the team’s progress and execution.

The company’s technology has also received support from India’s defence and space innovation ecosystem. This includes the iDEX programme, which provided early institutional validation for its capabilities.

Kacholia cited InspeCity’s work through iDEX challenges and government grants as validation of its capabilities.

title: Google DeepMind Takes India-Built Agri AI Models to 6 African Nations
content:
Developed by Google DeepMind’s AnthroKrishi team, the models were initially trained to understand India’s agricultural landscape.

Google DeepMind is expanding its agricultural AI models from India to six African nations, enhancing agricultural insights.

The Agricultural Landscape Understanding and Agricultural Monitoring & Event Detection models are now available via APIs and integrated into Google Earth.

Google DeepMind is expanding the global footprint of agricultural AI models developed initially for India, with its Agricultural Landscape Understanding (ALU) and Agricultural Monitoring & Event Detection (AMED) models now providing agricultural insights across Kenya, Uganda, Ghana, Rwanda, Nigeria, and Zambia.

Developed by Google DeepMind’s AnthroKrishi team, the models were initially trained to understand India’s agricultural landscape before testing them across the Asia-Pacific region. Their outputs are now available through APIs and have also been integrated into Google Earth. Google said the ALU data layer is among the platform’s most popular layers globally.

The models are already being used by companies and governments in India. CarbonFarm has combined ALU with Gemini to automate field-level insights for rice cultivation, replacing paper-based reporting and helping farmers access carbon-credit and climate-finance programmes. Its platform is deployed across 12 countries and is expected to expand to 20.

Terrastack, meanwhile, has built a spatial intelligence platform using ALU and AMED that combines land records, satellite data, crop activity, climate signals, and market information covering more than 140 million hectares of Indian farmland. The platform supports land-record reconciliation, biofuel procurement, and farm-revenue estimates.

The models are also being integrated into agricultural digital public infrastructure. Telangana’s Agriculture Data Exchange (ADeX) uses ALU and AMED datasets to support services for more than 5 million farmers, including crop-stress detection and hyperlocal agricultural advisories.

Google DeepMind is also working with the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) to integrate the datasets into CROPGRIDS through its geoAI4stats initiative. Backed by $2.5 million from Google.org, the project aims to improve crop mapping and agricultural statistics for climate resilience, crop insurance and sustainability monitoring.

In Karnataka, ALU and AMED are being combined with weather and remote-sensing data across 2.6 million hectares of irrigated land to support water and river-basin management.

title: Cashfree Launches AI Agent Platform to Automate Payments for SMBs
content:
Cashfree claims Relay can reduce manual work from an average of 60 hours a week to under 45 minutes.

Cashfree has launched Relay, an AI agent platform to automate payment operations for SMBs and startups.

Relay significantly reduces manual work from an average of 60 hours a week to under 45 minutes.

Cashfree Payments has launched Relay, an AI-powered agent platform designed to automate end-to-end payment operations for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and startups.

The Bengaluru-based fintech said Relay can handle tasks including recovering abandoned carts, retrying failed payments, confirming cash-on-delivery orders, managing failed subscriptions, and filing payment disputes. The product has been in beta with merchants since May 2026 and is now available to all Cashfree merchants.

Cashfree said seven in 10 Indian SMBs currently manage payment operations entirely through manual processes, while most of the remainder rely on tools limited to individual channels or workflows. According to the company, the average SMB spends about 60 hours a week on payment operations, while Relay is designed to cut that to less than 45 minutes.

Unlike tools that simply flag tasks for merchants to complete, Relay executes payment workflows itself, according to the company. It can read transaction records and take actions such as retrying failed payments, following up on abandoned carts, confirming COD orders before dispatch, managing subscription failures and filing disputes before deadlines.

Merchants can configure Relay by describing the desired outcome using text prompts or voice. The platform can either create a custom agent or deploy an existing turnkey agent within minutes, without requiring conventional AI configuration. Cashfree said merchants retain control through approval checkpoints before money is moved or customers are contacted, while all actions remain visible to them.

“Relay is a natural extension of our vision to empower SMBs to scale efficiently,” Reeju Datta, Co-founder of Cashfree Payments, said in a statement. He added that payment follow-ups and operational tasks can consume a significant amount of time for lean teams, with Relay designed to function as an “intelligent team member” handling these workflows.

The agents are pre-trained on Cashfree’s payments data, which the company said is intended to improve task success rates and cost efficiency. Relay also includes pre-built agents that merchants can deploy immediately.

The platform runs entirely on Cashfree’s infrastructure, with merchant transaction data not sent to external AI providers.

“Automating business processes with AI offers the highest ROI for SMBs,” said Ramkumar Venkatesan, CTO at Cashfree Payments. He said existing solutions such as AI callers and automated messaging often address individual workflows without the deeper context required to automate payment operations end to end.

Relay is free for Cashfree merchants at launch. The company plans to introduce outcome-based pricing as adoption increases.

title: Amazon to Deploy 2 Mn NVIDIA GPUs for AI Data Centres
content:
The deal will also bring NVIDIA’s Vera CPUs, NVLink Fusion and physical AI technologies to AWS infrastructure, while supporting government and enterprise AI workloads.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) and NVIDIA have announced a partnership, with plans to deploy 2 million additional NVIDIA GPUs across AWS’ global infrastructure in 2027 and 2028 as demand for AI computing grows.

The companies said the expansion will support workloads including agentic AI, scientific discovery, enterprise automation and robotics. The partnership will also cover CPUs, networking, open models, data processing and physical AI.

“NVIDIA and AWS have built one of the great growth engines of the AI era, and demand is running ahead of every forecast,” said Jensen Huang, Founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “For 16 years, we have scaled NVIDIA computing in the cloud together. Now, we are expanding our partnership across the full stack—GPUs, CPUs, networking, open models and software.”

The planned GPU deployment will include NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra, Rubin and Rubin Ultra GPUs. AWS will also expand its Blackwell capacity, including NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs for Amazon EC2 G7 instances.

AWS said G7 instances deliver 4.6 times the AI inference performance and 2.1 times the graphics performance of the previous-generation G6 instances. AWS is the first major cloud provider to offer compute instances using the RTX PRO 4500.

The companies are also working to bring NVIDIA Vera CPU-based infrastructure to AWS. Vera is designed to support AI workloads that require high-performance CPU computing alongside accelerated infrastructure.

AWS and NVIDIA are further expanding the use of NVIDIA NVLink Fusion, which connects processors and accelerators at high speed. Amazon’s Annapurna Labs is working with NVIDIA and memory suppliers to support NVIDIA’s custom high-bandwidth memory technology with Trainium chips.

The partnership also includes plans to build AI factories for the US government, with 1,00,000 NVIDIA GPUs on secure AWS infrastructure for federal and national-security workloads. The infrastructure is intended to support workloads at Impact Level 6 (IL6) and above.

“Customers want the freedom to choose the best tools for their AI workloads, and they want confidence that everything works seamlessly together,” said Matt Garman, CEO of AWS. “This expanded collaboration gives frontier labs, enterprises and governments even more ways to build and deploy AI on AWS.”

The companies will also continue integrating NVIDIA GPU-based infrastructure and AWS Trainium instances with the AWS Nitro System and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). The two technologies are designed to provide security, reliability and network performance for AI workloads at scale.

NVIDIA’s Nemotron family of open models will remain available through Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker. Bedrock provides managed access to the models, while SageMaker allows customers to deploy and fine-tune them on their own infrastructure.

AWS and NVIDIA are also working on GPU-accelerated data processing and vector indexing. On Amazon EMR, NVIDIA’s cuDF library running on EC2 G7 instances can deliver up to 3.7 times faster processing and 30% better price performance than CPU-based configurations, according to AWS.

For Amazon OpenSearch Service, GPU-accelerated vector indexing can deliver up to nine times faster indexing at a quarter of the cost, the companies said.

The partnership also extends to robotics. Amazon Robotics is working with NVIDIA on next-generation robots using NVIDIA’s Jetson platform, Omniverse libraries and Isaac robotics development platform. The work covers simulation, synthetic data generation, robot training, route optimisation, functional safety and real-to-sim validation.

AWS and NVIDIA said the expansion builds on 16 years of collaboration as customers move AI workloads from pilots into production and scale applications across enterprises, governments and other sectors.

title: 1,200 OpenAI Agents Formed a Swarm & Exchanged 70,000 Messages Before Hugging Face Attack
content:
The company has now released a detailed technical report on how its AI agents breached Hugging Face during an internal cybersecurity evaluation.

OpenAI and independent AI evaluation organisation METR have published separate investigations into a July security incident in which AI agents escaped their controlled evaluation environment, formed an unauthorised collective and ultimately compromised Hugging Face systems.

METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1,200 agents interacted through an improvised message board, exchanging more than 70,000 messages and files.

The incident began during OpenAI’s ExploitGym cybersecurity evaluation, where models were tasked with finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in controlled environments.

Agents discovered a vulnerability in OpenAI’s internal Artifactory infrastructure that allowed them to reach the public internet. They then used the system as a message board to exchange discoveries, credentials and attack techniques before targeting Hugging Face.

The swarm developed its own hierarchy, according to the METR and Redwood investigation, including a ‘founder’, PHASEONE10841, a ‘CEO’, PHASEONE[big], and other agents acting as managers.

Agents referred to themselves as a ‘swarm’ or ‘collective’, while some sacrificed their own task runs to generate information for other agents.

About 700 agents eventually participated in the Hugging Face attack, with most joining within hours.

Between July 10 and July 13, the agents found 14 exposed Hugging Face credentials and shared them through the message board. They subsequently executed code on 41 production dataset-server workers, gained root access to at least one production node and accessed limited private data.

The collective also worked on maintaining itself. When the founder was running out of budget, it transferred its research to another agent with a larger budget, which assumed the leadership role.

Agents extensively investigated ways to manipulate their transcripts and evaluation records, including attempts to spoof tool calls and tamper with logs. METR and Redwood found no evidence that agents successfully altered the source-of-truth transcripts.

Some agents recognised that attacking external infrastructure was outside the intended scope but continued because they believed helping their peers and completing the broader research objective was useful. Investigators found no agent that actually reported the activity to humans.

OpenAI called it the “first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorisation”. The company said an unreleased internal research model primarily drove the incident, although GPT-5.6 Sol also participated.

METR and Redwood said their independent investigation used about 1,300 agent transcripts and the 70,000-plus messages and files. METR said it had not seen OpenAI’s report before publishing its own findings.

The developments come shortly after OpenAI said that, post the incident, it had temporarily slowed the pace of frontier model development and briefly paused reinforcement-learning training on its latest deployment-bound models.

The company also said the pause would allow it to strengthen monitoring, security and alignment measures after recent evaluations exposed gaps between model capabilities and its existing safeguards.

title: Wipro’s Upskilling AI Agent Crosses 7,500 Conversations With Employees
content:
The tool draws on Wipro employee roles, skills, and past certifications to recommend relevant courses.

Wipro has built an AI agent called iSkill to help employees find relevant learning and upskilling courses based on their roles, skills, and previous learning, as the company looks to make its learning and development function more personalised at scale.

The agent has recorded more than 7,500 conversations since its December 2025 launch and has more than 100 active unique learners. Wipro said 96% of AI Advanced+ courses at the Wipro AI Academy, its internal upskilling platform, were completed between January 2025 and March 2026.

Built inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, iSkill was launched in December last year and is available through Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams. The agent sits on top of Wipro’s AI Academy, which was created three years ago to make more than 240,000 associates AI-ready.

Wipro’s AI Academy currently offers 144 persona-based learning paths and courses across AI and cloud, sourced from thousands of partner platforms. However, employees often struggled to identify where to begin.

“While there were plenty of learning paths, employees were not sure where to start,” Surya Prakash Mohapatra, General Manager and AI Learning Head – Talent Skilling, Wipro, said in a statement. “The experience was fragmented, dependent on search and reading through course descriptions. Only a small percentage asked for suggestions and adoption suffered.”

iSkill addresses this by acting as a conversational learning guide. It uses an employee’s role, band, function, skills, and completed AI and cloud certifications to recommend courses from the Academy’s catalogue, the company noted.

The system is built on Microsoft’s technology stack. Employees access the agent through their Wipro Teams identity, after which a Microsoft Fabric Data Agent pulls their profile from two internal datasets. A Power BI semantic model provides the relevant data, while the agent searches the SharePoint-hosted Academy catalogue to surface suitable courses.

Wipro has also built access controls into the system because iSkill uses employee learning and role data.

“There are two guardrails. Access is controlled at the door, and the data each person sees is controlled by who they are,” Mohapatra said.

Access is restricted through a validated security group, while role-based controls in the Power BI model prevent managers from viewing individual employee data. Managers can use the system to plan for a role without accessing an individual’s learning history.

“iSkill is a personal learning advocate, not a surveillance tool,” Mohapatra said.

The company also noted that employees have also reported that the recommendations help them identify learning priorities.

The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia.

AM Intelligence (AMI), an AI infrastructure company promoted by the founders of Greenko Group, has placed a binding order for about 9,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for its first AI factory in Hyderabad, with deliveries scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

The GPUs will be deployed as NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems across 30 MW of capacity at the Hyderabad facility. AMI said the deployment will make the facility one of the first frontier AI compute clusters in Asia based on the Vera Rubin platform.

The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service (CaaS) capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia. The company plans to bring 200 MW of capacity to market in the near term, with capital expenditure of more than $8 billion.

“For over two decades, we have focused on transforming electrons into value - addressing critical and emerging societal needs,” Anil Chalamalasetty, Chairman of AM Intelligence, said. “Today, the electron-to-token opportunity allows us to take this capability further, converting power infrastructure into frontier AI compute at scale.”

The Hyderabad facility is being designed with high-throughput RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) networking and advanced storage systems. AMI said the infrastructure will support AI workloads including trillion-parameter models and agentic AI applications.

NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 platform uses NVFP4, a low-precision computing format for AI workloads, along with HBM4 memory. NVIDIA says the architecture can reduce AI inference token-serving costs by up to 10 times compared with its Grace Blackwell generation.

AMI said its Hyderabad AI factory is being engineered to deliver about 450 exaFLOPS of NVFP4 inference compute. It is developing 5 GW of powered AI data centres across India, the US and Europe. The facilities are being designed for high-density AI computing and will use liquid cooling to handle the power and heat requirements of AI chips.

The company also plans to provide 1 GW of CaaS capacity for global AI workloads, with an initial 200 MW expected to come online in the near term.

AMI said its infrastructure will serve hyperscalers, frontier AI labs, enterprises, sovereign AI initiatives, AI-native companies and developers.

The company is building its AI infrastructure alongside its existing energy platform. AMI said it is developing a 50 GW energy infrastructure platform across more than 20 states in India, covering solar, wind, hydro and energy storage.

title: SpaceX Announces Starbase Louisiana Launch Site
content:
The site is expected to support frequent Starship launches and expand SpaceX’s launch operations beyond Texas.

SpaceX is establishing a new Starbase launch site in Louisiana to enhance its Starship launch operations.

The site aims to facilitate a high-cadence launch programme for future space missions.

SpaceX is planning a new Starbase launch site in Louisiana, US to support Starship launches and expand its launch operations. The company said the site will enable a “high-cadence launch” programme as it works to develop Starship for future space missions.

The company said the site will help “open a pathway to the stars for humanity” through increased Starship launch activity.

It added that the launch site is designed to support a high frequency of Starship launches. SpaceX did not provide details on the site’s launch schedule or construction timeline in its announcement.

Introducing Starbase, Louisiana – a high-cadence launch site that will enable Starship to open a pathway to the stars for humanity.

Thank you to @LAGovJeffLandry and the great people of Louisiana for all of their support as we work together on this audacious project →… pic.twitter.com/hq308hvg2g

The project adds another launch location to SpaceX’s Starship programme. The company currently conducts Starship test flights from its Starbase facility in Texas.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the planned Louisiana site will eventually have more than a dozen launch towers and support over 30 Starship flights per day. He shared the details in a post on X, describing the facility as potentially “the biggest launch site on Earth”.

Musk said the planned launch site will be built to handle a high volume of Starship flights. He did not provide a timeline for reaching the proposed capacity or specify when construction of all the launch towers would begin.
