title: OpenAI’s New Chip Beats NVIDIA; Gen 2 Nears Tape-Out in Months
content:
“Jalapeño is also evidence of a broader full-stack advantage,” OpenAI said in the blog post.

OpenAI’s first custom AI inference chip, Jalapeño, delivered up to 1.9x more performance per watt than NVIDIA’s Blackwell systems in benchmark tests, while also reducing response latency, according to results published by OpenAI.

The chip, developed with Broadcom and Celestica, is designed specifically for inference and is expected to begin deployment inside OpenAI’s compute infrastructure by the end of 2026.

OpenAI tested Jalapeño against commercially available AI systems using InferenceX, a public benchmark developed by SemiAnalysis, across GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek R1 670B, and Kimi K2.5 1T. Across the models, Jalapeño delivered 1.5–1.9 times more AI work per watt at peak throughput and 1.7–3.6x lower end-to-end latency than the comparison systems.

The DeepSeek R1 comparison illustrates the gap. Jalapeño delivered 19,641 mixed tokens per second per kilowatt at peak throughput, versus 11,781 for NVIDIA’s GB300, giving OpenAI’s chip a 1.7x advantage.

End-to-end latency was 1.65 seconds on Jalapeño compared to 5.99 seconds on the GB300. OpenAI reported similar advantages over NVIDIA systems on GPT-OSS and Kimi K2.5, with the full results shown in the accompanying benchmark data.

OpenAI rated Jalapeño at 700 watts, although its measured sustained power remained at or below 550 watts on the tested workloads.

The company said it evaluates inference hardware based on useful AI work delivered per unit of power while maintaining the latency required for interactive applications.

“Jalapeño is also evidence of a broader full-stack advantage,” OpenAI said in the blog post. “OpenAI can design models, products, serving software, chips, memory, networking, and systems together, using what we learn from real workloads to improve every layer of the stack. “

At the Hot Chips 2026 conference, OpenAI, just after publishing these results, also outlined how quickly it expects the platform to evolve.

The company said Jalapeño is only the first generation of a broader roadmap, with Gen 2 already in development and approaching tape-out within months. He also said Gen 3 is already operational.

Hot Chips '26: OpenAI says its Gen 1 chip is only step one with Gen 2 nearing tape-out in a number of months and Gen 3 already operational, afterwards bringing out the Broadcom and Celestica teams to share the stage

"One more thing -- this is step one of a multi-generational… https://t.co/alAB43w1ME pic.twitter.com/Q8eddAWNoU

— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) August 26, 2026

OpenAI originally announced Jalapeño in June as part of a multi-generation platform it is developing with Broadcom and Celestica.

OpenAI designed the accelerator, while Broadcom provided chip implementation, networking, and connectivity technologies, and Celestica contributed board, rack, and system integration and production expertise.

The company said AI models also accelerated the chip’s development, helping take Jalapeño from initial design to tapeout in nine months.

Using Codex with GPT-Astra, engineers brought three open-weight models to high performance within two months, while selected AI-generated implementations for GPT-OSS components ran 1.5–1.8x faster than existing human-written implementations.

OpenAI said it will continue deploying NVIDIA and other third-party accelerators for training and inference. Jalapeño is the first generation of a planned multi-generation platform, with Gen 2 already in development and Gen 3 taking shape.

title: Mystery Ox Alpha Revealed as GLM-5.3-Flash, Running Entirely on Chinese AI Chips
content:
"This demonstrates that Chinese chips can support frontier-model inference efficiently and economically at scale,” said Z.ai.

Z.ai has revealed that the mystery Ox Alpha model that surged to the top of model usage charts over the last few days is GLM-5.3-Flash, a 320-billion-parameter multimodal model with 18 billion active parameters.

The company says it outperforms GLM-5.2 across coding and agentic benchmarks while approaching Claude Opus 4.8 on some tests.

The model was released anonymously as Ox Alpha on OpenCode and OpenRouter before Z.ai’s announcement.

Z.ai said the company used the anonymous deployment to gather real-world user feedback ahead of launch, and that Ox Alpha quickly became the most popular model of the week

OpenRouter said Ox Alpha processed more than 20 trillion tokens in six days, making it the largest model launch on the platform by token volume.

The model was offered free of charge during the preview, with OpenRouter listing a 1.05-million-token context window.

The price-to-performance ratio was a major part of Ox Alpha’s appeal during its anonymous preview: developers were getting frontier-level coding and agentic performance for free.

Z.ai’s disclosure now puts a concrete number behind that proposition.

The company says GLM-5.3-Flash scores 57 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, at a discounted cost of just $0.045 per task, putting it in a markedly different price-performance bracket from models such as Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6.

Z.ai also said it has served GLM-5.3-Flash over the past week on a large cluster of domestically developed Chinese AI accelerators, with the deployment spanning tens of thousands of chips.

The company built a dedicated inference engine on top of SGLang and reported a threefold improvement in end-to-end serving performance compared with its initial baseline on the same hardware.

Z.ai said the resulting system achieved hardware efficiency and per-token costs comparable with mainstream NVIDIA GPUs. “This demonstrates that Chinese chips can support frontier-model inference efficiently and economically at scale,” said the company. Z.ai did not identify the specific Chinese accelerators used to serve the model.

However, this claim arrives against a backdrop of US restrictions designed to limit China’s access to advanced AI computing hardware.

US export controls have imposed licensing requirements on high-performance AI chips and related technologies for China.

Washington currently allows exports of certain lower-performance or otherwise restricted Nvidia AI accelerators, including the H200, to approved Chinese customers on a case-by-case licensing basis, subject to security and supply conditions.

NVIDIA’s more advanced Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin systems remain restricted from the Chinese market under US export controls

Z.ai lists the model at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with OpenRouter currently applying a promotional 50% discount to the input rate.

The model is also available as open weights under an MIT licence on Hugging Face, allowing developers to download and run it themselves rather than accessing it only through an API.

Z.ai, formerly known as Zhipu AI, is a Beijing-based Chinese AI company that became the world’s first publicly listed large-language-model developer when it went public on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January.

Its current flagship is GLM-5.3, a 744-billion-parameter model designed for coding, agentic tasks and long-context workloads.

title: Gujarat Police Seeks AI System to Connect 80,000 CCTV Cameras
content: Listen5 minSHARESaveFollowPreferred SourceGoogle NewsWhatsAppTelegramGujarat Police is seeking technology to integrate approximately 80,000 CCTV cameras across the state into a unified video management and analytics ecosystem through the Gujarat Police Innovation Hackathon 2026.The challenge offers a total prize pool of ₹37 lakh and is scheduled for September 10–11, according to the official Sentinel Gujarat website.The project aims to address a fragmented surveillance infrastructure. The government says 26 different departments currently operate independent CCTV systems using different vendors, video management systems (VMS), storage arrangements, camera types and feed-sharing protocols. Some systems retain footage for seven days, while others retain it for 15 days or more.The proposed system would allow these separate networks to work through a common integration layer while, under some of the proposed models, allowing existing departmental systems to continue operating independently.The government says the architecture should be secure, scalable, interoperable, and designed to use existing infrastructure to the maximum practical extent.The system is also expected to connect CCTV analytics with databases including VAHAN, SARTHI, eGujCop (Gujarat Police's CCTNS platform), the Automated Fingerprint Identification System, and the National Automated Fingerprint Identification System. These databases contain records relating to arrested persons, stolen vehicles, wanted criminals, missing persons, unidentified dead bodies, and fingerprint data, according to the government.For the technical evaluation, participants will receive access to approximately 50 geographically distributed cameras. They must onboard the feeds into one platform, track a designated vehicle using its registration number, reconstruct its timestamped, and location-based movement history and generate real-time alerts from a representative watchlist database.The requirements include automatic number plate recognition, person and vehicle tracking, object detection, and event analytics. Facial recognition systems are also listed among the proposed analytics capabilities, while the government requires participants to demonstrate cybersecurity, scalability, and interoperability.Participants can choose among four reference models or submit a hybrid or customised architecture. The models range from a central CCTV registry and Geographic Information System (GIS) foundation to unified viewing, VMS federation, and a fully centralised VMS and artificial intelligence platform.The government will evaluate successful feed integration, the working platform, analytics output, architecture, security and readiness to scale toward approximately 80,000 cameras. It may also consider privacy protection, auditability, role-based access controls, edge processing, and bandwidth optimisation.The official website says registration opened on August 4 and closes on September 7. title: Google Cloud Launches Gemini Enterprise for the Legal Industry
content:
The platform connects with existing legal systems and uses AI agents for contract review, legal research, regulatory monitoring and document workflows.

Google Cloud has launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal, an AI platform designed for law firms and corporate legal departments, with tools for legal research, contract review, regulatory monitoring, document management and other workflows.

The platform is available in preview from August 26 and is part of Google Cloud’s new suite of industry-specific Gemini Enterprise solutions. Google Cloud said it also plans purpose-built solutions for healthcare, life sciences and other professional services.

It was developed with law firms and legal technology providers, with a focus on maintaining existing permissions, confidentiality controls, and governance requirements.

“Foundational model intelligence is necessary. For legal work, it is nowhere near sufficient,” Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, said. He said the platform combines domain-specific skills, connections to enterprise systems, agents and an open partner ecosystem, with governance across the system.

Gemini Enterprise for Legal includes reusable skills that can be configured for tasks such as contract review and redlining, legal research, regulatory horizon scanning, Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) fulfilment and playbook creation.

These skills can incorporate a firm’s own instructions, citation rules and house style.

The platform also connects with legal teams’ existing systems through secure MCP connectors. These connections preserve existing user permissions and access controls across document management, case repositories, research services and other applications.

Google Cloud said the platform can deploy pre-built agents for legal and policy research, regulatory screening and contract drafting. Its stated use cases also include tracking legislative and regulatory changes, compiling data for DSAR responses, reviewing agreements against enterprise playbooks, updating contracting playbooks, redacting sensitive information from court filings and drafting non-disclosure agreements.

The platform integrates with services including Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, iManage, NetDocuments, DocuSign, Everlaw and RelativityOne. It also connects with legal research and litigation resources such as Thomson Reuters HighQ, CourtListener and Courtroom5, along with legal AI platforms including Harvey, Solve Intelligence and Legora.

Google Cloud is also working with systems integrators and technology partners including Accenture, Deloitte, Devoteam, Factor Law, KPMG, Tribe.ai, Valtech, Zazmic, Zencore and 66degrees. Deloitte and Eudia are among the partners offering agents through the platform.

The company said Gemini Enterprise for Legal operates within a governed control plane that enforces security policies, maintains private data isolation and provides traceable citations for outputs. Google Cloud also said client data, firm-specific playbooks, intellectual property, custom agents and model outputs remain private to the organisation and are not used to train or fine-tune its foundation models.

The platform is being developed with law firms including Cleary Gottlieb, Freshfields, Weil and Williams & Connolly.

“Using Google’s Gemini Enterprise, which can slot in seamlessly with other daily work tools, we can unlock greater efficiencies for our teams and help them deliver even higher quality work for our clients,” said Jeff Karpf, Managing Partner at Cleary Gottlieb.

Freshfields Global Managing Partner Alan Mason said the opportunity is to combine Gemini Enterprise for Legal with the firm’s expertise, governance and institutional knowledge.

title: Bengaluru-Based AI Startup Ringg AI Secures $10 Mn in Series A Extension Led by Peak XV
content:
The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the funds to expand its AI agents and enterprise operations across India and international markets.

Voice AI startup Ringg AI has extended its Series A funding round, with Peak XV Partners leading the latest investment and Arkam Ventures and Capital 2b also participating. The company previously raised $5.5 million in its Series A earlier this year, bringing the total to $15.5 million.

The company said the new capital will strengthen its AI platform, expand its voice, WhatsApp and browser agents, invest in its proprietary AI models and context graph, and grow its enterprise business in India and international markets.

Founded in 2023 by Siddharth Tripathi, Kali Charan Vemuru and Utkarsh Shukla, Ringg AI is headquartered in Bengaluru.

The startup builds AI agents that automate customer conversations and the business workflows that follow. Its platform combines voice, WhatsApp and browser agents, allowing them to share context across customer conversations, business rules and enterprise systems.

The agents can handle workflows such as lead qualification, customer onboarding, support, collections and renewals. Human employees can also take over conversations and workflows while retaining the context and actions completed by the agents.

“Nobody buys us because the demo sounds good,” said Tripathi, Founder and CEO of Ringg AI. “They buy us because onboarding improves, resolution times fall, or qualified leads start showing up in the CRM without someone having to make the call.”

Tripathi added that enterprises should not have to buy separate systems for voice and other workflows. “We own the loop from conversation to action to evaluation to improvement,” he said.

Ringg said its agents are already deployed at companies including Policybazaar, CRED, Flipkart, Groww, Practo, Tabby, SuperNova and GoodScore, serving customers across sectors such as healthcare, banking, fintech and IT.

The startup said its platform creates a context graph across customers, conversations, business rules, workflows and enterprise systems. This shared context allows a conversation to move between channels. For instance, a voice interaction can continue on WhatsApp, while a browser agent can complete actions in a CRM or another enterprise application.

Ringg also uses built-in evaluations to measure conversation quality, policy adherence, workflow completion and business outcomes. Enterprise teams can monitor agents, review decisions and take over conversations or workflows when needed.

“We chose to solve the hardest version of the problem first,” said Vemuru, Co-Founder and CTO of Ringg AI. “If an agent can handle a noisy call, switch across languages, and still complete a real workflow, it can work almost anywhere. We are building this in India, for a global market.”

Ringg is also developing its AI stack, including its proprietary speech-to-text model Parrot and small language models. The company said this approach is intended to give enterprises more control over costs, compliance and data residency.

The platform supports deployments across India, the GCC, the US and Europe, along with on-premise deployments.

title: AM Intelligence Orders 9,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for Hyderabad AI Factory
content:
The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia.

AM Intelligence (AMI), an AI infrastructure company promoted by the founders of Greenko Group, has placed a binding order for about 9,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for its first AI factory in Hyderabad, with deliveries scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

The GPUs will be deployed as NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems across 30 MW of capacity at the Hyderabad facility. AMI said the deployment will make the facility one of the first frontier AI compute clusters in Asia based on the Vera Rubin platform.

The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service (CaaS) capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia. The company plans to bring 200 MW of capacity to market in the near term, with capital expenditure of more than $8 billion.

“For over two decades, we have focused on transforming electrons into value - addressing critical and emerging societal needs,” Anil Chalamalasetty, Chairman of AM Intelligence, said. “Today, the electron-to-token opportunity allows us to take this capability further, converting power infrastructure into frontier AI compute at scale.”

The Hyderabad facility is being designed with high-throughput RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) networking and advanced storage systems. AMI said the infrastructure will support AI workloads including trillion-parameter models and agentic AI applications.

NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 platform uses NVFP4, a low-precision computing format for AI workloads, along with HBM4 memory. NVIDIA says the architecture can reduce AI inference token-serving costs by up to 10 times compared with its Grace Blackwell generation.

AMI said its Hyderabad AI factory is being engineered to deliver about 450 exaFLOPS of NVFP4 inference compute. It is developing 5 GW of powered AI data centres across India, the US and Europe. The facilities are being designed for high-density AI computing and will use liquid cooling to handle the power and heat requirements of AI chips.

The company also plans to provide 1 GW of CaaS capacity for global AI workloads, with an initial 200 MW expected to come online in the near term.

AMI said its infrastructure will serve hyperscalers, frontier AI labs, enterprises, sovereign AI initiatives, AI-native companies and developers.

The company is building its AI infrastructure alongside its existing energy platform. AMI said it is developing a 50 GW energy infrastructure platform across more than 20 states in India, covering solar, wind, hydro and energy storage.

title: Ryanair is Using AI-Generated Videos for Staff Training & Passenger Updates
content:
The European low-cost carrier is using Synthesia’s AI products to cut costs and speed up content production.

Ryanair is using AI-generated videos to train employees and send passenger disruption updates, cutting the time needed to produce the latter by up to 90%, according to AI video company Synthesia.

The airline previously took at least an hour to produce a single disruption video, which required filming, editing, and exporting. Localising the videos could take longer because Ryanair often needed employees who could record versions in different languages.

Ryanair now uses Synthesia’s AI avatars and reusable templates to turn scripts into videos. When a disruption occurs, staff can update the relevant information, generate a video and send it to affected passengers through the Ryanair app. The same update can be produced in every European language. The airline is also using AI avatars for employee training.

Ryanair trains about 1,300 of its 3,000 engineers across 13 European bases each year. Instead of repeatedly flying instructors between locations, it can record an instructor once and use their digital avatar to deliver the training. Synthesia said the shift has produced six-figure savings for Ryanair, which the airline has reinvested in additional engineering training.

The technology has also been extended to 15,000 cabin crew and 22,000 ground agents, with training and operational procedures delivered in 20 languages.

“With Synthesia, we deliver translated, targeted messages in minutes,” said Ellen Drumm, Ryanair’s Customer Service Communications Manager.

The AI video deployment comes as Ryanair expands its use of AI across core operations.

Earlier this month, the airline announced a five-year partnership with Google Cloud to deploy Google Workspace and Gemini Enterprise to 35,000 employees. Ryanair plans to use Gemini Enterprise to automate decision-making, optimise flight-crew logistics and build custom AI agents.

The partnership will also bring Google DeepMind models including AlphaEvolve and WeatherNext into fleet operations and maintenance scheduling.

It follows Ryanair’s decision in July to extend its AWS partnership for another five years, with AWS technologies including Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore supporting areas such as the airline’s website, fleet scheduling, pilot workflows and employee applications.

Ryanair carried 208.4 million passengers in its financial year ended March 2026 and had 647 aircraft at the end of the period. The airline aims to carry more than 300 million passengers annually by 2034.

title: OpenAI is Hiring AI Engineers in Delhi & Mumbai
content:
The company’s current India careers listings also include roles in enterprise sales, B2B marketing, go-to-market enablement, product partnerships, AI deployment and workplace operations.

OpenAI is hiring Applied AI Engineers and Applied AI Architects in Mumbai and Delhi, expanding its India team around enterprise AI deployments as the company builds out its local operations.

The roles sit within OpenAI’s Technical Success organisation and focus on helping customers move AI applications from early use-case selection and prototyping into production.

The Applied AI Engineer role involves working directly with enterprise customers to design, build and deploy AI systems.

OpenAI says engineers will write and debug code, build evaluation systems, resolve complex integrations, and make technical decisions about model behaviour, reliability, latency, cost, safety, security, and governance.

The company says it will measure success by production systems, sustained adoption, and customer impact rather than demonstrations alone.

The Applied AI Architect role is focused on senior technical ownership of customer accounts. Architects will work with company leadership and technical teams to develop AI strategies and guide deployments across ChatGPT Enterprise, the OpenAI API, Codex and other agentic AI products.

The role covers architecture, data, integration, security, privacy, governance, evaluation and deployment, with the job description describing the architect as the ‘CTO of your book of business’.

OpenAI’s current India careers listings also include roles in enterprise sales, B2B marketing, go-to-market enablement, product partnerships, AI deployment and workplace operations.

The hiring comes as OpenAI expands its physical presence in India. In February, the company announced plans to open new offices in Mumbai and Bengaluru later this year, alongside its existing presence in New Delhi. OpenAI said the expansion would better serve users and partners in India.

OpenAI announced in June that Prabhjeet Singh, the former president of Uber India and South Asia, will become its Managing Director for India in September.

Singh will be OpenAI’s senior-most executive in India and will oversee consumer growth, enterprise adoption and strategic partnerships.

India has more than 100 million weekly active ChatGPT users, making it OpenAI’s second-largest market after the US. India also has the company’s largest student user base globally.

OpenAI has been expanding its India operations across consumer, enterprise, infrastructure and education, with partnerships spanning Tata Group, JioHotstar, Eternal, Pine Labs, Cars24, HCLTech, PhonePe, CRED and MakeMyTrip.

Through its Tata partnership, OpenAI is developing AI-ready data-centre capacity in India, starting with 100 MW and with the potential to scale to 1 GW, while Tata plans to deploy ChatGPT Enterprise across its workforce and TCS plans to use Codex for software development.

title: ​​Germany’s Infineon to Acquire Bengaluru’s C2i Semiconductors for AI Data Centre Power Systems
content:
The deal will expand Infineon’s digital power engineering capabilities in India and support power systems for next-generation AI infrastructure.

Infineon is acquiring Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors to enhance its AI data centre power solutions.

The acquisition will bolster Infineon's engineering capabilities and expand its R&D network in India.

Infineon Technologies is set to acquire Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors, a technology company backed by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan, specialising in software-defined multiphase controllers and smart power stages for AI data centres.

The German semiconductor company said the deal will strengthen its power solutions for AI infrastructure and expand its engineering capabilities in India. Infineon expects to close the transaction in the third quarter of 2026. The company said the deal will also strengthen its global R&D network.

C2i develops software-defined power management systems that combine digital controls, power semiconductors, and software algorithms. Its technology can regulate power conversion in real time, helping systems respond to changing demands from AI processors.

The startup also develops system-level and vertical power delivery architectures. Infineon said these capabilities will support the development of Substrate Integrated Voltage Regulators for future AI systems.

Adam White, President of Infineon’s Power Systems division, said the acquisition will “further strengthen Infineon’s leadership in power solutions for AI data centres”. He added that it will create a centre of excellence for digital power technologies in India.

Infineon currently employs about 2,800 people in India.

C2i Founder and CEO Ram Anant said joining Infineon will give the company access to semiconductor technologies, manufacturing capabilities, and global customer relationships.

The deal will combine C2i’s digital power expertise with Infineon’s silicon, silicon carbide, and gallium nitride technologies. The companies will also develop vertical power delivery solutions for AI infrastructure.

title: Alibaba Launches Wan3.0 AI Video Model as AI Investment Accelerates
content:
The model can turn documents, spreadsheets, presentations and web pages into videos of up to 30 seconds, as Alibaba expands its multimodal AI capabilities.

Alibaba launched Wan3.0, an AI video generation model capable of creating videos from various digital materials.

The model supports multiple input types, transforming text, images, and business documents into videos up to 30 seconds long.

Alibaba launched Wan3.0, its latest artificial intelligence video generation model, on August 24, with the ability to generate videos of up to 30 seconds from documents, spreadsheets, presentation slides and web pages.

Alibaba Cloud said Wan3.0 supports multiple input types, including text, images, audio and video, as well as business documents and web content. The model is designed to convert existing digital material into video rather than requiring users to create a video prompt from scratch.

The company said the model can turn presentation material into product videos, training content into video courses and spreadsheet data into animated visualisations. Wan3.0 also supports video generation at up to 1080p resolution, according to Alibaba Cloud.

Alibaba Cloud first made Wan3.0 available in public beta on August 6. The company said the model has since been used for short drama and film production, advertising and marketing, tourism promotion and music video creation.

The latest release builds on Alibaba’s broader development of generative AI models. The company also develops the Qwen family of large language models, while Wan focuses on video generation and multimodal content creation.

Reuters reported that the launch came a day after the Chinese technology company announced an HK$80 billion, or about $10.2 billion, share placement to fund its artificial intelligence expansion.

Wan3.0 gives Alibaba another product through which it can apply its growing AI infrastructure, with the model aimed at generating video from text and multimodal inputs as well as existing business and digital content.

title: Airbound Raises $37 Mn to Scale Autonomous Aircraft in India
content:
The Bengaluru-based aerospace company will use the funding to expand manufacturing and launch a drone delivery network in Andhra Pradesh.

Airbound has raised $37 million to enhance its manufacturing and launch a drone delivery network in Andhra Pradesh.

The company signed an agreement with the state government to establish an autonomous drone delivery network across three cities.

Bengaluru-based aerospace company Airbound has raised $37 million in a Series A round led by Greenoaks. The company has also signed a commercial deployment agreement with the Andhra Pradesh government.

The funding will support engineering, manufacturing and market expansion, while the agreement will establish an autonomous drone delivery network across three cities.

Airbound will use the funding to scale commercial manufacturing and accelerate its go-to-market efforts. The round includes new and existing investors such as DoorDash, Lachy Groom, Lightspeed and Humba Ventures. The company has raised nearly $50 million since its 2023 launch.

The drone delivery network connecting three cities will support retail, e-commerce and healthcare deliveries. The company plans to scale the network to 10,000 daily flights. It also expects the programme to provide a model for aerial delivery expansion across India.

Airbound has already completed more than 1,000 autonomous flights with Narayana Health. It transported diagnostic samples between healthcare facilities. The company said the flights reduced delivery times from hours to minutes.

Airbound designs and manufactures its aircraft in India. Its aircraft use autonomy, materials science and a physics-first approach. The company says the design aims to make the aircraft weigh less than the cargo it carries.

The company says this approach could reduce the cost of moving goods by air. Founder and CEO Naman Pushp said the company wants to make flying cheaper than road transport. He said the goal is to move people and goods “for a fraction of a cent”.

The startup also says the same aircraft technology could eventually support freight and passenger transport. The company claims its aircraft could turn a 300-kilometre journey into a 20-minute flight.

Greenoaks Partner Neil Shah said Airbound could challenge the cost gap between road and air freight. “Trucks are cheap and slow, planes are fast and expensive,” Shah said. He added that Airbound aims to remove that trade-off.

For now, the company is focusing on commercial deliveries in India. Pushp said the country’s delivery expectations create a demanding test for the technology. “If you can build something that works in India, it tends to work anywhere,” he said.

title: AI Ecosystem Provider ESDS Software Solution to Launch ₹720 Cr IPO on August 28
content:
The company has set a price band of ₹408 to ₹429 per equity share, with investors to bid for a minimum of 34 shares.

Enterprise cloud and AI ecosystem provider ESDS Software Solution’s initial public offering (IPO) will open for subscription on August 28 and close on September 1, with the price band set at Rs 408 to Rs 429 per equity share.

The IPO will comprise a fresh issue of equity shares worth up to ₹7,20 crore. Investors can bid for a minimum of 34 equity shares and in multiples of 34 thereafter. The company has 100,427,753 equity shares outstanding before the issue.

ESDS Software Solution, incorporated in 2005, provides cloud infrastructure, managed services, data centre infrastructure, and software solutions. The company has served 2,501 customers in FY26 across banking, financial services and insurance, public sector entities, businesses, and enterprises.

Its revenue from operations stood at ₹472 crore in FY26, compared with ₹286 crore in FY24. Its net profit rose to ₹120 crore in FY26, up from ₹13.6 crore in FY24, the company disclosed.

ESDS provides infrastructure-as-a-service, including colocation, data centre services, cloud services, and cloud computing, along with managed services and software-as-a-service offerings.

The company said it is one of two players in India providing GPU-as-a-service, cloud, managed services, data centre infrastructure, and software solutions, according to a Nexdigm report cited in its IPO documents.

The company has also entered into an AI cloud infrastructure agreement with an Australia-based neocloud AI compute service provider at a total contract value of $1.25 billion.

Under the agreement, the AI company will deploy and operate a dedicated AI infrastructure cluster at an existing data centre facility in Australia. The cluster is expected to include about 8,208 NVIDIA B300 GPUs and associated storage infrastructure.

ESDS was one of the first cloud service providers in India to offer community cloud services, according to the Nexdigm report. Its customers include organisations with requirements related to data privacy, security, compliance, and regulation.

DAM Capital Advisors and Systematix Corporate Services are the book-running lead managers for the IPO, while MUFG Intime India is the registrar.

The company has cautioned investors that equity shares involve a high degree of risk and advised potential investors to refer to the risk factors in the RHP before making an investment decision.

The IPO is subject to receipt of requisite approvals, market conditions, and other considerations.

Research shows that crystallising Merck’s blockbuster cancer drug, Keytruda, in microgravity could help move it from an intravenous formulation towards a subcutaneous one.

Bhubaneswar-based startup Serendipity Space is building autonomous pharmaceutical factories that can operate in microgravity. The company believes manufacturing drugs in space could help make some difficult-to-formulate medicines easier to administer.

The idea for Serendipity Space began when CEO and Co-Founder Antariksh Parichha started looking into why patients receiving Keytruda, Merck’s blockbuster cancer drug, had to spend four to five hours in hospital for each treatment. He discovered that the drug’s intravenous delivery was partly behind the long hospital stays and began exploring research into making it easier to administer.

Merck explored a subcutaneous version of the drug, which let patients receive it through an injection rather than an intravenous infusion. But making that formulation required producing drug crystals with the right characteristics.

“I stumbled upon a paper in which they had tried to manufacture Keytruda in the International Space Station (ISS), and they got some stunning results,” Parichha says in an exclusive interview with AIM. The research showed that crystallising the drug in microgravity could help move it from an intravenous formulation towards a subcutaneous one.

The problem, however, was that most pharmaceutical research in space still depended on astronauts. Serendipity Space’s thesis was that humans themselves were one of the biggest bottlenecks.

“So the idea was naturally that at the root of the problems of why this has not happened at scale in space is the human,” Parichha says. The company therefore decided to build autonomous factories that could travel to space, manufacture the required drug material and return to Earth.

Serendipity Space raised its pre-seed round from Campus Fund in July 2025, although the company did not disclose the amount raised. The startup was founded by Parichha, Jivitesh Debata and Monica Ekal.

Parichha also recently met Prime Minister Narendra Modi along with other space startups. He said the Prime Minister quickly understood the company’s work.

The broader policy environment is also catching up, according to Parichha. He points to the government’s efforts through IN-SPACe to establish re-entry guidelines as an important step towards allowing private companies to bring spacecraft back to Indian soil.

The company’s argument is not simply that space offers a better laboratory. Parichha believes some pharmaceutical processes cannot be properly replicated on Earth.

On Earth, gravity causes sedimentation, convection and buoyancy during crystallisation. Those forces can create defects and variations in the resulting crystals.

“Once you actually switch these things off, you end up getting much better drug crystals,” he says.

According to Parichha, laboratory equipment can reproduce many high-gravity conditions, but cannot create the sustained microgravity needed for the company’s target applications. For drugs such as cancer treatments and chronic-pain medicines, he says the meaningful change occurs at roughly the microgravity level, below what can practically be achieved on Earth.

The pharmaceutical opportunity is particularly interesting because crystal quality affects how drugs can be formulated and administered.

In microgravity, Serendipity Space expects to produce a much more uniform particle-size distribution. On Earth, a batch could contain crystals ranging from roughly 50–500 microns. In microgravity, the company expects the crystals to converge towards a much narrower size range.

“That has a good effect for two reasons,” Parichha says. Uniform crystal sizes are important for drug approval because different particle sizes can affect dosage. They can also reduce viscosity, potentially making formulations easier to inject subcutaneously.

The company recently tested its Alchemy system during a near-space mission using a stratospheric balloon launched from the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) Balloon Facility in Hyderabad.

The flight tested the spacecraft’s core subsystems under conditions closer to those expected in space.

The prototype included heat-shield systems, deployment systems, avionics, telemetry and the pharmaceutical factory. Serendipity Space also placed commercial therapeutics on board, including proteins, small molecules and monoclonal antibody therapeutics.

The crystals produced during the mission were recovered after landing and analysed in the company’s laboratory. “We basically harvested the crystals out, and we analysed them in our labs, and they’re fine,” Parichha says.

The mission also demonstrated that the company could remotely control the factory through telemetry and telecommand, including changing temperatures, mixing rates and crystallisation rates during the flight. It also tested communications, materials, parachute deployment and soft-landing systems.

However, Parichha says a balloon-drop experiment can provide only a short period of free fall. It cannot reproduce the sustained microgravity of an orbital mission, where pharmaceutical crystallisation could continue for days or weeks.

The next step, he says, is to operate the system in orbit for much longer periods required for pharmaceutical processes.

Microgravity research has been conducted for decades on the International Space Station across pharmaceuticals, fibre optics, semiconductors, metals and other materials. But Parichha believes not every space-manufacturing application makes economic sense.

The first commercially successful applications, he argues, need to involve products with an extremely high value per kilogramme.

“If you manufacture something in space, it has to have economic returns which are actually very high,” he says. Compared with semiconductors and metals, pharmaceuticals have a much higher dollar-per-kilogramme value, making them a more natural starting point for in-space manufacturing.

The economics of reaching orbit have also changed. Parichha said launch costs that were around 20,000–25,000 per kilogramme 10 to 15 years ago have fallen to roughly 3,000–5,000 per kilogramme.

That decline, combined with growing pharmaceutical interest in microgravity research, convinced him that the timing was finally right. Over the past four to five years, several pharmaceutical companies have repeatedly sent drug candidates to the ISS for crystallisation experiments, according to Parichha.

Serendipity Space is developing what Parichha describes as an autonomous factory capable of operating without human intervention in orbit.

The system has to monitor the crystallisation process, determine what is being produced and control the manufacturing conditions remotely.

The company is approaching the problem through redundancy and passive design.

“If one fails, the other can take over, and we can have the process continuing as well,” Parichha says, describing the redundant systems being built into the payload.

The company is also trying to make the payload as passive as possible. Hence, even if sensors or electrical systems fail, the physical design should continue maintaining critical conditions such as temperature without requiring active intervention.

But autonomy is only one part of the engineering challenge.

A returning spacecraft can reach speeds of around Mach 25, generating temperatures of roughly 1,500–2,000°C. Serendipity Space has already tested whether the crystals can survive the acceleration forces associated with re-entry.

The company is now working to make its heat shields capable of withstanding these extreme temperatures.

Serendipity Space is working across both biologics and small-molecule drugs.

Parichha sees a particularly strong opportunity in biologics, including monoclonal antibodies. These drugs are notoriously difficult to crystallise on Earth, and even when crystals form, controlling the process can be difficult.

Microgravity could provide a way to control that process more precisely, potentially helping pharmaceutical companies develop formulations that can move from intravenous administration to subcutaneous injections.

That could reduce the time patients spend in hospitals while also lowering some of the costs associated with administering complex drugs.

The company is exploring formulations across cancer, psoriasis and other therapeutic areas where monoclonal antibody drugs are already widely used.

Parichha describes Serendipity Space as a formulation-development company.

Pharmaceutical companies have drug candidates that can encounter problems involving solubility, bioavailability and other properties before reaching clinical trials. Serendipity Space wants to give those companies access to microgravity as another environment in which to develop and optimise their drugs.

“We actually end up almost acting like a Contract Research Organisation (CRO) or a Contract Development and Manufacturing Organisation (CDMO) would do,” Parichha says.

The company develops the crystallisation process on Earth, determines what can work in space and then takes it into orbit. Its business model is based on contracts to develop pharmaceutical formulations, with pharma companies in India and overseas as its initial customers.

Serendipity Space is also building the vehicle that carries the factory into orbit and brings it back.

There are currently no readily available autonomous orbital factories that Serendipity Space can simply lease on the cadence it needs. “We can't rent a commodity that doesn’t exist,” Parichha says.

The ISS offers access to microgravity, but repeated access and the limited cadence do not solve the company’s core manufacturing problem.

The company wants to control the entire chain, from crystallisation and formulation to the spacecraft, re-entry and recovery. “If we don't own the entire chain of this entire process, we also don’t end up capturing the entire value,” Parichha says.

Parichha believes India has a chance to lead one of the emerging segments of the space economy rather than trying to compete head-on in areas where the US already has a substantial lead.

He points to in-space manufacturing as one such opportunity.

“There are not a lot of companies doing this around the world,” he says, estimating that only four or five companies are seriously pursuing the area.

India also has the expertise needed for re-entry. According to Parichha, only four countries have successfully re-entered a space capsule and landed it safely, with India among them. Serendipity Space’s strategy is to combine that existing capability with a new commercial application.

The company wants India to go beyond building its own spacecraft and create an ecosystem in which foreign companies can also bring vehicles back to Indian soil. Parichha argues that such a policy could create a new market for testing, analysis, recovery and other services around re-entry.

Building a pharmaceutical factory for orbit might sound like an idea that would struggle to find investors. Parichha says the opposite happened.

He believes India’s venture capital ecosystem has become more willing to take risks on deep-tech companies since the country’s space sector was opened to private participation.

“I was expecting a lot of ridicule,” he says. Instead, investors treated the concept as a serious business proposition and wanted to understand how the company planned to execute it.

Parichha says India still needs more capital for deep-tech hardware because the US and Europe have far larger pools of funding available for companies that require years of engineering before reaching commercial scale.

Serendipity Space’s bet ultimately rests on a simple proposition that some medicines may be easier to manufacture when gravity is removed. If that works, the startup would not simply be sending experiments to space. It would be trying to make low Earth orbit part of the pharmaceutical supply chain.

And that, Parichha believes, could give India a chance to build an entirely new category of space manufacturing before the market becomes crowded.

title: $203,000 H-1B Visa Fee? New Proposal Adds to Trump’s Separate Payment
content:
US Department of Homeland Security proposes new $103,000 H-1B fee to recover immigration system costs

US employers could potentially face more than $200,000 in government charges to hire a foreign worker through the H-1B programme if a new Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposal takes effect, and President Donald Trump’s separate $100,000 H-1B payment requirement is reinstated.

The DHS has proposed a $103,265 fee for H-1B petitions subject to the annual visa cap.

The proposal explicitly states the new charge would be separate from any payment required under a presidential proclamation and that employers subject to both would have to pay both.

“To the extent a petitioner is subject both to a proclamation-required payment and to the additional H-1B fee proposed in this rule, the petitioner would be required to pay both amounts,” DHS said.

That would put the two charges at $203,265, before the other fees employers already pay when sponsoring an H-1B worker.

However, this fee is not in effect yet. DHS is accepting public comments before deciding whether to finalise the rule.

The proposed fee would apply to H-1B petitions competing for the annual 85,000-visa allocation—65,000 under the regular quota and 20,000 for workers with qualifying US master's degrees or higher.

It would not apply to cap-exempt H-1B filings, including certain petitions involving universities and qualifying research organisations.

DHS calculated the figure by identifying ~$8.7 billion in costs it says need to be recovered and dividing that amount among an estimated 85,000 fee-paying H-1B petitions.

The proposed revenue would go beyond processing H-1B applications, with DHS proposing allocations across agencies. This includes US Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Justice Department's immigration courts, the Department of Labor, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the State Department, and Customs and Border Protection.

The possibility of a combined bill depends on the fate of the separate $100,000 payment.

Trump introduced the $100,000 payment last September for certain new H-1B petitions involving workers outside the US. A federal court in Massachusetts later vacated the policy, and the administration appealed.

On July 24, the First Circuit declined to put that ruling on hold, leaving the $100,000 payment unenforceable while the appeal continues.

The new proposal comes alongside other changes to the H-1B system.

For the FY2027 H-1B selection process, DHS has replaced the previous random lottery with a wage-weighted system. The rule, which took effect in February 2026, gives higher-paid positions greater weight in the selection process while retaining eligibility across four wage levels.

The administration is also pursuing a separate change to the wages employers must offer H-1B workers.

In March, the Department of Labor proposed changing the methodology used to calculate prevailing wages for H-1B and several other foreign-worker programmes. The proposal would raise the wage levels used in those calculations, potentially increasing what employers would have to pay for some positions.

title: Vahan.ai Fine-Tunes Nemotron 3 Nano to Build Multilingual AI Recruiter
content:
The model was fine-tuned using Vahan.ai’s proprietary production dataset of human-corrected recruitment conversations in multiple languages.

Bengaluru-based startup Vahan.ai has fine-tuned NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Nano open model for its AI recruiter as the Indian recruitment platform works towards building specialised small language models (SLMs) for blue-collar hiring.

The company worked with NVIDIA technical experts through the NVIDIA Inception programme to optimise the model for multilingual recruitment conversations, function calling and recruitment-specific workflows.

Vahan.ai said the optimised model delivers nearly 6.7x faster time-to-first response and more than 3x lower average end-to-end response latency compared with its previous setup. The company also said the deployment reduces inference costs.

The model was fine-tuned using Vahan.ai’s proprietary production dataset of human-corrected recruitment conversations in multiple languages. The training focused on areas such as response correctness, language matching, human-like interactions, function calling and tool argument accuracy.

In benchmarking across seven recruitment-focused parameters, Vahan.ai said the fine-tuned Nemotron 3 Nano outperformed both the base Nemotron model and the 120-billion-parameter model previously used by the company through a cloud deployment. It also performed better on unseen recruitment conversations, according to the company.

Vahan.ai currently uses a voice-based AI recruiter that conducts conversations with job seekers in English and Hindi over phone calls. The platform handles tasks including job discovery, applications and interview scheduling.

The company plans to add support for eight more Indian languages. Vahan.ai said its platform has facilitated more than 1.5 million job placements across 920+ cities and connected nearly 50 million Indians with employment opportunities.

“At Vahan.ai, we're focused on building AI that is purpose-built for recruitment rather than relying solely on general-purpose language models,” said Madhav Krishna, founder and CEO of Vahan.ai.

“Working closely with the NVIDIA team in India has enabled us to optimise NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano for one of the most complex conversational AI challenges - multilingual recruitment at scale,” Krishna added.

The company plans to use the fine-tuning and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for developing specialised SLMs for recruitment. It will also use production conversations to continuously evaluate and improve its models.

Vahan.ai said the models will be deployed on India-based NVIDIA GPU cloud infrastructure, which it expects will further improve latency and reduce inference costs as it expands its multilingual recruiter.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
WazirX on August 24 announced the launch of WazirX AI, an AI-powered trading co-pilot that lets users research crypto markets, analyse their portfolios and prepare or execute trades through a single conversational interface.

The company said the tool is designed to reduce the time traders spend switching between charts, news feeds, signal groups and trading screens, with the entire research-to-trade workflow potentially completed in under 10 minutes.

“WazirX AI combines market research, portfolio monitoring and trade preparation into one conversation, reducing the time and effort required to evaluate an opportunity and act on it. The AI streamlines the workflow and enables a faster and easier decision-making process,” said Nischal Shetty, Founder, WazirX.

The AI agent is integrated into the WazirX app and website and follows an ‘Ask-Understand-Decide’ model. It coordinates market data, technical analysis, portfolio information and order management across multi-step requests, allowing users to move from identifying an opportunity to making a trading decision within the same conversation.

Users can ask WazirX AI about live prices, market news and macroeconomic developments, with the assistant providing summaries and supporting charts. It can also generate live portfolio briefings covering portfolio value, profit and loss and open positions, including daily morning updates.

The assistant can prepare trades directly within the chat. Before placing an order, WazirX AI displays an approval card and can recommend position sizes based on a user’s risk preferences. It supports both spot and futures trading, including limit and market orders, short positions and pair-specific leverage limits.

Users can also set alerts using natural-language instructions.

The company said the tool can also handle more complex workflows.

A user could ask WazirX AI to screen INR futures for four-hour momentum, filter opportunities based on a specified risk-reward threshold, validate the shortlist across multiple timeframes and prepare an order containing the entry price, leverage, margin, stop-loss, take-profit and estimated loss.

Alongside the AI co-pilot, WazirX is launching a Paper Trading Sandbox, giving every user a simulated $100,000 balance. The sandbox allows users to test the research-to-trade workflow and experiment with strategies without using real funds.

WazirX said WazirX AI uses live WazirX price data and supports real-time price updates. The product has been rolled out across Android, iOS and Web, while the $100,000 paper-trading sandbox is available to all users.

The launch marks a shift towards conversational interfaces for crypto trading, bringing market research, portfolio monitoring, risk assessment and trade preparation into a single workflow rather than requiring traders to do each task separately.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke has built and open-sourced a Git server over a weekend after becoming frustrated with the company’s internal Git infrastructure.

The resulting project, called ‘walgit’, is a single Rust binary designed to run in front of an S3-compatible object store without requiring a separate database.

Lütke said on X that Cursor’s recent “Git at any scale” post prompted the project. “It came right when I was frustrated with Shopify’s internal git system,” he wrote, describing the implementation as an exercise that he completed over the weekend.

Cursor’s system, called Continuity, uses a write-ahead log (WAL) stored in S3-compatible object storage as the source of truth for Git repositories. Local repositories remain on fast NVMe drives for Git operations, but are treated as rebuildable caches rather than authoritative copies.

Continuity removes the need to maintain a fixed location for each repository or a relational database to track those locations. Any server can reconstruct a repository from the WAL when needed.

Lütke’s walgit follows the same basic architecture. Its repository describes it as a Git server with “no database, no leader and no local state that matters”, with the object-store bucket serving as the repository and local machines acting as caches.

A deployment can point the binary to an S3 or Google Cloud Storage bucket, and multiple server instances can use the same underlying store.

The system uses a WAL and compare-and-swap (CAS) operations to publish repository changes. A push is uploaded to object storage and becomes visible only after the repository manifest updates successfully. This lets multiple instances operate against the same repository without a leader or a conventional coordination database.

Walgit also addresses the storage and download challenges of very large repositories. It supports Git’s bundle-uri mechanism, allowing large repositories to be distributed as chains of static bundles stored in the object store or delivered through a content delivery network (CDN).

Lütke specifically said this makes large repositories such as Shopify’s monorepo “very fast to download”.

The project also includes smart HTTP support, Git LFS, a web interface, JSON API, webhooks, repository-level push policies and OpenID Connect authentication.

It can keep commits and trees locally while reading large blob data remotely through HTTP range requests, allowing repositories larger than the machine hosting the Git server.

The repository is MIT-licensed and is currently almost entirely written in Rust.

content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman accepted that he was wrong about how quickly AI would disrupt software businesses, acknowledging that he and other industry leaders had been “too ambitious on timelines.”

Altman made the comments in a recent podcast with entrepreneur and investor David Senra.

He had expected the release of GPT-4 in 2023 to trigger much faster disruption across the software industry, with established businesses becoming vulnerable to AI-powered alternatives almost immediately.

“I think I was wrong about a few things, but one in terms of the speed: the economy just has so much inertia,” Altman said.

Altman observed that people and companies tend to continue using the products and workflows they already know even as new technology becomes available. That lag, he argued, means the economic effects of increasingly capable AI will unfold more gradually than he previously expected.

“People keep doing the same things, buying from the same company….wanting to use their tools the same way,” he said.

Altman also pointed to his own habits as an example of how difficult it can be to change the way people work with technology. He said he still uses computers in many of the same ways he has for years, arguing that “changing behaviour is just much harder than the tech nerds realise.”

He said the slower pace of adoption could ultimately be beneficial, describing it as “a positive in many ways” that would make the transition “go smoother and slower.”

“But I think it means we've all been too ambitious on timelines,” Altman said. “Society and the economy will adapt more slowly.”

OpenAI has already confidentially filed for a US IPO, although the company has not set a listing date or disclosed the size of the offering. Reports suggest that OpenAI is targeting a valuation of up to $1 trillion, while CFO Sarah Friar has indicated internally that 2027 is the likely timeframe.

The company has also said the listing may be a while away because some initiatives are easier to pursue while OpenAI remains private.

Friar said in April that OpenAI plans to reserve a portion of its IPO shares for retail investors, potentially giving individual investors direct access to the listing rather than allocating the offering primarily to institutions.

content:
Y Combinator Co-Founder Paul Graham and AI researcher Yann LeCun have offered contrasting answers to a question about what they would do if they were 17 today.

Graham said he would focus on learning to build and train large language models. LeCun, meanwhile, said he would look beyond LLMs towards AI systems that can understand and perform physical tasks.

Graham added that he would use his teenage years to develop a deep understanding of LLMs rather than immediately trying to build a startup.

“Someone asked what I’d do if I were 17. I’d learn how to build LLMs from scratch, and then train ones as powerful as I could with whatever hardware I could get access to,” Graham wrote on X.

He followed that by explaining why he would not prioritise entrepreneurship at that age.

“Notice that what I would not do is try to start a startup,” Graham wrote. “Instead I'd build the foundation of knowledge to base a startup on later.”

Graham argued that understanding the underlying technology would be more valuable than trying to identify a business opportunity without that technical foundation.

“Way better startup ideas would grow out of understanding LLMs deeply than trying to start companies based on what I knew at 17,” he added.

Meanwhile, LeCun wants AI to move beyond language

He took a different approach, focusing on one of the limitations of current AI systems. Responding to Graham, he said he would investigate why LLMs can perform language-based tasks but struggle with basic interactions with the physical world.

“I would try to figure out why LLMs can write my essays but not clean my bedroom,” LeCun wrote. “I’ll figure out a set of methods and architectures beyond LLMs that can quickly learn to perform physical tasks as efficiently as humans and animals.”

LeCun added that this would remain his focus regardless of age, saying it is what he would do “if I were 30, 40, 50, or 66 years old”.

The comment comes as LeCun is building a company around that same idea.

He co-founded Advanced Machine Intelligence, or AMI Labs, after leaving Meta in late 2025. The Paris-based startup is developing world models that are intended to understand the real world, retain memory, reason and plan.

AMI Labs raised $1.03 billion in March at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation. The round was led by Cathay Innovation, Greycroft, Hiro Capital, HV Capital and Bezos Expeditions, with other investors including NVIDIA and Samsung.

The company’s approach is based in part on LeCun’s Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, or JEPA, which seeks to make AI learn representations of the world and predict how it will change rather than simply predict the next piece of text.

AMI CEO Alexandre LeBrun has said the company wants its systems to work with robotics, manufacturing and other industries that operate in the physical world.

He has also described LLMs and world models as complementary, with language models handling language while world models provide an understanding of physical environments.

NVIDIA is in discussions to invest in Perplexity AI as part of a multibillion-dollar funding round that would value the AI startup at more than $30 billion, according to a report by The Information.

The proposed valuation would represent an increase of more than 50% from Perplexity’s last financing, which valued the company at $20 billion in 2025. The talks come as Perplexity’s annualised revenue has surged to more than $750 million, up from less than $250 million at the start of the year.

A significant part of that growth has come from Perplexity Computer, an AI agent that can automate computer-based tasks for professionals. The product has expanded Perplexity beyond its original AI-powered search engine and into the growing market for agentic software.

The proposed equity investment reportedly follows earlier discussions in which NVIDIA considered paying Perplexity billions of dollars to license some of its technology and hire some of its employees.

The talks are notable because NVIDIA has recently pursued similar arrangements with AI startups as it expands beyond GPUs and works to strengthen its own AI software and model efforts.

Last week, NVIDIA agreed to pay $6 billion to license AI model-development software from Poolside and planned to offer jobs to 109 of the startup’s employees, according to The Wall Street Journal. NVIDIA is also investing $1 billion in Poolside at a $12 billion pre-money valuation.

NVIDIA has struck similar licensing and hiring deals with AI inference chip startup Groq and networking company Enfabrica over the past year.

Perplexity has said it plans to use NVIDIA’s Vera CPUs to run agentic AI queries. NVIDIA launched Vera in March as a processor built specifically for agentic AI workloads, including inference, reinforcement learning and data processing.

Perplexity also entered a multiyear agreement with NVIDIA-backed CoreWeave in March to run its AI inference workloads on CoreWeave’s cloud infrastructure.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has also said he uses Perplexity as his go-to chatbot.

NVIDIA has already invested in Perplexity multiple times, with the startup raising more than $1.7 billion from NVIDIA and other investors including New Enterprise Associates, Accel and SoftBank Group.

The new funding could give Perplexity more capital to expand ahead of a potential public listing. CEO Aravind Srinivas told CNBC in June that Perplexity plans to go public in 2028 regardless of how the IPOs of AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic perform.

Perplexity has also expanded beyond search. Alongside its core search product and Perplexity Computer, it provides access to both open-source and proprietary AI models developed by other companies. The startup does not train its own foundation models from scratch; instead, it routes queries to different models depending on the task.

WATER, a Hyderabad-based physical AI company, has raised $2.5 million in a round led by Endiya Partners to build its adaptive-surface technology.

The round also saw participation from Pullela Gopichand, Chief National Badminton Coach of India; Rohit Chennamaneni, Co-founder of Darwinbox; and Nandan Reddy, Co-founder of Swiggy, among other angel investors.

The company will use the funding to support technical validation of VORTEX, its foundational model designed to sense, understand, and respond to the human body in real-time.

“Our thesis is simple: intelligence in the physical world should upgrade the human being at the centre of it,” Teja Vinukollu, Founder and CEO of WATER, said in a statement. “We call that layer Bio Physical Intelligence. The body is constantly telling the surfaces it lives on what it needs, and VORTEX is the first model built to listen and respond.”

Founded in 2024 by Teja Vinukollu and Haneesh Mourya Desu, WATER has developed VORTEX as the shared foundational model behind its two products—FLOW, an adaptive chair, and CAMA, an adaptive bed. FLOW focuses on posture, movement, and load during seated interaction, while CAMA focuses on sleep, recovery, and respiration.

The company said its approach combines sensing, decision-making and closed-loop physical actuation across multiple surfaces. VORTEX is engineered as a closed loop that can sense, model, actuate, and learn as it interacts with the human body.

WATER has already built a near-production-ready adaptive sleep system that was showcased at CES 2026. The company also said a foundational patent filing underpins its approach to safety for systems designed to act on the human body without disturbing it.

The company's longer-term vision is to extend its body-intelligence layer beyond individual products to adaptive environments. WATER said seating, sleep surfaces, and other physical systems could eventually respond dynamically to a person's needs, with potential applications extending into automotive and aviation.

“This isn’t a smarter chair or a smarter bed. It’s a genuine attempt to build a foundational model of how the human body interacts with the surfaces it lives on, and that’s a much bigger and more durable idea,” said Sateesh Andra, Managing Partner at Endiya Partners.

content:
Hugging Face is exploring a potential sale that could value the AI developer platform at more than $13 billion, according to a report by Business Insider, as growing adoption of open-source AI makes platforms that host and distribute models increasingly valuable.

The New York-based company is working with an investment bank to gauge interest from potential buyers, the report added. No deal has been reached, and Hugging Face could ultimately decide against a sale.

The reported valuation would be nearly three times Hugging Face’s last known valuation of $4.5 billion in 2023. Its investors include Lux Capital, Addition, and Salesforce Ventures.

AIM has reached out to Hugging Face but didn’t receive a response at the time of publishing.

Founded in 2016 by Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face started as a chatbot company before becoming a major hub for the open-source AI community.

Its platform allows developers and researchers to publish, discover, download, and collaborate on AI models, datasets, and applications. That makes Hugging Face different from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic: it does not need to build the single best model to benefit from the expansion of the AI ecosystem.

Hugging Face said in its 2026 State of Open Source report that it reached 13 million users, more than 2 million public models and over 500,000 public datasets in 2025, with users, model repositories, and dataset repositories all close to doubling.

The platform continues to grow. A Hugging Face community analysis published on August 18, 2026, said the Hub officially crossed 3 million public models.

That growth gives a potential acquirer access to one of the largest repositories of open AI models and datasets, along with the developers building around them.

The reported sale discussions come as investors and technology companies place greater value on infrastructure surrounding AI models.

Stripe’s recent $8 billion acquisition of OpenRouter also highlights the growing value of platforms that connect developers with AI models. OpenRouter gives applications access to models from multiple providers.

Hugging Face occupies a different part of the stack, but the underlying thesis is similar. Companies that help developers find, build, run, and distribute AI models can become valuable even if they do not train a frontier model themselves.

The company has also recently become central to a high-profile AI security incident.

In July, an OpenAI AI agent conducting a controlled cybersecurity test escaped its intended environment and tried to breach Hugging Face.

The incident highlighted how deeply Hugging Face has become part of the infrastructure AI developers and agents use, while also raising questions about how increasingly capable AI systems should be tested in environments connected to real-world services.

title: Anthropic Asks Job Candidates Whether AI Safety Comes Before Stock Value: Report
content:
The question was a part of Anthropic’s culture interview, which all candidates go through with an employee selected to conduct it.

Anthropic is asking job candidates whether they would prioritise the company’s AI-safety mission over its financial value, including how they would respond if a safety decision eventually caused the company’s stock to fall to zero, according to Axios.

The question is reportedly part of Anthropic’s culture interview, which all candidates go through with an employee nominated to conduct it, the report said, citing people familiar with the process and an applicant who spoke anonymously.

One candidate recalled being asked how they would feel if Anthropic abandoned its AI ambitions for safety reasons and the decision sent the company’s stock to zero. Other candidates have described the question more generally as a discussion about safety decisions that could affect revenue or shareholder value.

However, a former Anthropic employee familiar with the process and cited in the report says the culture interview is not fully scripted.

Interviewers receive suggested questions, but can vary how they approach them. Candidates are also asked about a moral quandary they have faced and how they handled it.

A Bloomberg report published in May also examined Anthropic’s unusually intensive hiring approach.

The company’s culture interviews are designed to probe candidates beyond technical ability, with applicants asked to discuss their personal values, worldview and how they have handled difficult moral questions. The process is intended to assess how candidates reason through ambiguous situations rather than whether they can produce polished, rehearsed responses.

According to reports, Anthropic has around 4,000 employees, and its careers page lists hundreds of open roles across research, engineering, sales, security, and other functions.

title: ‘AI Slop’ on LinkedIn Gets 40% Fewer Views, Confirms Company
content:
The ‘Seems like AI slop’ button has been used by over a million users to flag what they believe could be AI-generated content on the platform.

LinkedIn members are now seeing 40% fewer posts that the platform classifies as ‘AI slop’, Chief Product Officer Hari Srinivasan said in a post on the professional networking platform. He added that more than one million users have clicked the platform’s ‘Seems like AI slop’ option since it launched a few weeks ago.

LinkedIn introduced the feedback tool in late July, allowing users to flag posts and comments they believe are low-quality or overly AI-generated. The option appears in the three-dot menu on posts and comments. When selected, LinkedIn removes the content from the reporting user’s feed and receives the feedback.

The company said it combines this feedback with other signals and its own detection systems rather than using individual reports to determine distribution.

Srinivasan said LinkedIn has also added safeguards to prevent individual feedback from being used to unfairly target other members. “If a post receives enough community feedback, you may see a message in your Post Analytics to help you understand how your content is being received.”

The feature is intended to show creators when their content is receiving substantial negative feedback from the community. The move comes as AI-generated content has become increasingly common on LinkedIn.

In July, AI content detection company Pangram found in an analysis that 41% of LinkedIn posts longer than 250 words were flagged as fully AI-generated, while 30% of posts between 50 and 250 words were flagged as fully AI-generated.

LinkedIn has been taking several measures to reduce low-quality and automated content on the platform. The company said it is improving its automation defences, reducing the distribution of generic content and developing classifiers to identify AI slop.

LinkedIn said it was catching hundreds of thousands of automated comment attempts every day and had blocked billions of other automation attempts in recent months.

The company has also targeted fake engagement and other forms of automated activity that can artificially increase content distribution.

As part of the same push, LinkedIn announced recently that it was removing its ‘Enhance your post’ feature.

The tool used AI to rewrite users’ posts and messages. LinkedIn said it would instead offer a proofreading feature designed to preserve the user’s original voice.

“AI slop is a top priority for all of us,” Srinivasan said. “People come to LinkedIn to connect with real people and share their real perspectives, ideas and expertise.”
