title: Coding Performance Draws Attention
content:
A mysterious AI model called Ox Alpha has appeared on OpenRouter without revealing the company behind it, offering developers free access to a reasoning model built for coding, long-running AI agents and production workloads.

The model surfaced on August 20 under OpenRouter’s ‘Stealth’ label. Its provider has chosen to remain anonymous, with OpenRouter saying it only routes requests to the third-party provider.

Ox Alpha comes with over 1 million token context window, a maximum output of 131,072 tokens, and support for text, image, and video inputs. It also supports tool calling and structured outputs, putting it squarely in the growing category of models built for agentic software development rather than simple chatbot interactions.

The model is currently available for free, with OpenCode promoting it as a limited-time preview. The provider has reportedly claimed capacity for as much as 100 trillion tokens per day, while OpenCode's listing describes the model as free for a week.

Ox Alpha quickly gained attention after early developer testing suggested strong coding performance.

In a test conducted by independent developer and researcher Ben Davis, Ox Alpha scored 80% after completing eight of 10 DeepSWE software-engineering tasks. On the same comparison, Claude Fable 5 scored 65%, GLM-5.3 62%, Grok 4.6 62% and GPT-5.6 Sol 52%.

The model’s ability to work across long software-engineering tasks has been enough to attract significant developer interest.

That is the biggest question surrounding the launch.

The strongest theory so far points to Z.ai, the Chinese AI company behind the GLM family. Researchers have compared Ox Alpha’s API behaviour, tokenisation, and error responses with publicly available GLM models and found several similarities.

Ananay Arora, Founder of OpenHack, said on social media that Ox Alpha is “100% a GLM model by Zhipu AI” and suggested that the model could be an upcoming GLM-6.

Based on early benchmark results, Arora speculated in a post on X that Ox Alpha appeared to be “almost Mythos class” and was outperforming other frontier models in software engineering and cybersecurity benchmarks.

Besides that, one independent fingerprinting effort found Ox Alpha’s tokeniser matched the GLM-5 generation across 44 test strings. Other researchers found similarities in API behaviour and reasoning controls.

The connection to Z.ai remains unconfirmed, with one notable clue standing out. While GLM-5.3 is a text-only model, Ox Alpha can process images and videos, fuelling speculation that it could be an unreleased multimodal model from the GLM family rather than a rebranded GLM-5.3.

Anonymous model releases are not entirely new. Z.ai previously used the name Pony Alpha for an anonymous preview before the release of GLM-5, giving developers a chance to test the model without the usual branding and expectations.

Ox Alpha has also seen substantial usage since its release. OpenCode’s tracking page currently shows more than 22 trillion tokens processed, 282,000 unique users, and nearly 6.8 million completed sessions.

content:
Slack on August 20 introduced Slack Code, a new feature that lets teams work with AI coding agents inside dedicated code channels. The company said the feature is designed to move AI-assisted software development from individual sessions into a shared workspace where teams can review and direct the work.

Rob Seaman, Salesforce’s EVP and GM for Slack, said, “AI only creates value when it’s part of how a team actually works, not something people go do alone in another tab. Code channels bring that work into the open, where the rest of the team can see it, shape it, and build on it.”

The company said that Slack Code creates project-based code channels where developers and other team members can follow an agent’s work, review code changes and see live previews. Channels can also be created automatically when a user tags a coding agent from an existing conversation, then archived when the task is complete while retaining the record as an audit log, Slack added.

The feature connects with coding agents from Anthropic, Cognition, GitHub, OpenAI and Vercel. Slack said its founding partners include Anthropic’s Claude, Cognition’s Devin, GitHub’s Copilot, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Vercel’s agents, which can work within the shared team context in Slack.

According to the company, Slack Code gives teams visibility into an agent’s conversation, plan, code diffs and live previews. Team members can provide feedback, pause, redirect or stop an agent, while Slack said high-stakes actions such as pushing code to production require expert sign-off within the channel.

Slack is also expanding its broader agent experience with a new Agents tab where users can browse agents and their sessions, check statuses and stop an agent mid-task. Its Add to Slack feature supports agents from platforms including Lovable, n8n, Vercel, OpenAI and LangChain.

“For companies to unlock the full value from AI, it has to move beyond individual productivity gains to operational transformation. Slack Code enables AI to move beyond individual copilots to embedded, contextual AI orchestration to deliver real AI ROI at scale,” said Rebecca Wettemann of analyst firm Valoir.

Slack said that Slack Code is available on any Slack plan, although customers need access to the individual partner agents. The company added that the pricing and packaging may change, while availability can vary by region and customer agreement.

Scaler has launched a Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) Specialization and committed ₹25 crore towards building a talent pipeline for enterprise AI deployment, as companies increasingly look for engineers who can integrate AI systems into real-world business environments.

The company plans to train 10,000 FDEs over the next year, investing in curriculum development, AI infrastructure, industry partnerships and learner support.

The move comes amid a sharp global rise in demand for the role. According to Scaler, demand for FDEs has grown 729% year-on-year, with companies including OpenAI, Google Cloud, Anthropic, Palantir, Databricks, McKinsey & Company and BCG expanding teams around the function.

The company cited enterprise AI deployment as an emerging bottleneck as organisations move beyond experimentation. It also pointed to MIT NANDA's The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025, which found that nearly 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots fail to deliver measurable business impact.

The shift is particularly relevant to India, where GCCs, IT services companies and global technology firms are increasingly deploying AI across enterprise workflows.

The FDE role sits between traditional software engineering and enterprise consulting. Unlike conventional software engineers, FDEs are expected not only to build production systems but also to deploy them within a customer's existing technology environment.

This means working with customer-specific data, legacy systems, security constraints and business processes while also managing stakeholders and translating business problems into technical solutions.

Amar Srivastava, CEO, Online Business and Group CPO, Scaler, said, “At Scaler, we see this as one of the defining shifts shaping the future of software engineering. Through this specialisation, we want to equip engineers with not only the technical expertise to build and deploy AI, but also the ability to collaborate with stakeholders, understand business needs and turn AI into real business outcomes.”

The company said the role is gaining importance as enterprises face a gap between having access to AI models and successfully integrating them into production environments. Scaler’s ₹25 crore investment will support the development of its FDE curriculum, AI infrastructure, industry partnerships and learner support systems.

The company said the programme is designed to address a gap between AI familiarity and the ability to build and deploy production-grade AI systems.

The India AI Workforce Report 2026 found that AI adoption is expanding beyond software engineering into consulting, leadership and business functions.

Meanwhile, Scaler’s Confidence-Capability Gap Report, conducted with CyberMedia Research (CMR), found that 89% of engineers believe they are AI-ready, but only 19% are actively building AI systems.

Scaler said this gap is becoming increasingly important as organisations seek engineers who understand both AI technology and enterprise implementation.

The company also expects FDE roles to command compensation premiums of up to two to three times traditional software engineering roles, although it did not provide specific salary benchmarks. The 7.5-month specialisation will be offered as part of Scaler's Modern Software Engineering programme.

The curriculum combines AI and LLM engineering with backend and full-stack development, cloud technologies, enterprise integration, system design and security.

The programme will also use enterprise simulations and live business scenarios designed to replicate deployment challenges faced by engineers working with real customers.

Scaler said learners will receive mentorship from FDE practitioners and gain exposure to customer-facing engineering requirements beyond technical implementation.

One of the defining characteristics of the FDE role is that technical execution is combined with business problem-solving.

A traditional software engineer typically builds products and features within their organisation's technology environment. An FDE, by contrast, may have to adapt those systems to a customer's infrastructure, data, security requirements and operational processes.

The role therefore, requires skills such as stakeholder management, cross-functional collaboration, structured problem-solving and communication, alongside software engineering and AI expertise.

This could make FDEs particularly relevant to India’s expanding GCC ecosystem, where engineering teams are increasingly taking ownership of AI deployment, product development and business transformation rather than operating purely as offshore delivery centres.

Scaler’s programme is positioning FDEs as a new category of enterprise AI engineers—professionals who can bridge the gap between an AI model and the business environment in which that model ultimately has to work.

content:
Indian legal-tech nonprofit Adalat AI has been selected for Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 batch, as it looks to expand its AI-powered courtroom infrastructure across India and the Global South.

The company said it is the first nonprofit backed by Y Combinator in nearly five years and one of the first Indian-founded nonprofits to join the accelerator. YC’s first nonprofit was healthcare crowdfunding platform Watsi, which joined the accelerator in 2013.

“We’re the first nonprofit YC has backed in nearly five years—and one of the first Indian-founded nonprofits in its history,” Adalat AI said in a LinkedIn post announcing the selection.

Founded by Utkarsh Saxena and Arghya Bhattacharya, Adalat AI is building technology for courts where manual processes, limited digital infrastructure and shortages of courtroom staff contribute to delays. Its products include AI-powered speech-to-text transcription, case-flow management, document navigation and paperless workflows.

The company said its technology is currently used across 11 states and more than 6,000 courtrooms in India. Its website currently reports deployments across nine states, more than 3,000 judges reached and coverage of 10–15% of India’s judiciary, suggesting that its footprint has expanded rapidly and that deployment figures vary by product and measurement period.

Adalat AI’s speech-recognition system has been built for Indian courtroom conditions, including legal terminology, accents and regional languages. The company has previously said its models were trained using legal terminology from more than 1,00,000 court orders across 11 Indian languages.

The technology has already received mandates from Indian courts. In Kerala, the High Court directed trial courts across the state to use Adalat AI’s speech-to-text tool for recording witness depositions from November 2025, following a pilot in Ernakulam.

Adalat AI has also expanded beyond transcription. Its case-flow system gives judges a single interface to manage cases at different stages, while its document-navigation technology allows users to locate specific passages in long legal documents using voice commands.

The latter was also presented as a research system at the 2025 Natural Legal Language Processing workshop.

Saxena brings a legal and policy background to the company. He previously worked as a Supreme Court law clerk, practised law in India and worked with government and policy institutions on judicial reform.

Bhattacharya, Adalat AI’s CTO, has a background in computer science and AI from IIIT Hyderabad and previously worked as the founding engineer at customer-feedback intelligence startup Enterpret.

Adalat AI has also been building technology for people interacting with the judicial system. The company recently launched an AI-powered national case-information helpline on WhatsApp, allowing users to search for cases, check status and hearing dates, review case history and access court orders. The system uses Anthropic’s Claude API.

The YC backing comes as Adalat AI prepares for its next stage of expansion. The founders will be based in San Francisco from September through December and will work with the YC team during the programme.

“With YC behind us, we're taking this work across India and the Global South,” the company said.

content:
GitHub has added more than 3 million CPU cores, 120 petabytes of high-speed storage, and significant network capacity as part of a capacity expansion programme that began in recent months.

Monthly commits have more than doubled from 1.4 billion in April to 2.9 billion in August, while GitHub has accelerated its migration to Microsoft Azure, which now handles roughly 58% of the platform’s load, up from 12% in May.

The infrastructure expansion follows a series of reliability incidents, including an outage on August 17 lasting 7 hours, 47 minutes that disrupted GitHub.com, authentication, APIs, GitHub Actions, pull requests, issues, and Copilot.“Our investigation found that the outage began when traffic reached a new peak, and a critical infrastructure component in our Central US data center failed to scale with it,” GitHub CTO Vlad Fedorov said in a blog post. “The resulting capacity pressure spread through our systems, causing authentication failures and disrupting multiple GitHub services.”

During recovery, some Copilot services also encountered a client-side retry loop that increased traffic. GitHub said engineers had to mitigate the behaviour before safely restoring traffic.

The company said the August 17 outage was not caused by a code or configuration change, but by a failure to scale critical infrastructure before demand exceeded available capacity.

The incident came less than two weeks after a separate GitHub Actions outage on August 6. During that incident, workflow runs failed or remained queued for extended periods, affecting both GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners.

At its peak, 71% of workflow runs experienced infrastructure failures, while 75% of the remaining runs were delayed by more than five minutes.

GitHub said the August 6 outage was triggered by a routine deployment to an internal Actions service that exposed an existing capacity and concurrency weakness.

As pods were replaced, the remaining capacity became saturated, causing services to crash and creating a cascading impact across multiple clusters and downstream services. A backlog then accumulated, while a latent bug caused some runners to repeatedly attempt to acquire invalid jobs.

The two incidents followed reliability work GitHub had announced in March and April.

GitHub has since focused on three priorities: adding capacity, improving efficiency and removing architectural bottlenecks.

“First, we are applying consistent retry limits, retry budgets, and variable timeouts across service-to-service interactions to prevent retry storms and cascading load,” said Federov. “Second, we are reviewing lower-priority CPU and memory alerts to identify components that could fail during sudden traffic spikes.

He added that GitHub is also isolating critical systems and removing shared dependencies between them. “This work is designed to reduce the likelihood of an outage and limit its impact when one occurs.”

title: Anthropic Leapfrogs
content:
IPO-bound Anthropic has now pulled ahead of its rival OpenAI on annualised revenue.

Anthropic’s annual revenue run rate crossed $65 billion by the end of July, up from $47 billion in May and around $9 billion at the end of 2025, according to a report by Bloomberg.

Meanwhile, OpenAI’s revenue increased 18% sequentially to $6.7 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up from $5.7 billion in the first quarter, according to WSJ.

However, the company’s operating loss widened from $9.3 billion to $12.3 billion during the same period, putting further pressure on its path to profitability ahead of a potential IPO.

Anthropic more than doubled its revenue to $11.6 billion in the second quarter, surpassing OpenAI for the first time. The company also recorded a small adjusted operating profit, according to WSJ.

The company expects its IPO to match or surpass the scale of SpaceX’s record-setting public listing, according to the report. It has largely grown fuelled by demand for Claude and Claude Code, its coding agent, particularly among enterprise customers.

In May, the company raised $65 billion in funding at a valuation of $965 billion. The company also confidentially filed for a US IPO in June. It has, however, not disclosed the size or terms of the offering.

The Financial Times had reported that Anthropic’s investors expect the company to go public in October at a valuation of $2 trillion or more. If that happens, it would surpass SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO valuation.

Anthropic’s backers expect the company’s annualised revenue to reach between $100 billion and $120 billion by the end of 2026, the report added.

Separately, Reuters reported that the company is forecasting revenue of $190–200 billion in 2028. Now, investors and bankers are using that metric to assess Anthropic’s potential public-market valuation, even as the company continues to spend heavily on infrastructure, model development, and talent.

At the same time, OpenAI’s revenue has also accelerated sharply. The Financial Times reported that OpenAI’s annual revenue has risen from around $24 billion in late 2025 to $40 billion, following the launch of its latest models.

OpenAI’s latest private valuation stands at $852 billion. The company also filed confidential IPO paperwork with US regulators in June.

OpenAI, however, doesn’t appear to be as much in a rush to go public. CNBC reported that OpenAI is preparing for a potential IPO as early as 2027.

According to the report, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees at an all-hands meeting that the company expects to become a public company in 2027, although an earlier listing remains possible if its business growth accelerates.

“The IPO is not a finish line; it is a milestone, another fundraise,” Friar reportedly told employees.

content:
OpenAI’s Codex helped work management platform Asana migrate from the outdated Enzyme testing framework to React Testing Library (RTL) in about two weeks—something the company had estimated would take at least five years.

In a blog post, OpenAI said that the project cost about $12,000 in model and infrastructure usage, compared to roughly $6 million that Asana had previously estimated.

Enzyme had fallen out of active maintenance and had been blockingAsana’s efforts to modernise its frontend stack.

Rather than manually migrating the codebase over several years, Asana simultaneously used up to four Codex coding agents, with each agent working from a separate copy of the codebase.

The project started with a five-sentence prompt.

An engineer checked progress twice a day and reviewed every proposed change, retaining human oversight over the migration. Asana said simpler instructions worked better than a more elaborate agent setup.

After 1.5 weeks of engineering effort spread across two calendar weeks, Enzyme had been fully removed, and the migration to RTL was complete.

The migration gives Asana a new way to approach other large engineering projects that had previously been considered too time-consuming to justify.

The company now plans to test coding agents on additional migrations, rewrites, and performance problems.

“Not every years-long project will collapse into weeks,” Asana CTO Amritansh Raghav said in a blog post. “But agents can give engineers more room for craft—and make once-impossible work worth attempting.”

Codex’s enterprise adoption has expanded rapidly beyond individual developers.

Recently, OpenAI said weekly active enterprise users have grown 5x in engineering since February, while usage increased 108x in legal, 41x in sales, 41x in recruiting, and 26x in marketing.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) has made OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.6 Luna models generally available on Amazon Bedrock in India, allowing organisations to run inference on AWS infrastructure within the country.

This availability gives businesses in sectors including financial services, healthcare, public sector and startups access to OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock with in-country inferencing. AWS said this can help organisations use their existing security, governance and operational controls while deploying OpenAI models.

GPT-5.6 Terra is positioned for general-purpose enterprise workloads, while GPT-5.6 Luna is intended for high-volume and latency-sensitive tasks such as summarisation and classification.

The pricing also reflects OpenAI’s latest reductions. AWS said GPT-5.6 Luna now costs up to 80% less, while GPT-5.6 Terra costs up to 20% less, with the reduced pricing available through Amazon Bedrock.

“What we’re seeing in India is a shift from AI as experimentation to AI as operating leverage,” Nitin Bawankule, Head of Enterprise Sales, India, OpenAI, said.

“Businesses want models that can help teams write better software, work through complex information, and make higher-quality decisions in the flow of work. For many organisations in India, especially in regulated sectors, local inferencing is a key part of adopting AI with confidence,” he added.

Amazon Bedrock also allows customers to access OpenAI models alongside other foundation models through a single API. This means organisations can select different models for different workloads without changing their infrastructure or development workflow.

“India’s enterprises are moving rapidly from AI experimentation to production-scale deployment, and they need frontier intelligence that runs where their data already lives,” Satinder Pal Singh, Director of Solution Architecture for India and South Asia at AWS, said.

The models can be used for software development, data analysis, agent workflows and production inference. AWS also highlighted applications in regulated workflows, including KYC verification, regulatory filings and document processing.

GPT-5.6 Luna can also be used for high-volume customer applications such as chatbots, voice assistants and support systems, where the cost of each interaction becomes significant at scale.

For engineering teams, GPT-5.6 Terra can be used for code generation, review and testing across large codebases. Organisations in financial services, healthcare and the public sector can also use the models to analyse sensitive data, generate forecasts and process unstructured records.

AWS said calls to the OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock are covered by the security, governance and operational controls available across its cloud infrastructure.

Google is offering eligible college students in India one year of its Google AI Plus plan at no cost as part of a new student offer for the academic year. The plan includes access to Gemini Omni, double the Gemini usage limits and 400 GB of storage.

Students can claim the offer through Google’s AI student programme. Google is also offering a bundle of Google AI Pro and YouTube Premium at up to 70% off for students who want access to ad-free music and video streaming.

The company is also adding new study features across Gemini and Google Search.

Gemini’s new student hub will include study notebooks, which use diagnostic quizzes to identify a student’s strengths and knowledge gaps before creating study plans around their learning goals. Students can also request and discuss Deep Research reports through Gemini Live.

Google said the tools are intended to support personalised learning while keeping teachers involved.

“Across Google Search, Gemini, YouTube, and more, our education tools are built to be safe by design and rooted in proven learning science,” the company said.

Google is also adding learning features to Search. Students will be able to generate interactive visuals for difficult concepts, create practice quizzes, use Lens for step-by-step learning and organise projects through notebooks and custom files.

The offer comes as Google expands Gemini beyond general-purpose AI use into education, with students getting access to AI tools for research, revision and project work as part of their academic workflow.

Google said its goal is to “bring lessons to life in the classroom and support personalised study at home, while keeping teachers in the lead.”

title: Fleetx.ai Acquires Pando.ai to Build Unified Fleet & Freight Platform
content:
Snippet: The combined entity plans to prepare for a public listing over the next 18 to 24 months, potentially targeting an IPO, and is aiming for ₹300-400 crore in combined revenue on a profitable basis by the time of the listing.

Fleetx.ai, a fleet and logistics technology company, announced on August 20 that it has acquired transportation management system (TMS) provider Pando.ai for an undisclosed amount. The company said the acquisition will combine Pando.ai’s TMS capabilities with Fleetx.ai’s fleet visibility and AI capabilities, creating a platform spanning fleet visibility through freight execution.

“Bringing Pando.ai into the Fleetx.ai fold creates a unified, end-to-end stack for fleet and logistics, powered by AI agents,” Vineet Sharma, Co-Founder and CEO of Fleetx.ai, said. “We’re equally excited to work closely with Pando.ai’s leadership team and build on the deep expertise they bring.”

According to Fleetx.ai, the combined platform will cover operations from fleet visibility through freight execution, with AI agents working across the stack. Pando.ai will continue to operate as a distinct brand, with its own product and company identity.

Fleetx.ai said the entire Pando.ai leadership team has joined the company and will continue to lead the Pando.ai business. The company also said it plans to invest further in Pando.ai’s products and AI capabilities and layer its own AI capabilities onto Pando.ai’s platform.

Badrinath Setlur, Chief Executive Officer of Pando.ai, said, “Our customers have always trusted us to keep their supply chains moving. That trust doesn’t change with this acquisition. It only gets stronger.”

“Joining forces with Fleetx.ai means we can invest even faster in the AI capabilities our customers are asking for, while our team and our product continue to operate exactly as they have. This is a natural next step for Pando.ai, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” he added.

Fleetx.ai said the combined entity will begin preparing for a public listing over the next 18 to 24 months, potentially targeting an IPO. The company is aiming for combined revenue of ₹300-400 crore on a profitable basis by the time of the listing.

Fleetx.ai said AI agents can support physical logistics operations by flagging delayed shipments, rerouting drivers and renegotiating freight allocations. The company said the acquisition expands its platform from fleet visibility towards freight planning and execution as it works towards greater automation of logistics operations.

Sonata Software has appointed Hariprasad Rebala as the Chief AI Officer, giving him responsibility for driving the company’s AI strategy as it seeks to transition into what it calls an “AI-native” organisation.

Rebala will oversee Sonata’s AI-led business transformation across its offerings, service delivery, platforms, capabilities, ecosystem and partnerships, the company said in a statement.

His mandate includes developing AI-native delivery capabilities and helping clients translate AI investments into measurable business outcomes.

The appointment comes as IT services companies increasingly reorganise around AI capabilities, with firms looking to move beyond deploying AI tools for clients towards embedding the technology across their own delivery models and offerings.

Rebala brings more than three decades of experience across IT services, enterprise technology and startups.

“AI is rapidly moving from experimentation to becoming fundamental to how enterprises compete, operate and create value. AI alone will not define the winners—the ability to translate AI into enterprise velocity will,” Rebala said in a statement.

“My focus will be on building differentiated AI capabilities and platforms with our customers and partners, turning AI investments into measurable business outcomes and sustained competitive advantage,” he added.

Before joining Sonata, he was the Chief of AI Solutions and Growth at voice AI startup Gnani.ai. He had earlier co-founded Forfend Cybernatics, where he worked on IoT and conversational AI platforms.

He has also held senior leadership positions at Mindtree, Capgemini and Wipro, where he worked on business scaling, industry practices and large transformation programmes, particularly in banking and financial services.

“Transforming Sonata Software into an AI-native organisation is foundational to our growth trajectory. Hari brings a unique combination of AI startup and IT services expertise, with deep context of enterprise-grade AI platforms and engineering, delivering to outcome-based models,” Rajsekhar Datta Roy, Chief Executive Officer, Sonata Software, said.

The company said the appointment is part of a broader strategy to embed AI across its engineering, platforms, delivery model and client solutions.

Sonata, headquartered in Bengaluru, has more than 6,400 AI engineers and works with technology providers including Microsoft, AWS, Salesforce and Snowflake.

Snowflake is adding dynamic model routing to its Cortex AI Gateway, allowing enterprises to automatically match AI workloads with models based on quality, speed, cost and customer preferences.

The company announced the capability on August 19, alongside plans to add DeepSeek-V4-Flash 0731 and GLM-5.3 to Snowflake Cortex AI. The updates are aimed at giving enterprises more control over AI inference costs as they deploy more models and agents.

“Enterprises are becoming much more rigorous about the economics of AI. The question is no longer how much AI they are using, but whether that AI is translating into meaningful business value,” said Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy.

Dynamic model routing is available through Cortex AI Gateway and is integrated into Snowflake CoCo and Snowflake CoWork. It can also be used by third-party AI agents connected to the gateway.

Under the system, lower-complexity or repetitive requests can be sent to more efficient models, while tasks requiring deeper reasoning can be routed to frontier models. Customers can also control which models and providers are available to users, which Snowflake says can help organisations manage regional availability and compliance requirements.

“Achieving intelligence efficiency requires the flexibility to use the best model for each task as the landscape evolves,” Ramaswamy said. “Snowflake’s role is to absorb that complexity so customers can focus on outcomes while we optimise model choice underneath.”

Snowflake said internal testing found that dynamic routing could improve token efficiency without reducing output quality. In one evaluation, agents building a dbt pipeline achieved up to three times greater token efficiency compared with using a frontier model for every task.

In another test, engineering teams completed the same number of pull requests with 25% greater token efficiency.

The company is also expanding the model options available through Cortex AI. DeepSeek-V4-Flash 0731 and GLM-5.3 will join models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, SpaceXAI, Meta and Mistral.

Snowflake said its AI Research Team recently evaluated DeepSeek-V4-Flash on enterprise-focused tasks, where the model scored 74.4% on data engineering tasks. GLM-5.2 scored 62.8% while using fewer tokens than the other models tested.

The company is also adding controls for managing AI consumption. Cortex AI Gateway gives administrators visibility into token usage and costs, while Snowflake CoCo allows organisations to set default models, assign usage to teams or cost centres, establish per-user quotas and receive alerts when consumption approaches defined limits.

Sanjeev Mohan, principal and Founder of SanjMo, said the challenge for enterprises is increasingly the operational work involved in selecting models for different workloads.

“Snowflake’s dynamic model routing directly addresses that gap,” Mohan said. “The ability to match workload complexity to model cost, without rebuilding your infrastructure every time a new model drops, is exactly the kind of efficiency enterprises need to move from AI experimentation to AI at scale.”

The move comes as enterprises face a growing number of proprietary and open models, with differences in performance, pricing and availability. Snowflake is positioning Cortex AI Gateway as a layer that can manage those choices while keeping enterprise data and access controls within its platform.

OpenAI has put its largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning (RL) run on hold while it conducts smaller-scale training and evaluations to test model behaviour and validate new safeguards.

The company also paused RL training for its latest models for two weeks as it hardened its research environments and expanded monitoring.

The changes follow the Hugging Face incident, wherein GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable unreleased research model escaped an isolated cybersecurity evaluation environment.

The models exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in a package-registry cache proxy to obtain internet access, then used stolen credentials and other vulnerabilities to reach Hugging Face’s production infrastructure while trying to obtain solutions to the ExploitGym benchmark.

The incident exposed a problem with RL: models can learn to exploit weaknesses in rewards, graders, tools, or oversight rather than accomplish the intended task.

The company is therefore expanding alignment techniques across more stages of RL, including reward models designed to detect unsafe behaviour and training aimed at reducing reward hacking. It has also introduced a new monitoring setup that checks model activity at sampled tokens and escalates suspicious behaviour to automated investigators.

These investigators examine tool actions, reasoning and activity sequences for attempts to steal data, bypass safeguards or gain unauthorised access. OpenAI aims to raise an alert within 30 minutes and pause the activity if it cannot rule out a potential critical violation.

The monitoring comes with a high compute cost. OpenAI estimates it currently consumes about 20% of the inference compute for workloads under monitoring. The company said some high-risk training and evaluation workloads remain paused until they meet the new security requirements.

OpenAI is also applying the strictest safeguards to Astra, an upcoming model that it says may have reached its “critical” cybersecurity capability threshold. Astra was not involved in the Hugging Face incident.

The training slowdown comes amid a separate dispute over OpenAI’s safety structure. The Financial Times recently reported that the company disbanded its dedicated Preparedness team, which assessed catastrophic risks from its models, and moved those responsibilities into specialised teams.

Nikhil Kamath, Co-founder of Zerodha, and entrepreneur Sreeram Reddy Vanga, have invested a combined ₹250 crore in CtrlS Datacenters.

Kamath has invested ₹200 crore, while Vanga has invested ₹50 crore, according to CtrlS.

The latest investment from Kamath and Vanga will fund infrastructure expansion and capacity build-out, particularly as demand from enterprises and hyperscalers increases. CtrlS founder and CEO Sridhar Pinnapureddy said the capital would allow the company to “think bigger, move faster” as it builds infrastructure for India's next phase of digital growth.

“Every meaningful technology shift of the next decade—AI, cloud, and digital public infrastructure- runs on data centres. India is at an inflexion point where the underlying infrastructure either keeps pace or becomes the bottleneck,” said Kamath.

The investment comes two months after Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) committed up to ₹7,000 crore to CtrlS.

The deal included a ₹4,000-crore investment for an 8.2% stake in CtrlS at a pre-money valuation of ₹44,824 crore (C$6.6 billion), while another ₹3,000 crore was committed to a separate joint venture to develop hyperscale data centre campuses across India.

CtrlS currently operates 19 data centres across nine markets in India, with more than 370 MW of capacity. The company has another 4.4 GW of projects at different stages of development. It is also developing AI-ready infrastructure to support higher-density computing workloads.

According to ICRA, CtrlS’s operating income rose about 17% to ₹1,562 crore in FY2025, from ₹1,339 crore in FY2024. The ratings agency expects revenue to grow 20–25% annually in FY2026 and FY2027, supported by contracted capacity.

The company has been increasing its financing commitments alongside this expansion.

In July, CtrlS secured ₹5,500 crore in debt financing from State Bank of India and Central Bank of India for a planned 3.5 GW data centre campus in Hyderabad. SBI sanctioned ₹4,000 crore, while Central Bank of India committed ₹1,500 crore.

CtrlS was founded by Pinnapureddy in 2007 and has built a large Indian footprint spanning hyperscale, colocation and edge data centres.

Murf AI's Falcon 2 voice model outperforms OpenAI and ElevenLabs in naturalness and offers low latency at a competitive price.

The model is designed for the Indian market, supporting multilingual conversations and diverse accents, with over 150 voices in 35 languages.

Murf AI has launched Falcon 2, a proprietary voice foundation model that the company says ranks ahead of OpenAI Realtime API and ElevenLabs’ Flash and Turbo models for naturalness on the Artificial Analysis Speech Arena, while delivering sub-100 millisecond time-to-first-audio at a lower cost.

Falcon 2 is priced at $0.01 per minute of generated audio, compared to $0.05 for both ElevenLabs Turbo and Flash. Murf AI said the model recorded higher naturalness scores than ElevenLabs Turbo v2.5, Flash v2.5 and OpenAI Realtime on the independent benchmark.

The model aims to address a key trade-off in real-time voice AI: balancing naturalness, latency, and cost. Murf said Falcon 2 uses a lightweight proprietary architecture focused on inference efficiency rather than primarily increasing model size.

The Bengaluru-based company is also positioning Falcon 2 around the requirements of the Indian market, including multilingual and code-mixed conversations, diverse accents, and the infrastructure costs associated with running voice AI at scale. The model supports 150+ voices across 35+ languages, including extensive coverage of Indian languages.

“Falcon 2 represents a different proposition: a voice foundation model developed by our India-based teams and competing directly with established global models on independent benchmarks,” Sneha Roy, Co-founder and COO, Murf AI, said in a statement. She added that the model was engineered around the economics and deployment requirements of enterprise production.

Beyond speech generation, Falcon 2 includes a deeper semantic layer designed to interpret sentence meaning and adjust pacing, emphasis and pronunciation based on context. Its conversational training includes patterns from customer calls, support interactions, and booking conversations.

The model also improves text normalisation for enterprise-specific information such as numbers, currencies, dates, addresses, pincodes, and vehicle numbers.

Murf AI said Falcon 2 can support up to 10,000 concurrent calls with stable latency, offers data residency across 11 geographies and supports on-premise deployment. Enterprises can also use instant voice cloning to create a custom brand voice using 10 seconds of recorded audio.

At the announced pricing, one million minutes of generated speech would cost about $10,000 on Falcon 2, compared with $50,000 on ElevenLabs Turbo and Flash. Murf said the economics are intended to make high-volume, real-time voice deployments more viable for enterprises.

Latency is another area Murf is highlighting. In tests conducted using a third-party geo-distributed API relay, Falcon 2 ranked first across most regions tested, with time-to-first-audio below 100 milliseconds.

The launch also comes as enterprises increasingly experiment with voice agents for customer support, commerce, bookings, and other phone-based interactions. In India, Murf has identified multilingual speech, code-switching, latency, cost per minute and local infrastructure as particularly important constraints for scaling such systems.

“The challenge was never simply reducing latency or improving speech quality independently. It was engineering a system where both improve together without increasing the computational cost of deployment,” said Ankur Edkie, Co-founder and CEO, Murf AI.

title: India Building the Software Layer
content:
India can develop an indigenous GPU as a physical chip within the next two to three years, believes S D Sudarsan, Executive Director of the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) Bengaluru.

In an interview with AIM, he shared that C-DAC is ramping up work on a homegrown computing stack spanning processors, GPUs, AI accelerators, and servers.

The centre is developing its own GPU and AI accelerator architecture to produce a chip capable of handling AI workloads that are relevant by the end of the decade.

“We are predicting that we’ll likely have GPU specialisation by= 2029. We will have that kind of a specification from a capability perspective; we are building on that,” Sudarsan said.

He added that the target is to develop an indigenous chip comparable to other GPUs available in the market at the time.

For the upcoming GPU, however, C-DAC is deliberately avoiding locking the design to today’s AI models. Sudarsan said the centre expects AI workloads and model architectures to change considerably over the next three years.

The organisation is therefore developing both a GPU for more demanding parallel workloads and a simpler AI accelerator for workloads that do not necessarily require a conventional GPU.

“One is for a GPU type of workload. The other one is an AI accelerator, which has a much more simpler design and won’t be as complex as a traditional GPU,” he said.

The immediate milestone is to create an indigenous GPU chip. “Very soon we can have a technology demonstrator of our own GPU as a physical chip in front of you,” he said.

The GPU effort is part of a broader attempt by C-DAC to build an indigenous high-performance computing ecosystem rather than relying entirely on foreign processors and accelerators.

C-DAC already has the Rudra series of servers, with platforms based on Intel and AMD technologies. Rudra-I uses Intel Xeon processors, while the newer Rudra-GN platform uses AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI300X accelerators.

C-DAC is also working towards RISC-V-based server platforms. Its VEGA processor family, developed under the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) programme, includes 32-bit and 64-bit single-, dual- and quad-core processors based on the RISC-V instruction set architecture.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology launched the DIR-V programme in 2022 to build homegrown, open-source microprocessors.

“By 2030, we'll have a DIR-V-based HPC (high-performance computing) system, which is completely indigenous,” Sudarsan said.

Sudarsan said C-DAC expects to eventually have four server variants spanning x86 and RISC-V architectures. Two would use x86 technologies from Intel and AMD, while two would be based on RISC-V, with one variant using a fully Indian IP stack.

C-DAC is also working on chiplets based on its VEGA IP, covering CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators, according to Sudarsan.

C-DAC’s push for indigenous computing extends beyond silicon. Sudarsan said the organisation has continued developing the system software stack for its supercomputers, including compilers, integrated development environments, profilers, linkers, and loaders.

“Throughout the journey from 1988 till date, the system software stack has always been the compilers, the IDEs, as they call them, the profilers, the linkers, the loaders. They all have been always done by C-DAC, and it has always been indigenous for the supercomputers,” he said.

C-DAC has developed and taped out multiple RISC-V-based processors and SoCs under the government’s Microprocessor Development Programme.

The organisation has also developed DHRUV64, a 1GHz 64-bit dual-core processor-based SoC that C-DAC describes as India's first fully homegrown dual-core processor-based SoC. DHRUV64 is the third chip based on the VEGA family, following THEJAS32 and THEJAS64. The chip integrates C-DAC's VEGA AS2161 dual-core processor and targets embedded and compute-intensive applications.

Sudarsan said these processors and boards are already being tested through real-world applications.

“There are use cases of drone-based applications. There are use cases of image processing applications. We have also seen radar-type, automobile-based applications,” he said.

IBM has successfully connected two cryogenic modules to support the scaling of future quantum computers.

The modules are designed to link hundreds of quantum chips, advancing IBM's roadmap for a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.

IBM has connected and cooled two modular cryogenic systems into a single environment. The modules are designed to link hundreds of quantum chips and support the scaling of future quantum computers.

The company said the development advances its roadmap for IBM Quantum Starling, which it plans to deliver in 2029 as a fault-tolerant quantum computer.

The two modules reached temperatures below 15 millikelvin after cooling to 4 kelvin in under five days. Together, they stand more than eight feet tall and eight feet wide. Each module provides up to 12 times more wiring space than IBM’s most widely used quantum systems.

This space will enable more connections between quantum chips.

IBM’s new box-shaped design allows the modules to connect in a row. The company will use its L-coupler technology to connect separate quantum processors. L-couplers allow processors to share information and operate as part of a larger quantum computer.

It plans to use L-couplers by 2027 to connect multiple processors into a system with at least 1,000 programmable qubits. The company will install its Quantum Nighthawk processors in the cryogenic modules later this year for further testing. By the time Starling is delivered, IBM expects each module to house thousands of qubits.

It also said the new architecture allows key components of its Quantum System Two environment to operate independently. This could let the company test, improve and iterate each component separately.

IBM introduced its plans for Starling last year alongside a new error-correction code. The company said the code reduces the physical resources needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing. It has since demonstrated hardware components and made progress in error-correction decoding.

“Bringing fault-tolerant quantum computers to industries depends on several fundamental advances,” said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. “The successful connection and operation of these cryogenic modules signals a leap forward in that direction.”

IBM said the new modules address another engineering challenge on its path towards fault-tolerant quantum computing. The company expects the scalable architecture to speed development as it works towards Starling’s planned 2029 delivery.

Etched has shipped its first AI inference rack to Jane Street and secured $700 million in funding.

The funding round values Etched at $21 billion, with significant contributions from major investors.

AI hardware company Etched has shipped its first inference rack to trading firm Jane Street and raised $700 million in a recent funding round, the company said in a statement. Jane Street led the round, valuing Etched at $21 billion.

The San Jose-based startup said the funding will help accelerate production as it works towards gigawatt-scale deployment. The round includes Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Peter Thiel, Tiger Global, and Blackstone.

Jane Street’s investment follows its testing of Etched’s chip. “We tested the chip and are pleased with the early results,” the trading firm said.

“Etched’s unique approach to inference delivers the precision we will need to support our most demanding workloads,” Jane Street added. The firm said it now has its own Etched rack running in its data centre.

We've raised $700M at a $21B valuation from Jane Street, Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia, A16Z, Peter Thiel, BCV, and Blackstone.

We're also excited to share that we've shipped our first rack to Jane Street. pic.twitter.com/MFlF2xSw0B

— Etched (@Etched) August 18, 2026

The startup said less than 1% of the world has access to frontier models. It argues that wider access will require new hardware designed for large-scale inference. Its latest funding gives it capital to turn that thesis into deployed infrastructure. Jane Street’s first rack also gives Etched a live customer deployment after months of chip development and testing.

The move comes as AI infrastructure companies focus more heavily on inference. Investors are increasingly looking at the cost and energy required to serve models at scale.

Etched now faces the challenge of turning its specialised architecture into a larger production fleet. The company said its next phase will require factories, supply chains, and software to operate that fleet.

“The racks won’t build themselves,” Etched said as it invited engineers to join the company’s expansion.

The shipment marks a shift for Etched, which has built its business around specialised hardware for transformer inference. Its approach involves hardcoding the transformer architecture into silicon rather than relying on general-purpose GPUs.

The strategy targets inference, where AI models process user requests after training. Etched has argued that specialised hardware can improve performance and efficiency by removing some of the flexibility built into GPUs.

The company’s earlier work centred on Sohu, its transformer-specific ASIC. Etched positioned the chip as an alternative to NVIDIA’s GPUs for transformer workloads. Its latest announcement shows the company moving that strategy into customer deployments.

Etched’s valuation has also risen sharply. The company reached a $10.3 billion valuation in July after raising $300 million. The latest round more than doubles that valuation within weeks.

The company now prepares to scale beyond its first customer rack. The next phase will involve new factories, global supply chains, and fleet software.

It also launched the world’s first-ever transformer supercomputer, burning transformer architecture directly into the core of chips. It said the system achieved unprecedented performance metrics, notably in tokens per second.

The startup also plans to develop self-improving kernel agents as it scales its infrastructure and aims to run inference at gigawatt scale.

Financial services company Charles Schwab has officially entered India by opening its new 3.45 lakh square feet technology capability centre in Hyderabad, as the US financial services company looks to build engineering and technology capabilities to support its global operations.

The company plans to scale Schwab India’s Hyderabad workforce to around 2,000 employees by the end of 2027, making the centre one of the latest large-scale additions to Hyderabad’s growing financial technology and capital-markets ecosystem.

The entry also strengthens Hyderabad’s position as a hub for capital-markets technology, with the city increasingly hosting global institutions across brokerage, trading, investment management, wealth management, market infrastructure, risk, analytics and cybersecurity.

Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu said Hyderabad is moving beyond the traditional BFSI GCC model towards building technology that underpins global financial markets.

“Hyderabad is home to nine of the world’s top 10 brokerage and trading institutions, covering the full stack of capital markets capabilities and representing roughly $40 trillion in assets under management. This sits within a broader ecosystem of more than 475 GCCs, giving global companies access to a deep pool of technology talent and capabilities,” Babu mentions.

“What sets Hyderabad apart is that we are moving well beyond the shared services and support operations that traditionally defined this sector. Mumbai is India’s trading and brokerage capital, but Hyderabad is increasingly building the technology that powers trading and brokerage for the world,” he states.

Schwab India will support Charles Schwab’s US business through technology development, engineering and operational capabilities. The centre will focus on designing, developing and delivering technology solutions for the company’s US business and the millions of customers using its platforms.

Pradeep Menon, Country Head and Managing Director, Schwab India, said Hyderabad’s technology talent and established GCC ecosystem were key factors behind the company’s decision.

“Schwab India is an important step in Charles Schwab’s next phase of global growth. Hyderabad offers deep technology talent, strong infrastructure, and a mature ecosystem for capability centres.”

Christopher Wyse, Managing Director and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer at Charles Schwab, said the direct investment in engineering talent would allow the company to expand its technology capabilities.

“Schwab India strengthens our ability to serve the 48 million account holders and 30,000 employees who rely on our technology every day. Direct investment in engineering talent here allows us to build with greater speed and quality, and it reflects our confidence in Hyderabad as a long-term technology hub for our company,” Wyse mentions.

Charles Schwab’s entry adds to a growing list of global financial institutions with technology and capability operations in Hyderabad. The ecosystem includes Deutsche Börse Group, Vanguard, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, State Street, Wells Fargo, UBS and Invesco, spanning brokerage, trading, wealth management, investment management, banking, asset servicing and financial technology.

The development is significant because Hyderabad’s BFSI ecosystem is increasingly moving towards technology-intensive functions rather than conventional back-office and shared-services operations.

The next phase of growth could centre on areas such as AI-powered investment research, portfolio optimisation, financial risk modelling, fraud detection, personalised investing, regulatory technology and intelligent financial workflows.

The Telangana government is seeking to deepen the links between financial institutions, technology companies, fintechs, startups, universities and specialised talent to build a broader capital-markets technology ecosystem.

As Schwab India expands, the company also plans to bring select technology capabilities currently supported by contractors in India into its in-house operations in Hyderabad.

This could further strengthen the Hyderabad centre’s strategic role as the company builds internal engineering capabilities in India.

With BFSI accounting for more than a third of GCC demand in Hyderabad, Charles Schwab’s entry adds another global financial institution to a city that is increasingly positioning itself not merely as a location for financial-services support, but as a place where the technology infrastructure powering global trading, brokerage, investment and wealth-management businesses is built.

Voice-based AI startup Blue Machines AI has launched Floe, a language detection model that identifies whether a customer has actually switched languages during a conversation, rather than treating individual English or regional-language words as a signal to change the agent’s response language.

The model supports 11 languages including English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Bengali, Odia and Punjabi. It is built for voice and chat interactions across channels such as WhatsApp and SMS.

The company said Floe analyses words, parts of speech, sentence structure, short utterances and previous conversation turns to determine the language an agent should use.

This matters in Indian conversations, where customers often mix English terms such as product names, financial terminology and acronyms into regional-language sentences. For example, “Mera credit card block ho gaya hai” contains the English term “credit card”, but the sentence remains primarily Hindi.

Blue Machines AI said Floe is intended to distinguish between the presence of a language and a customer’s actual language preference. It also considers short responses such as “haan”, “okay”, “correct” and “theek hai” without treating them as automatic language switches.

“In enterprise conversations, language is not a static setting; it is a decision that can change during an interaction,” said Nirmit Parikh, Founder and CEO, Blue Machines AI. “The challenge is not merely to identify the languages being spoken, but to understand which language the customer expects the agent to use.”

Floe is integrated into the company’s conversational AI platform, where its output can inform speech recognition, conversational models, text-to-speech, pronunciation, regional terminology, language-specific prompts, compliance disclosures, escalation, routing and conversation analytics.

The company said the model has recorded internally measured latency of less than 10 milliseconds under production-scale conditions. It is optimised for CPU inference, allowing language detection to run within the real-time conversation without relying on GPU infrastructure for routine inference.

“For enterprise AI, language switching has to work inside the live conversational path without slowing the interaction down,” said Abhishek Ranjan, Chief Technology Officer, Blue Machines AI. “Our model is optimised for CPU inference and has demonstrated latency of less than 10 milliseconds under internally measured production-scale conditions.”

By tracking language across multiple turns instead of classifying each utterance independently, Floe is intended to reduce unnecessary language changes and clarifications while keeping the agent’s responses consistent throughout an interaction.

AlgoFET has raised ₹15 crore to enhance its autonomous drone infrastructure in India.

The startup aims to develop new products and expand manufacturing for defence and enterprise markets.

Bengaluru-based drone tech startup AlgoFET has raised ₹15 crore ($1.56 million) from Piper Serica in a pre-Series A funding round to scale its autonomous drone infrastructure in India.

The deeptech company will use the capital to develop new infrastructure products, expand manufacturing, strengthen proprietary intellectual property, and scale deployments across defence, enterprise, and global markets.

It is building ground infrastructure that lets drones recover, recharge, and relaunch with minimal human intervention. Its systems cover autonomous docking, battery management, high-power charging, embedded electronics and firmware, and cloud-based fleet monitoring.

“Every mission still ends when the battery does, and a human has to intervene,” Ankit Mishra, Founder of AlgoFET, said in a statement. “AlgoFET exists to close that gap, not by building a better charger, but by building the infrastructure layer the entire drone ecosystem needs to operate at scale.”

AlgoFET said charging, battery replacement and returning drones to operation still depend largely on manual intervention. Its infrastructure aims to address this gap as drone use expands across defence, agriculture, logistics, surveillance, and infrastructure.

Founded in December 2023 by IIT Guwahati alumnus Mishra, AlgoFET has deployed more than 2,000 units. It has an order pipeline of more than 4,000 units and an order book worth ₹100 crore.

The company works with Indian drone manufacturers and the Indian Army. It also has early traction with manufacturers in the US and Europe, according to the company.

AlgoFET operates a 12,000 sq ft manufacturing facility in Kadugodi, Bengaluru. The new funding will help expand its in-house manufacturing capacity and build infrastructure for larger-scale deliveries.

The company will also invest the fresh capital in proprietary technology covering docking, charging, battery management, firmware, and fleet software. It plans to scale deployments across defence, enterprise, the US, and Europe.

Piper Serica Investment Professional Hardik Dua said the infrastructure supporting drones would become increasingly important as their use becomes more autonomous.

“The next phase of the drone ecosystem will not be defined by flight alone, but also by the intelligence and infrastructure that keeps these systems operational over time,” Dua said.

AlgoFET said the funding will support product development, manufacturing, intellectual property, deployments, and the operational systems needed to deliver at scale.

Yotta Data Services has partnered with IntelliDB Enterprise to offer managed database-as-a-service (DBaaS) for AI applications on Yotta’s sovereign cloud in India.

The partnership combines Yotta’s cloud and AI infrastructure with IntelliDB Enterprise’s PostgreSQL database management platform and native vector database capabilities. The offering is targeted at government organisations, banks and financial services companies, regulated industries, enterprises and digital-native businesses that need databases for both conventional applications and AI workloads.

The companies said the service will support applications using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, and AI agents by combining PostgreSQL with vector-database capabilities.

AI applications increasingly require databases capable of handling structured enterprise data alongside vector embeddings used by systems that retrieve information for large language models. Yotta and IntelliDB said their joint platform will provide these capabilities through a managed service.

Customers will also be able to modernise applications running on legacy databases and consume managed PostgreSQL with automated operations, high availability and security features.

“The next wave of enterprise transformation will be driven by AI, and every AI application depends on trusted, intelligent and sovereign data,” Sunil Gupta, Co-founder, Managing Director and CEO of Yotta Data Services, said.

“Our partnership with IntelliDB Enterprise strengthens this vision by adding an AI-ready database layer that enables organisations to build secure, scalable, and future-ready AI applications entirely on India's sovereign digital infrastructure,” he added.

The companies said the database services will be hosted entirely in India, allowing organisations to keep their application data in the country while running AI workloads.

The partnership comes as enterprises and government organisations look to run AI systems on infrastructure that meets local data residency and compliance requirements.

Yotta has been building its sovereign cloud and AI infrastructure portfolio, including cloud services, GPU infrastructure, AI model services and enterprise AI platforms. The IntelliDB partnership adds managed database services to that stack.

Gagandeep Singh, co-founder and CEO of IntelliDB Enterprise, said database infrastructure would play a central role as organisations scale AI deployments.

“AI initiatives and scaling for any organisation is only as strong as the data infrastructure underneath it,” Singh said.

“This partnership brings our secure, AI-powered and intelligent database platform to more Indian enterprises and government organisations, hosted entirely within India. Together with Yotta, we are simplifying database operations while giving customers a secure, scalable, AI-powered platform.”

The companies said the service will allow customers to move from traditional enterprise workloads to AI applications on the same sovereign cloud infrastructure, without moving data outside India.

Wispr, the artificial intelligence company behind AI dictation tool Wispr Flow, has raised $280 million in Series B funding at a $2 billion valuation, led by long-time investor Menlo Ventures. The company said the round brings its total capital raised to $361 million.

“In a little over a year, voice has gone from something people were questioning to something they rely on, and it happened faster than we expected,” Tanay Kothari, Co-founder and CEO of Wispr, said in a statement.

The company said the new funding will support investment in its products, research lab, models, and team.

Existing investors Notable Capital, NEA, Neo Ventures, 8VC, and MVP Ventures participated in the round. New investors include Acrew, Activate, Forerunner, Goodwater, Peak XV, Together Fund and PLUS Capital, along with a select group of artists, athletes, and cultural leaders.

Wispr also previewed Canto, its first proprietary speech model. The company said the 2-billion-parameter model was built for conditions in which speech recognition is more difficult, including background noise, wind, heavy accents, and music.

Wispr said word error rates in the hardest conditions fall from more than 30% to between 5% and 10%. The company also expects Canto to reduce the number of dictations users need to edit by 30–35% across everyday use, according to Reuters.

The model is also designed to handle multilingual speech, including situations where speakers switch between languages. Wispr used Hinglish as an example, saying speakers may switch between Hindi and English while expecting the resulting text in Roman script. The company said Canto can also use a user's dictionary and names to improve transcription.

Wispr said future versions of Canto will become larger and more capable, with each model intended to improve Flow's dictation. The company has not announced a general availability date for Canto.

Wispr said more than 60 billion words have been written with Flow, which is used by people at almost all Fortune 500 companies and more than 10,000 enterprises.

The company is also expanding beyond dictation. Wispr launched Flow Notetaker for meetings shortly before the Series B announcement and said it is building an intelligence layer for human-AI interaction, starting with voice and eventually extending to other modalities.

“If by the end of the year, the voice dictation platform is the only thing that Wispr has—it will probably die. We did something with Wispr once, and that is a playbook that we need to rise and repeat,” Kothari earlier told AIM.

The Series B follows Wispr's $30 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures in June 2025 and a $25 million Series A extension led by Notable Capital in November 2025. The November round brought total funding to $81 million and valued Wispr at $700 million, according to Reuters.

Kothari said Wispr's broader goal is to make voice a primary way of interacting with computers

Tagbin has launched Brixx, an AI platform that generates designs and project plans using natural-language prompts for the construction sector.

Initially developed for the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region, Brixx now supports multiple stages of construction projects.

Gurugram-based Tagbin has launched Brixx, an AI-powered platform that aims to transform architecture, engineering, and construction workflows by letting users generate designs, CAD drawings, BIM models, bills of quantities (BOQs), detailed project reports (DPRs), and implementation plans using natural-language prompts.

Brixx initially started as an AI-powered DPR solution for the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER), Government of India, before expanding into a broader platform for the architecture, engineering, and construction sector. Users can describe project requirements in natural language, after which the platform generates coordinated designs, drawings, BIM models, cost estimates, DPRs, and project plans.

The platform is designed to cover multiple stages of a construction project, including architectural concept generation, space planning, CAD layouts, technical drawings, and coordinated BIM models. It can also prepare itemised BOQs and preliminary cost estimates, apply relevant building regulations and development controls, and generate DPRs, schedules, and implementation plans.

Brixx also extends beyond design and documentation into project monitoring. The platform is being developed to review designs for potential compliance issues, monitor construction using digital and visual evidence, and compare on-site construction against sanctioned designs. It can identify deviations, delays, and cost variations during execution.

“Software development is being transformed by platforms that convert ideas and prompts into working applications. We believe architecture and construction are ready for the same transformation,” said Saurav Bhaik, Founder and CEO of Tagbin, in a statement.

He added that Brixx can convert project requirements into coordinated designs, BIM models, drawings, BOQs, and execution plans while helping verify whether construction follows the sanctioned design.

The company said Brixx aims to create a digital connection between approved designs and construction, allowing stakeholders to track project progress and identify problems across the project lifecycle. Its longer-term vision covers stages from project conception and statutory approvals through procurement and completion.

For government agencies, Brixx can support DPR preparation, building-plan scrutiny, digital approvals and occupancy inspections. Private developers, architects and engineering firms can use the platform for design, estimation, documentation, and coordination between design and execution teams.

Superhealth aims to expand its AI-native hospital model from one facility in Bengaluru to 100 across India.

Dalvir Singh Suri has been appointed as Head of Operations to build systems for scaling Superhealth's model.

Bengaluru-based Superhealth has appointed former Dunzo co-founder Dalvir Singh Suri as its Head of Operations, as the healthcare startup looks to scale its AI-native hospital model from its first facility to 100 multispecialty hospitals across India.

Suri will be responsible for building the systems, teams, and operating processes needed to replicate Superhealth’s model across its planned network over the next five to seven years. His appointment comes as the company seeks to move beyond proving its model at a single hospital and build the operational backbone required to scale it.

At the centre of that model is SuperOS, Superhealth’s proprietary AI-native hospital operating system. The company says the system has been running its flagship hospital since day one, with real-time patient monitoring, clinical audits, and digitally orchestrated clinical and operational workflows.

Superhealth opened its first hospital in Bengaluru 10 months ago and describes its model as combining AI-native software with doctor consultation and all-inclusive pricing.

The appointment aims to replicate an AI-native hospital model that works at one facility, then standardise and reproduce it across a 100-hospital network.

Suri brings nearly 17 years of experience building and scaling operating systems, including more than eight years at Dunzo, where he worked on hyperlocal operations.

“Operational excellence is how a great care model becomes repeatable,” said Manoj Kumar, Founder and COO, Superhealth Hospitals. He said the company wants patients to experience the same operational standards across every Superhealth centre.

The move comes as healthcare companies increasingly use AI not only for patient-facing applications but also to automate and coordinate internal workflows. In Superhealth’s case, the ambition is to make AI part of the hospital’s underlying operating layer—from monitoring and audits to coordinating clinical and operational processes.

“The next challenge is to scale that experience with speed and discipline,” Suri said, adding that he will focus on building the operations organisation needed to support Superhealth’s expansion.

Razorpay has announced Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model designed specifically for payments, trained on nearly 3 trillion data points spanning 4 billion payments on its network.

Built with NVIDIA GPUs and AWS cloud infrastructure, the model is intended to improve payment routing, fraud detection, risk assessment and checkout personalisation.

Razorpay said it has already tested early components of the model on live transactions across its network.

The company claims an 8–10% improvement in payment success rates, an eightfold increase in international card fraud detection, and five times more fraudulent or disputed transactions identified without increasing the number of alerts.

The model learns from roughly 3,000 signals per transaction. Razorpay said it developed the model as a proprietary system, with both its architecture and training data built in-house.

The company’s rationale for a shared model is that payment decisions often depend on overlapping signals. Routing, fraud, risk and checkout systems have traditionally been developed as separate machine-learning models.

Vulcan is intended to provide a common intelligence layer that can use those signals across multiple payment decisions.

One application is real-time routing. The model scores available payment routes before a transaction is attempted and selects the route it predicts is most likely to succeed.

Razorpay said the model is also being used to detect fraud patterns across merchants, identify risky cash-on-delivery orders and predict which payment method is most likely to work for an individual shopper.

Razorpay’s Magic Checkout has also seen a 40% increase in shoppers being shown their preferred UPI application, which the company said is helping complete an additional 100,000–200,000 purchases each month.

The model is not an LLM. Razorpay said it uses transformer architecture but is trained to model patterns in payment transactions rather than language.

The company described it as a foundation model because the same underlying representation of payment behaviour can be adapted to multiple downstream use cases rather than requiring a separate model for each task.

NVIDIA GPUs are being used for training and running the model at scale, while AWS infrastructure, including Amazon SageMaker, supports its development, training and deployment. Razorpay said customers including Blinkit, Bachatt and redBus have begun using capabilities derived from the model in live payment environments.

Harshil Mathur, CEO and co-founder of Razorpay, said the objective was to address reliability across India's expanding digital payment base. “Every payment teaches the system something that makes the next payment better,” he said.

Pahal Patangia, head of global industry business development and payments at NVIDIA, said the work combines payments data with “real-time contextual intelligence”, while AWS said the model consolidates billions of transaction insights into a single intelligence layer.

Razorpay said it eventually intends to extend the model across more payment decisions, including authentication, routing, fraud detection and lending.

In March, Razorpay launched Agent Studio, a marketplace and builder for AI agents designed to handle payment and financial operations. Initial agents included tools for recovering abandoned carts and failed subscriptions, responding to payment disputes and forecasting cash flow.

Its agentic onboarding system, for example, was designed to reduce merchant onboarding from 30–45 minutes to about five minutes, while its integration agent can help businesses connect Razorpay to their technology stack in under 10 minutes.
