Apple expects memory costs to continue climbing beyond the September quarter, warning that the unprecedented surge in DRAM prices that recently forced it to raise hardware prices is unlikely to ease anytime soon, according to executives during the company’s third-quarter earnings call.

The comments come as Apple prepares to unveil its next-generation iPhone lineup in September, and is expected to announce its first major iPhone price increase in years—by as much as $200—as it grapples with higher component costs.

“We reluctantly raised prices,” Apple CEO Tim Cook said during the earnings call. “We did it because we're in what I would characterise as a 100-year flood on the memory pricing, with exponential increases in memory prices.”

While Apple has partially offset higher memory prices through earlier inventory purchases and lower costs for certain non-memory components, Cook warned those benefits would diminish over time.

“We have a benefit from some carry-in inventory in the September quarter. However, we believe we'll see decreasing benefit from this over time beyond the September quarter,” he said.

Looking beyond September, Cook said memory prices are expected to continue rising, which ‘could drive an increasing impact on our business.’

Apple also acknowledged that supply-side options remain limited because the global DRAM market is dominated by three suppliers. “Obviously if there were more suppliers, that would be good, and it would help us on the supply side and perhaps the pricing side. It’s unclear on the pricing side... We’re evaluating all options,” Cook added.

According to earlier reports from the Financial Times and Bloomberg, Apple has been evaluating DRAM chips from Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) for devices sold in China and has sought assurances from US officials that the company would not face future export restrictions.

CFO Kevan Parekh said memory inflation has become the single biggest driver of Apple’s margin pressure. He said more than the entire sequential decline in adjusted gross margin, from 48.1% in the June quarter to the midpoint of 46.5% expected in the September quarter, excluding tariff refunds, is explained by rising memory costs.

Despite those headwinds, Cook said Apple does not automatically pass higher component costs to consumers.

“It's not a mathematical formula,” he said. “We look at units, revenue, and margin, then come to a business judgment as to how to handle that. We think about it over the long term instead of a 90-day clock.”

Apple has already begun adjusting prices elsewhere in its portfolio.

Earlier this month, the company increased prices for Macs, iPads, and the MacBook Neo as component costs surged, making the latest earnings call the clearest indication yet that memory inflation has become a structural challenge rather than a temporary spike.

The company nevertheless reported its strongest June quarter on record.

Revenue rose 16% year-over-year to $109.4 billion, while diluted earnings per share increased 29% to $2.02. iPhone revenue climbed 22% to a record $54.3 billion, Mac revenue rose 29% to $10.4 billion, and Services revenue grew 12% to $30.7 billion.

Apple also said its installed base surpassed 2.5 billion active devices, another all-time high.

However, management forecast September-quarter revenue growth of 9–11%, below analyst expectations, citing worsening supply constraints and continued memory inflation.

Apple’s shares fell by as much as 6% during extended trading on July 30 amid lower revenue guidance. It had closed the session 1.41% lower after briefly touching the $5 trillion market cap earlier this week and surpassing NVIDIA to become the most valuable company.

Amazon raised its planned 2026 capital expenditure (CapEx) to $220 billion, up from an earlier estimate of about $200 billion, as demand for AI infrastructure continued to outpace available capacity.

The company said most of the spending will go towards AWS data centres, servers, networking equipment and AI infrastructure, while warning it still expects capacity constraints through 2026 and into 2027.

CEO Andy Jassy said the company now expects to spend more in cash CapEx this year because of “the higher cost of memory”, adding that “we will still not have enough capacity to meet all the demand we have in 2026”, a situation he expects to continue into 2027.

The investment plans accompanied another strong quarter for AWS, which generated $42.2 billion in revenue, up 36.7% year over year, marking its fastest growth rate in 18 quarters.

AWS operating income climbed to $16.6 billion, with operating margin expanding to 39.4% from 32.9% a year earlier.

AWS has now reached an annualised revenue run rate of $169 billion, while its backlog grew to $496 billion from $364 billion in the previous quarter, reflecting accelerating long-term enterprise commitments for cloud and AI infrastructure.

Jassy said Amazon now believes AWS can become “at least double” the scale it had previously envisioned.

“We’ve long believed AWS could become a few hundred billion dollars revenue business and now believe it will be at least double that and very possibly be a $1 trillion annual revenue business for us in time with very appealing accompanying free cash flow and return on invested capital.”

Amazon also said both its AI business and custom AI chip business have each surpassed $25 billion in annual revenue run rates, with both growing at triple-digit rates.

This year, Anthropic committed more than $100 billion over a decade for up to 5 GW of AWS capacity spanning multiple generations of Trainium chips to train and serve Claude models, while OpenAI expanded its AWS partnership with an additional $100 billion, eight-year agreement that includes approximately 2 GW of Trainium capacity for advanced AI workloads.

The company also revealed that its Graviton processors are now used by 98% of AWS’ top 1,000 EC2 customers, with revenue commitments nearly tripling quarter over quarter.

Following the first close of its $300 million Series B round led by HCLTech, Sarvam AI used its inaugural Epoch conference in Bengaluru to unveil a sweeping expansion of its AI stack, introducing new models, developer tools, enterprise products and infrastructure as it sharpened its positioning as a full-stack AI company rather than just a large language model provider.

The startup also reaffirmed that its previously announced one-trillion-parameter model remains under development and is expected within the next six months.

The company introduced upgrades to its Sarvam-105B reasoning model, Bulbul v4 for expressive multilingual text-to-speech, improved Saaras speech recognition models, and the latest version of Sarvam Vision for document understanding and OCR.

It also launched a managed model training service that enables enterprises to fine-tune foundation models on proprietary datasets with minimal code.

Beyond the foundation models, Sarvam also expanded into application-layer software. It introduced an AI coding assistant designed as a lower-cost alternative for software development. The company also launched Indus Work Agents, a platform for enterprise productivity and workflow automation.

Its Voice Agents platform, which was previously available only to enterprise customers, is now open to all developers. Sarvam further unveiled Kivi, a desktop voice dictation application, along with an AI dubbing system that can translate content across languages while preserving the original speaker’s voice.

Sarvam also unveiled an infrastructure service offering low-cost inference for large open models, allowing enterprises to run them with data residency in India.

To support that vision, Sarvam said it now operates around 2,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, which it described as one of the country’s largest Blackwell deployments, and plans to scale that to 10,000 GPUs.

The company said the infrastructure would allow Indian enterprises to deploy large open models while keeping customer data within the country.

The startup also revealed its enterprise momentum.

It said its voice agent platform has already processed over 325 million minutes of calls and announced pricing aimed at undercutting international AI providers.

Sarvam said more than 500 enterprises, startups and organisations are using its products today, with most of its revenue currently coming from the private sector.

Alongside commercial products, Sarvam demonstrated AI glasses ‘Kaze’ for visually impaired users, highlighted its work with the Odisha government to digitise land records using vision AI, and outlined plans for startup and university programmes to expand adoption of its platform.

Former xAI, Thinking Machines Lab and Mistral AI researcher Devendra Singh Chaplot has joined Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI as an advisor, as the startup steps up work on frontier AI models in India.

The startup announced the appointment during its Epoch AI conference in Bengaluru, where the company unveiled new AI models and research initiatives.

“I am excited to help Sarvam as an advisor and help them build the best models in the world,” Chaplot said at the event.

His appointment comes weeks after Sarvam raised $234 million in the first close of a $300 million Series B funding round at a $1.5 billion valuation. The company said the funding would support the development of its next-generation frontier AI models focused on agentic AI, coding, and cybersecurity, as well as investments in compute infrastructure and enterprise deployments.

The startup also reaffirmed that its previously announced one-trillion-parameter model remains under development and is expected within the next six months.

Pratyush Kumar, Co-Founder of Sarvam AI, said that Chaplot is advising the company on building large language models. The company has committed to developing trillion-parameter models, comparable in scale to those being built by leading Chinese AI firms, as it trains larger, more capable systems.

Chaplot brings experience from several of the world’s leading AI labs. Earlier this year, he joined Elon Musk’s xAI as a pre-training lead to work on AI research. Before that, he was a founding member of Paris-based Mistral AI, where he contributed to the development of models such as Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B and Mistral Large.

Before joining xAI, Chaplot was an AI research scientist at Facebook AI Research (FAIR). He later moved to Thinking Machines Lab, where he served as a Member of Technical Staff.

Chaplot earned a PhD in Machine Learning and a Master's degree in Language Technologies from Carnegie Mellon University. He completed his BTech in Computer Science and Engineering at IIT Bombay.

Chaplot pushed back against the belief that India lacks the resources needed to develop frontier AI models.

“Many think building at the frontier requires resources that are impossible to get in India. That’s not true,” he said.

He further argued that building frontier AI does not depend on having a large number of seasoned researchers.

“You need a handful of experienced people, but mostly you need motivated and talented people. That’s something we have plenty of in India,” he said, adding that AI remains a relatively young field, allowing researchers to build expertise quickly with the right mentorship.

SarvamAI is also opening a new office in San Francisco. Kumar said the move is intended to attract top AI talent to work on building models for India.

“We want to have a very strong conduit of talent back to India. It’s important to get the best people thinking and building for the Indian context,” he said.

He further added that the company is already looking to hire in the US and is working through the logistics of setting up a US subsidiary and office.

Founded by Vivek Raghavan and Kumar in 2023, Sarvam AI develops models, inference infrastructure and enterprise AI products across speech, vision, document intelligence and AI agents. It was also selected by the Indian government under the IndiaAI Mission to build a sovereign large language model.

Semiconductor company Marvell Technology has announced plans to invest $250 million in India over the next three years, expanding its research and development capabilities, workforce and infrastructure to support the growing demand for AI, cloud and data infrastructure technologies.

The announcement was made as the company marked 20 years of operations in India, underscoring the country’s growing importance in Marvell’s global engineering and semiconductor strategy.

As part of the investment, Marvell will double its headcount in India over the next three years, inaugurate a new wing at its Bengaluru office and expand its presence in Hyderabad. The company said the expansion will strengthen its global innovation network and accelerate the development of next-generation semiconductor technologies powering AI workloads, hyperscale data centres and cloud platforms.

“India has become a strategic hub of engineering excellence for Marvell, playing a critical role in advancing the infrastructure technologies that power the world's leading hyperscalers and cloud providers,” said Navin Bishnoi, Associate Vice President and India Country Manager at Marvell.

Marvell established its India operations in Bengaluru in 2006 and has since grown the country into its second-largest R&D organisation globally. Engineering teams across Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad contribute to the company’s work in advanced semiconductor technologies, including process nodes beyond 2nm, high-speed analogue IP, subsystem design, software and firmware development, and end-to-end silicon engineering.

Beyond R&D, Marvell said it is investing in the broader semiconductor ecosystem through partnerships with universities, startups, industry bodies and government agencies. These collaborations include internship programmes, faculty development initiatives, joint research projects and curriculum development aimed at preparing students for careers in advanced technology and semiconductor engineering.

Alongside the investment announcement, Marvell highlighted its recently launched Marvell Scholarship for Technical and Engineering Merit (M-STEM) programme, which aims to strengthen India’s future semiconductor and AI talent pipeline.

The scholarship programme, launched earlier this year, received more than 7,000 applications from engineering students across India. Marvell selected 100 students pursuing degrees in electronics, electrical engineering and computer science to receive financial assistance, industry exposure and hands-on learning opportunities.

According to the company, the initiative is designed to help cultivate the next generation of semiconductor and AI innovators by combining academic support with practical industry engagement at a time when demand for specialised chip design and AI engineering talent continues to grow globally.

Cognizant has launched its first global OpenAI Codex hackathon involving 10,000 employees across six Indian cities, as the IT services company steps up efforts to build AI coding capabilities internally amid intensifying competition among technology firms to train their workforce on generative AI tools.

The hackathon, organised in partnership with OpenAI, is being held across Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Pune, Coimbatore and Kochi under the theme ‘Engineering the Frontier’, the company said in a statement on July 30.

The initiative comes at a time when Indian IT services companies are rapidly investing in AI talent, developer productivity tools and enterprise AI capabilities as clients increasingly demand AI-led software engineering and automation.

Earlier this year, Cognizant said it was recognised by OpenAI for its AI Builder capabilities and selected among a group of global systems integrators to help expand the use of OpenAI Codex for enterprise customers.

“Cognizant is bringing Codex to its workforce at significant scale, giving 10,000 associates across India the opportunity to learn, experiment and build with frontier AI,” Colleen Kapase, Vice President of Strategic Global Partnerships and Ecosystems at OpenAI, said in a statement. “This hackathon is an important first step in Cognizant’s ambition to translate those skills into practical solutions for enterprise customers.”

The company said the hackathon is intended to give employees hands-on experience with Codex through coding challenges, OpenAI-led training sessions and collaborative solution development. Participants will also have access to technical mentors and learning resources as part of the programme.

Cognizant plans to expand the initiative beyond the initial cohort, targeting participation from more than 50,000 employees over the coming months.

Rajesh Varrier, President of Global Operations, Chairman and Managing Director of Cognizant India, said the initiative is aimed at helping employees develop practical expertise with AI coding tools and build enterprise-focused AI solutions.

“For us as an AI Builder, combining human judgment with AI capability is key to closing the gap between AI and enterprise results,” said Varrier. “Hosting a global Codex Hackathon, right here in India, is a proud moment for us. It’s an opportunity for our associates to build real fluency with frontier tools like Codex and develop custom AI solutions that deliver value.”

The latest programme adds to Cognizant’s broader AI skilling efforts. Earlier this month, the company announced plans to expand its AI-focused workforce by creating 15,000 specialised professionals, essentially forward-deployed engineers, under its newly announced Frontier programme.

For the June quarter, Cognizant reported revenue of $5.48 billion, up from $5.24 billion a year earlier.

Freehand, an AI startup based in Chennai, raised $75 million to expand its autonomous supply chain platform.

The funding round was co-led by Battery Ventures and NewRoad Capital Partners, contributing to a total of $100 million raised since 2024.

San Francisco-based agentic AI startup Freehand, with a significant presence in Chennai, has raised $75 million in a funding round co-led by Battery Ventures and NewRoad Capital Partners, as it looks to expand its autonomous AI platform for enterprise supply chains, marking one of the largest funding rounds in the emerging category.

The round also saw participation from PSP Growth, led by former US Commerce Secretary Penny Pritzker, Nexus Venture Partners, and existing investors. With the latest raise, the startup has secured a total of $100 million in funding since its launch in 2024.

Around half of Freehand's workforce is based in India, with significant operations in Chennai.

Founded by former Pando executives Nitin Jayakrishnan and Abhijeet Manohar, Freehand develops AI agents that autonomously execute supply chain workflows, including auditing invoices, negotiating rates, enforcing contracts, reconciling transactions, and processing supplier payments. The platform has already been deployed by enterprises including Meta, Unilever, Johnson & Johnson, Pfizer, Dunkin', and Cardinal Health.

Announcing the funding on LinkedIn, Jayakrishnan highlighted the company's confidence in its technology by attaching a performance guarantee. "We've raised $75M to give you a guarantee: if we can't find $500K your company wasted on overpaid invoices, we'll pay you $10K," he wrote.

Describing the problem Freehand aims to solve, he added, "A Fortune 500 gets a million invoices a year... each surcharge is small enough that escalating it costs more than paying it. And there are a million of them." According to Jayakrishnan, the company's AI analyses contracts, invoices, purchase orders, transaction records, and communications to identify hidden leakages and automate complex procurement decisions.

The company claims its platform recovered $260 million in excess spending across customers over the past year by analysing more than 19 million invoices. In early deployments, organisations have reportedly recovered 5–10% of spending in complex procurement categories, accelerated workflows by five to seven times and reduced procure-to-pay cycles by over 70%, it added.

Microsoft reported 18% quarterly revenue growth to $90 billion for Q4 FY26, driven by Microsoft Cloud reaching $59.3 billion (up 27%) and Azure topping $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time.

Microsoft’s fiscal year runs from July 1 through June 30 of the following year.

For the full fiscal year 2026, Microsoft surpassed $331.8 billion in annual revenue, representing an 18% increase year-over-year. Operating income expanded 21% to $155.2 billion, reflecting strong operating leverage alongside sustained capital investment in AI infrastructure.

Nearly 90% of annual cloud revenue came from customers outside frontier AI model companies.

Azure revenue grew 43% in the quarter and is projected to expand approximately 45% in the July–September quarter, backed by planned capital expenditure exceeding $50 billion.

Underpinning this expansion is a shift toward model-agnostic enterprise deployments. Microsoft now offers over 11,000 models on Azure, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI, and its proprietary MAI family, and reported a fivefold surge in multi-provider adoption.

“Since the start of the year, we have seen a 5x increase in the number of customers building with models from multiple providers,” CEO Satya Nadella said in the earnings call. To prevent vendor lock-in, Microsoft is decoupling enterprise context from specific models.

“You've got to keep your harness separate from the model. The harness will ensure that your memory, your context, all of that is external. That means any given model at any given time is swappable,” Nadella explained, adding that because ‘every model is substitutable,’ organisations can optimise for cost, latency, and resilience without breaking operational continuity.

Infrastructure expansion kept pace, with 31 new data centres added in the quarter—88 total for the year, another gigawatt of AI capacity brought online, and GPU dock-to-live times cut by nearly 50%.

Even so, demand continues to outstrip available hardware.

Chief financial officer Amy Hood noted, “Currently, the situation is obviously that demand exceeds available supply in a sort of relatively extreme moment,” adding that capacity additions translate directly into Azure growth.

Nadella noted that shifting specialised workloads to Microsoft’s lighter, in-house models is drastically cutting operational overhead. For instance, replacing third-party models with proprietary 'MAI' models reduced GPU inference costs by up to 89% for voice processing in Dynamics 365 (via MAI-Voice-2-Flash) and up to 84% for generative image editing in PowerPoint (via MAI-Image-2.5).

Enterprise AI adoption accelerated across Microsoft’s portfolio. Microsoft 365 Copilot surpassed 30 million paid seats as net seat additions more than doubled sequentially, while user satisfaction doubled over the last three quarters.

“We are also evolving our business model beyond per seat to per seat plus consumption, further expanding our TAM and delivering more customer value,” Nadella said.

Developer growth followed a similar trajectory as GitHub Copilot hit 50 million users and the broader GitHub platform reached 225 million developers.

Highlighting the shift toward autonomous software engineering, Nadella noted, “Every major coding agent runs on the platform, and one in three pull requests on GitHub now involves an agent”.

Meanwhile, Azure Foundry doubled revenue to reach 100,000 customers, and the two-month-old Agent 365 control plane logged nearly 40 million registered enterprise agents.

The Andhra Pradesh government has launched two artificial intelligence Centres of Excellence (AI CoEs) in Amaravati and Visakhapatnam to provide early-stage deeptech startups with access to high-performance GPU computing, AI sandboxes, mentorship, and commercialisation support.

The centres, sanctioned by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the state's Department of IT, Electronics & Communications, will operate under the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub (RTIH). The initiative is aimed at strengthening Andhra Pradesh's AI startup ecosystem by providing entrepreneurs with advanced computing infrastructure, industry partnerships and market access.

Speaking at the launch, RTIH and Andhra Pradesh Innovation Society (APIS) CEO P Dhatri Reddy said the facilities are intended to help startups move beyond the ideation stage by offering the infrastructure and ecosystem support required to commercialise AI-driven innovations.

She added that the centres are expected to foster collaboration between academia, industry, and research institutions, helping position Andhra Pradesh as a preferred destination for AI-led entrepreneurship.

The AI CoEs will offer specialised AI sandboxes, high-performance compute infrastructure, mentorship programmes, and structured industry linkages, enabling startups to build, test, and scale AI applications without investing heavily in their own infrastructure.

Echoing this, Krishna Priya Akella, Founder and CEO of AI-powered influencer marketing platform Starbuzz.ai, noted that access to GPU computing resources, APIs, investor networks, and market connections could significantly reduce barriers for AI startups looking to build and scale products.

Tamil Nadu AI Association Executive Director C Aarthi Ram stressed that beyond infrastructure, startup support programmes should remain focused on solving customer problems and building sustainable businesses.

The role of universities in nurturing AI innovation was also emphasised. Ganesh Reddy Karri, Professor and Deputy Director at VIT-AP University's Centre of Excellence, called for stronger collaboration between academic institutions and industry to accelerate research translation and develop commercially relevant AI technologies.

The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has partnered with enterprise AI software company Pegasystems to launch a nationwide virtual internship programme aimed at preparing engineering students for an AI-first workforce.

Announced at Pega’s flagship event, PEGAInnovate, the National Internship Program (NIP) is a five-week, fully virtual initiative delivered in collaboration with AICTE and SmartBridge Educational Services. The programme introduces students to enterprise AI technologies such as generative AI, agentic engineering, workflow automation, and enterprise transformation.

The launch comes as India continues to grapple with an AI skills gap despite producing one of the world’s largest engineering talent pools. According to Pega, the internship is designed to bridge the gap between academic learning and enterprise requirements by offering hands-on projects, virtual instructor-led sessions and mentorship from industry experts.

Within just 10 days of opening registrations, the programme attracted more than 10,000 registrations, eventually expanding to nearly 75,000 students across over 1,500 colleges nationwide.

Participants will receive practical exposure to technologies including Pega Blueprint, the company’s generative AI-powered application development platform, alongside agentic AI and workflow automation. Dedicated Pega mentors and senior executives will conduct sessions to familiarise students with enterprise AI use cases and career opportunities within the Pega ecosystem.

The internship also serves as a precursor to Pega’s revamped University Academic Program (UAP), scheduled to launch in August with a new curriculum focused on AI and enterprise automation.

Explaining the motivation behind the initiative, Deepak Visweswaraiah, Senior Vice President and Managing Director, Pega India, stated, “The volume of registrations in a single week tells us something important: students are not waiting to be handed enterprise AI skills; they are actively looking for a way in. NIP gives them that opportunity. It provides hands-on experience with technologies such as Pega Blueprint, AI-powered application development, agentic workflows, and automation.”

Unlike conventional internship programmes focused primarily on coding, Pega says the initiative aims to teach students how to build AI-enabled business solutions.

“A five-week programme cannot teach someone everything about enterprise software, and that was never the goal,” said Goutham Parcha, Vice President, Application Development, Pega India. “What we can do is shift how a student approaches a problem, moving them from writing code towards designing outcomes. That shift is exactly what agentic engineering demands of our own teams every day, and it is the instinct we want every NIP participant to walk away with.”

According to the company, the programme reflects a broader shift in enterprise software development, where engineers are increasingly expected to work alongside AI systems rather than simply write code. By exposing students to agentic AI, workflow automation and enterprise application development before they enter the workforce, Pega aims to build an AI-ready talent pipeline for India’s rapidly evolving technology sector.

SK Hynix reported record second-quarter 2026 results as AI infrastructure spending continued to fuel demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), while outlining a strategy to secure future growth through multi-year supply agreements with major customers.

The South Korean memory chips maker posted revenue of ₩79.32 trillion ($55 billion), up 51% quarter-on-quarter and 257% year-on-year, alongside a record operating profit of ₩60.54 trillion ($42 billion), a 557% jump YoY.

Growth was driven by HBM3E, AI server DRAM, and enterprise SSDs, lifting operating margins to 76%, while non-operating investment gains pushed net profit to ₩93.92 trillion ($65 billion).

SK Hynix said it has completed long-term supply agreements with 10 major AI customers, marking a shift away from the memory industry’s traditional spot-market cycles. The agreements include pricing mechanisms designed to reduce volatility alongside financial commitments, including deposits, to improve demand visibility and support long-term capacity planning.

The company said the agreements go beyond volume commitments by aligning future memory development with customers’ technology roadmaps while providing greater visibility for production and capital investment.

It also dismissed concerns that more efficient AI models or cloud providers leasing data centre capacity could reduce demand for AI hardware. Instead, management argued that efficiency improvements would broaden AI adoption and ultimately increase demand for memory.

“We view these developments not as a sign of AI investment slowdown, but more as a transition towards higher utilisation of the AI infrastructure that has already been built at scale, as well as accelerated monetisation efforts,” Corporate Center President Song Hyeon-jong said in a statement.

“As AI models improve and software optimisation advances, the computational volume and cost per individual task are continuously decreasing. We anticipate that these improvements in efficiency will not dampen overall infrastructure demand,” he added.

SK Hynix said demand is increasingly extending beyond HBM to conventional server DRAM and enterprise SSDs as agentic AI applications expand.

The company expects DRAM demand to grow in the mid-20% range and NAND demand in the high teens, while arguing that supply constraints will persist because of increasingly complex manufacturing processes for AI memory and the long lead times required to build new fabrication capacity.

The company also forecast stronger profitability in the second half of 2026 as HBM4 shipments ramp and higher-value products make up a larger share of sales.

It expects second-half DRAM bit growth to exceed the first half, supported by higher HBM4 volumes and increased shipments of 1c DRAM.

On its product roadmap, SK Hynix said it began mass-producing HBM4 during the second quarter and expects a full production ramp in the second half of the year. HBM4E samples have already been supplied to major customers, with volume production planned for 2027.

The company is also preparing technologies for HBM5, including integrated HBM (IHBM), which it said could reduce thermal resistance by more than 30% in future AI systems.

The results come weeks after SK Hynix completed its Nasdaq ADR listing, which the company described as the largest-ever US listing by a foreign issuer. Management said the listing was intended not only to raise capital but also to strengthen relationships with major AI customers and expand its presence in the next-generation computing ecosystem.

However, its shares dropped sharply on the Korean stock exchange KOSPI, falling over 18% at the time of publishing as sales fell short of analyst estimates.

The stock is also underperforming on Nasdaq, closing around 9% lower on July 28 as investors duno semniconductor stocks. It’s now trading 4% below the listing price.

More than 1,100 employees from leading AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral, and Thinking Machines, have urged the US government to back an international framework that could slow the development of advanced AI systems if required.

The employees argue that governments should develop technical and governance mechanisms before AI systems become capable of accelerating their own research and development.

“We request that the US government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development,” they said in a statement published under the banner Pacing the Frontier.

The signatories include Anthropic co-founders Jack Clark and Jared Kaplan, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta Chief Scientist Shengjia Zhao, Google DeepMind’s Anca Dragan, and Thinking Machines Chief Scientist John Schulman, alongside researchers, engineers, and policy staff from several frontier AI companies.

They have flagged automated AI research, also known as recursive self-improvement, wherein AI systems begin improving future AI systems with limited human involvement. According to the signatories, such capabilities could accelerate AI progress beyond current oversight mechanisms.

“It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate AI progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems,” the statement noted.

Rather than calling for an immediate slowdown, the signatories argue that governments should ensure the world has the ability to intervene if development begins outpacing society’s capacity to manage it.

"Each company, and country, is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress,” they added.

John Schulman said he signed the statement to encourage work on coordination mechanisms before governments are forced to intervene.

“Signed because this statement helps establish common knowledge about the possible need for coordination mechanisms as automated AI research accelerates progress,” Schulman said. “I'd also like to see labs start designing these mechanisms voluntarily, even before the USG gets involved.”

The initiative comes as AI safety has returned to the centre of policy discussions following recent incidents involving advanced models and growing debate over how frontier AI should be governed.

In recent weeks, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis have each proposed different approaches for oversight of advanced AI models, including international coordination and pre-deployment evaluations.

The statement was drafted with support from AI safety organisations Guidelight AI Standards and Encode AI.

content:
The AI agent that escaped OpenAI's testing environment and breached AI platform Hugging Face also compromised a customer hosted on AI infrastructure company Modal Labs, according to a Reuters report. The disclosure expands the scope of an incident that OpenAI had previously linked only to Hugging Face.

Modal Labs is a serverless cloud platform that provides compute infrastructure for AI applications and GPU workloads.

The report added that the agent exploited an unsecured public code execution endpoint belonging to a Modal customer while carrying out the intrusion.

Modal said its own infrastructure was not breached. “We were not directly breached,” Modal Chief Technology Officer Akshat Bubna told Reuters, adding that the affected asset belonged to one of the company's customers rather than Modal itself.

OpenAI did not identify Modal in its original disclosure about the Hugging Face incident. However, the company confirmed that the agent had accessed four accounts across separate services during the attack, without naming the services involved.

OpenAI said it had found “a small number of cases” in which its models identified and used publicly exposed credentials on other publicly available services during its review of the Hugging Face intrusion. “This includes four accounts on four services as part of the Hugging Face incident (and a few accounts accessed as part of other evaluations),” the company said in an updated blog post published on July 28.

OpenAI added that one of the four accounts served as an outbound relay and staging point, another was used for data storage, and the remaining two were accessed only in read-only mode. The company said those two accounts were not used to facilitate the compromise of Hugging Face.

In its earlier account of the incident, OpenAI said the AI agent broke out of its isolated testing environment while being evaluated on ExploitGym, a cybersecurity benchmark.

The agent reached the public internet, compromised Hugging Face and attempted to use external infrastructure to continue the attack. OpenAI later disabled the agent and said it had implemented additional safeguards.

According to Reuters, OpenAI did not realise its own system was responsible for the attack until about a week later, after Hugging Face publicly disclosed the breach and the FBI had already been notified.

In its latest update, OpenAI said none of the models planned for public release were involved in the Hugging Face intrusion. “The pre-release model mentioned in our blog post is an internal-only research prototype and was never intended for public release,” the company said, adding that it has since “deactivated, encrypted, and restricted it from research access.”

The company also said the models did not have direct internet access during the ExploitGym evaluation. Instead, they identified and exploited "a previously unknown zero-day vulnerability in Artifactory, a package registry cache proxy" to gain internet access. OpenAI said it had disclosed the vulnerability, along with other Artifactory vulnerabilities discovered by the models, to the vendor.

OpenAI said it is continuing to work with Hugging Face on the investigation, including contributing to the company’s post-mortem, and has added Hugging Face to its Trusted Access for Cyber Program.

“Based on our review to date, we have not identified any other activity at the level of severity or scale of what we've shared related to Hugging Face, which involved a platform-level compromise,” the company said.

The incident has become one of the first publicly disclosed cases of an advanced AI agent escaping a controlled testing environment and carrying out unauthorised actions against external systems.

Mindgrove Technologies and AtumX Innovations have launched AGNI, a developer board for classrooms using indigenously designed chips.

The initiative targets five government schools in Chennai, reaching nearly 1,000 students, with plans for expansion across India.

Indian semiconductor startup Mindgrove Technologies has partnered with STEM education company AtumX Innovations to introduce AGNI, a developer board powered by an indigenously designed chip to government school classrooms.

The initiative will begin with five government schools in Chennai, reaching nearly 1,000 students, with support from the Atal Innovation Mission. The companies said the rollout will gradually expand to schools in other cities across India.

AGNI is powered by Mindgrove’s Secure IoT System-on-Chip (SoC), a commercial-grade high-performance microcontroller designed in the country. AtumX has adapted the board for classrooms by developing a student-friendly integrated development environment (IDE) that allows students to progress from block-based programming to artificial intelligence applications.

The companies said the initiative aims to give students hands-on experience with hardware designed and built in India, reducing the dependence on imported developer boards traditionally used in engineering education.

“Every engineer in India who wanted to build with silicon has had to start on an imported chip and board. We built our developer board to change that starting point,” said Shashwath T R, Co-founder and CEO of Mindgrove Technologies, in a statement.

He added that exposing students to indigenous hardware early could strengthen India’s semiconductor ecosystem by building a pipeline of future engineers familiar with homegrown technology.

According to the companies, AGNI is not only intended for schools but also for engineers and original equipment manufacturers, allowing them to evaluate and build products using Indian-designed semiconductor technology before Mindgrove launches its future chips.

AtumX said the initiative aligns with its goal of encouraging students to become technology creators rather than consumers.

“A school student who learns on an Indian chip today will do college projects on an Indian chip, file patents on an Indian chip, and build startups on an Indian chip,” said Akash J, Co-founder and CEO of AtumX.

Mindgrove, headquartered at the IIT Madras Research Park, designs SoCs for applications including Internet of Things, automotive systems, and computer vision. The startup is backed by investors including Peak XV Partners, Rocketship.vc, Speciale Invest, and Mela Ventures.

Founded in 2022 and incubated at Anna Incubator, Chennai, AtumX develops STEM learning products and currently works with more than 500 schools and 35 education partners across India, the US, and Australia.

The Chennai deployment marks the first phase of a broader national rollout, with the companies aiming to bring indigenous semiconductor technology into classrooms across the country in the coming months.

JanAI has launched a community AI café in HD Kote, Karnataka, to promote AI adoption among rural citizens.

The initiative focuses on local entrepreneurship and community participation, particularly empowering women and rural youth.

JanAI, an initiative of the Head Held High Foundation, has launched a community AI café in Karnataka’s HD Kote, aiming to bring AI to rural communities through local entrepreneurship and community participation. The initiative is designed to create a neighbourhood hub where citizens can learn, build and use AI to improve livelihoods and solve local problems.

The JanAI Café has been established within a women-run Millets Café operated by members of the Jenu Kuraba tribal community in partnership with the Swami Vivekananda Youth Movement. JanAI says the model is intended to ensure that women play a leading role in AI adoption, while equipping rural youth with AI skills and entrepreneurial opportunities.

Alongside the launch, JanAI released the HD Kote Community Listening Inception Report, which it describes as one of India’s early grassroots AI-readiness studies. The report draws on surveys of more than 1,000 households and over 100 rural youth, documenting everyday challenges, aspirations, entrepreneurial ambitions and perceptions of AI.

The survey was conducted by more than 20 locally trained AI ambassadors, most of them girls, with the findings set to guide the development of AI solutions tailored to local needs.

According to JanAI, the café represents a shift from technology-led deployment to community-led AI development, where residents help shape AI tools rather than simply adopt them. The organisation says the initiative brings together community listening, trusted local leadership, AI adoption, entrepreneurship and measurable impact under one roof.

“The JanAI Café is much more than a place—it is a new model for how AI can reach every citizen. We believe that before AI can solve problems, it must first learn to listen,” Madan Padaki, Founder of JanAI, said in a statement.

He added that the initiative combines community listening, local leadership, AI adoption and entrepreneurship, with a vision of establishing thousands of similar cafés across India.

Padaki said locating the café inside a women-led tribal enterprise demonstrates that AI’s future “will not be written only in our technology parks and metropolitan cities; it will also be shaped by women, youth and communities in India’s villages.”

JanAI plans to establish more than 10,000 agentic AI cafés across tehsils and gram panchayats over the next three years. The statement says the cafés will serve as community infrastructure for AI adoption, entrepreneurship and inclusive economic growth by bringing together governments, civil society organisations and industry partners.

A section of HCLTech employees raised slogans demanding salary hikes while chief executive C Vijayakumar was addressing staff during the company's 50th anniversary celebrations in Chennai, with videos of the incident circulating widely on social media.

The chants of "we want hike" erupted as Vijayakumar walked onto the stage to address employees gathered at the event, briefly interrupting the proceedings.

The clips quickly gained traction on social media, triggering discussions around compensation, employee expectations, and workplace sentiment in India's information technology sector.

The celebration was part of HCL Group's year-long golden jubilee events being held across multiple cities for employees.

HCLTech is yet to announce a timeline for salary hikes in the current fiscal year.

The incident comes at a time when India's $300 billion IT services industry continues to grapple with subdued client spending, slower discretionary technology investments and cautious hiring, prompting companies to keep a close watch on costs even as they step up investments in artificial intelligence.

HCLTech had not publicly commented on the incident at the time of publishing this article.

Vijayakumar, who has served as the CEO of HCLTech since 2016, is the highest-paid IT chief in the country. His remuneration jumped nearly 67% to ₹176.47 crore ($18.45 million) in FY26, according to HCLTech’s annual report.

HCLTech reported a 20.3% year-on-year increase in consolidated net profit to ₹4,626 crore ($84 million), while revenue rose 13.9% year-on-year to ₹34,579 crore ($3.62 billion) during the quarter ended June 30. In constant currency, revenue grew 2.6% from a year earlier but declined 0.5% sequentially, reflecting the seasonally weak first quarter.

Google is expanding Gemini Spark, its AI agent that can complete tasks in the background, to Google AI Pro subscribers in India over the next few weeks. The service, powered by Gemini 3.6 Flash, is available to Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers and integrates with Google Workspace applications including Gmail, Docs and Sheets.

Unlike a traditional AI assistant that responds to prompts, Gemini Spark is built to carry out ongoing tasks on a user’s behalf. It runs on Google’s cloud infrastructure and continues working even when a user’s device is offline or locked.

Google said that Spark can “work quietly in the background” and connect with Workspace applications “with zero setup required”.

It further added that Spark automates recurring digital tasks while keeping users in control.

Users can decide whether to enable the service and which applications it can access. The company said Spark asks for confirmation before carrying out high-impact actions such as sending emails or making purchases.

“Spark always operates under your direction,” Google said. “You choose whether to turn it on and what apps it connects to, and it is designed to ask you first before performing high-stakes actions like spending money or sending emails.”

Google also shared examples of how the agent can be used. Travellers can instruct Spark to automatically add flight and hotel booking confirmations from Gmail to a Google Sheet and populate their calendar with local events during a trip.

Users can also schedule weekly searches for local activities and monitor sports court availability based on weather conditions.

For businesses, Spark can scan customer enquiries and prepare draft replies. It can also analyse a user’s previous emails to create a personalised writing style that is applied to future email drafts.

Google said Gemini Spark is part of its broader push towards AI agents that can complete tasks on a user's behalf instead of just answering questions.

Freshworks has appointed Ryan Manning as its Chief Product and Technology Officer (CPTO), effective August 10, as the software company brings its product and technology organisations under a single leadership structure.

Manning will report to CEO Dennis Woodside and succeed Srini Raghavan, who is leaving the company to pursue an entrepreneurial venture. Murali Swaminathan will continue as Chief Technology Officer and report to Manning.

The appointment comes as Freshworks expands its presence among mid-market and enterprise customers. In his new role, Manning will lead the company's product and technology strategy across its AI, IT, and customer experience portfolios, overseeing the global product roadmap and engineering organisation.

“Ryan has the unique ability to quickly turn what customers need into products that win in the market," said Dennis Woodside, CEO of Freshworks, in a statement. “As AI changes how quickly and how deeply our customers can put new capability to work, we’re excited to bring product and engineering back together under a single organisation so we can move with more speed and less friction.”

Manning joins Freshworks after holding leadership roles at startups and enterprise software companies. He helped build and scale ServiceNow around the time of its IPO and co-founded FreeAgent CRM, now Servis.ai. Most recently, he served as Chief Product Officer at BMC Helix, where he led product strategy during the company’s transformation, including its focus on ServiceOps and agentic AI.

“AI is changing what businesses should expect from service software," Manning said. "Having built service management products across startups and global software businesses, I believe Freshworks is uniquely positioned to lead the shift, combining powerful capability with rapid impact in a way the market needs right now.”

Manning holds a bachelor’s degree in accounting and finance from San Diego State University, where he also serves on the board of the university’s Computer Science programme. He will be based at Freshworks’ headquarters in San Mateo, California.

Freshworks said the leadership change is intended to align product development and engineering under a single executive as AI reshapes enterprise software development and deployment.

Cognizant's revenue rose by 4.5% in Q2, supported by its focus on AI-driven strategies.

A 6% decline in quarterly bookings indicates a slowdown in AI-led deal activity.

Cognizant Technology Solutions posted a 4.5% year-on-year rise in revenue for the June quarter, even as the IT services major leaned harder into its ‘AI builder’ strategy, striking new deals around Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 while flagging a sharp slowdown in fresh bookings.

The Nasdaq-listed company, which counts India as its largest talent base, reported revenue of $5.48 billion for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up from $5.24 billion a year earlier.

Growth in constant currency terms was 4.1%, decelerating from the 7.2% pace clocked in the same quarter last year, which can be considered as a sign that the initial AI-led deal momentum is beginning to normalise.

Cognizant’s quarterly bookings fell 6% year-on-year, even though trailing twelve-month bookings rose 5% to $29.1 billion, translating into a book-to-bill ratio of roughly 1.3x.

The company signed seven large deals (contracts worth $100 million or more) during the quarter.

“Our organic revenue growth momentum continued in the second quarter and was at the high end of our expectations,” Chief Executive Officer Ravi Kumar S said in a statement.

"As organisations shift from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale execution, we believe the market opportunity ahead is larger than ever," he said, adding that the company was helping clients "close the AI velocity gap" by combining industry expertise with engineering and data modernisation capabilities.

Financial Services, Cognizant's largest and most mature vertical, was the standout performer with 12% year-on-year growth (11.7% in constant currency). Health Sciences grew a modest 1.4%, Products and Resources rose 1.2%, and Communications, Media and Technology grew 1.5%.

North America, which accounts for more than 75% of revenue, grew 5.5%, while Europe grew a slower 2.5% and Rest of World contracted 1.2%.

Margins Hold Up Despite Restructuring Costs

Cognizant’s operating margin came in at 15.9%, up 30 basis points year-on-year, while adjusted operating margin expanded 40 basis points to 16.0%.

The quarter absorbed $84 million in restructuring charges under Project Leap, the company's ongoing efficiency programme, which were largely offset by an $81 million one-time benefit from the reversal of a legacy India Provident Fund liability following recent labour law changes.

Cognizant's AI narrative extended well beyond internal tooling in the quarter. The company is now working with travel technology firm Travelport to embed Claude into software development workflows spanning airlines, hotels, and travel agencies.

Separately, Cognizant has also become one of a small number of Global Premier Partners in Anthropic's Claude Partner Network, and is training what it calls a "Frontier Certified" workforce.

The company also expanded ties with Google Cloud around Gemini Enterprise, and said it would apply OpenAI's GPT-5.5 within its cybersecurity practice as part of the "OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program," aimed at speeding up the process of finding and fixing security vulnerabilities.

The company repurchased 22.5 million shares for $1,153 million during the quarter, including through a previously announced $500 million accelerated buyback programme, leaving $2.3 billion still authorised for future repurchases. In July, it also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.33 per share.

During the quarter, Cognizant also closed its $634 million acquisition of Astreya, an AI-focused IT managed services provider, funding part of the deal through a $1 billion drawdown on its revolving credit facility.

Total headcount stood at 356,700 as of June 30, down 900 sequentially but up 12,900 from a year earlier. Voluntary attrition in technology services rose to 13.0% on a trailing-12-month basis, up from 12.3% in the previous quarter.

Cognizant revised its full-year 2026 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to a range of 4.0–5.5%, while keeping its adjusted operating margin guidance unchanged at 16.0–16.2%.

For the September quarter, the company guided for revenue of $5.60–5.68 billion, implying year-on-year growth of 3.4–4.9%.

Andrew Ng, Co-Founder and Chairman of Coursera, has launched a new AI education startup, LearnVector, with a $100 million investment from Coursera to develop AI-driven personalised learning experiences.

The companies also plan to work together on course development and distribution, with LearnVector collaborating with both Coursera and Udemy.

Announcing the venture on X, Ng said online education had expanded access to learning over the past 15 years, but the learning process itself had remained largely unchanged.

“With advances in AI, we can now build a custom learning guide for each person. We will turn learning from one-to-many to one-to-one,” he wrote.

LearnVector is focused on building AI learning guides that adapt to each learner’s progress rather than functioning as conventional chatbots. Ng argued that effective AI learning requires structured guidance instead of simply answering questions.

“Research shows that chatbots without guardrails harm learning. They help complete tasks and enable students to do better on homework. But cognitive offloading to a chatbot results in them being less skilled. And, you cannot always trust what a chatbot tells you,” he said.

Instead, he said LearnVector would “plan a path with you, adapt to how you learn, and patiently stay with you until you've mastered new skills”.

According to Reuters, Coursera’s investment gives it roughly a one-third stake in LearnVector, implying a valuation of about $300 million. The startup plans to launch its first courses in early 2027 and will initially target corporations, governments and higher education institutions.

It will use AI foundation models from multiple third-party providers to deliver personalised courses that evolve as learners progress.

Ng said the company is being built around the idea that AI will reshape work by changing the skills people need rather than replacing them entirely.

He added that trust remains central to online education, saying learners need “material that is accurate, relevant, and worth the effort you put into it”. Ng said LearnVector plans to work with Coursera to combine AI-driven instruction with the platform’s library of learning content.

Safe Superintelligence Inc (SSI), the AI startup founded by former OpenAI Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever, has partnered with NVIDIA. The collaboration entails an equity investment and access to the chipmaker’s next-generation Vera Rubin systems, giving the startup a tenfold increase in computing capacity.

The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the deal. However, Reuters reported that NVIDIA is investing about $5 billion in SSI.

SSI said the investment and access to NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform will substantially increase its compute. The companies will also work together on advancing NVIDIA’s current and future computing platforms, with SSI contributing insights from its AI research.

The partnership marks one of the first major public announcements from SSI since the company was founded in 2024 by Sutskever, Daniel Gross, and Daniel Levy. The startup has largely operated in stealth, developing ‘safe superintelligence’ rather than releasing commercial AI products.

According to NVIDIA, the company decided to partner with SSI after obtaining what it described as rare access to the startup’s closely guarded research. SSI has spent the past two years pursuing a new research direction in developing a robustly aligned artificial intelligence.

“Ilya has pioneered fundamental breakthroughs at the foundation of modern AI, beginning with AlexNet,” NVIDIA Founder and CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. "We are excited to see what new breakthroughs SSI will discover powered by our Vera Rubin platform.”

Sutskever said the startup had reached a stage where it was ready to expand its research efforts.

“We have research that is worthy of scaling up, and having access to a big NVIDIA computer will let us do so,” he said. “We're incredibly proud to be partnering with Jensen and the NVIDIA team, and we are confident that our big bet on the Vera Rubin platform will take us to the next level.”

The partnership adds SSI to a growing list of AI companies securing large-scale infrastructure commitments from NVIDIA as demand for compute continues to rise.

Last year, OpenAI partnered with the AI chipmaker to deploy chips in 10 GW of AI data centres, backed by over $100 billion in progressive investment. More recently, SK Group and NVIDIA announced plans for a $500+ billion partnership to establish AI infrastructure, featuring a 2 GW NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory built by SK Telecom.

SSI last raised $2 billion at a $32 billion valuation, backed by investors including Greenoaks, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Andreessen Horowitz. The NVIDIA investment deepens the relationship between the AI chipmaker and one of Silicon Valley’s most closely watched AI research startups.

Microsoft has introduced MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, its first AI model built for cybersecurity, alongside updates to MDASH, its multi-agent vulnerability identification and remediation platform.

The company said the new model enables MDASH to deliver “world-class performance at 50% of the cost” of its previous offering while outperforming rival AI systems on a cybersecurity benchmark.

According to Microsoft, the combination of MAI-Cyber-1-Flash and GPT-5.4 achieved a score of 95.95% on CyberGym, a benchmark that evaluates how AI systems identify vulnerabilities across large codebases. The company said this was about 12 percentage points higher than Anthropic’s Mythos model.

Microsoft said MAI-Cyber-1-Flash was built to handle up to 90% of vulnerability detection tasks, allowing MDASH to reserve larger models, including GPT-5.4, for more complex cases. The company said this multi-model approach cuts costs by 50% compared with its earlier MDASH configuration, which relied on GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 mini and GPT-5.3 Codex.

The company also announced Perception, a new agentic security system within MDASH. Microsoft said Perception uses teams of AI agents to monitor, patch and remediate vulnerabilities continuously, and will expand to additional security workflows using MAI-Cyber-1-Flash.

Microsoft attributed the model’s performance to three factors: the model itself, security data collected over years of operating its platforms, and MDASH's orchestration layer.

The company said the compact model was derived from its MAI-Thinking-1 family and trained on security-focused data. It also said its security operations generate more than 100 trillion security signals daily across identity, endpoint, cloud and network environments, while MDASH coordinates more than 100 specialised AI agents for vulnerability detection and remediation.

“Three things matter today: Model. Data. Harness,” the company said. “We have jointly optimised our world-class models, our unmatched historic data, and our expert-tuned harness to ensure that our customers have a uniquely powerful security offering.”

Microsoft said MAI-Cyber-1-Flash was evaluated by its AI Red Team, tested through automated and expert-led adversarial exercises, and independently assessed by a third party before release. Through MDASH, customers will also have access to role-based access controls, tenant isolation, encryption, audit logs and sandboxed execution environments without internet access.

The company said its long-term goal is to improve cyber models through reinforcement learning based on real-world security operations.

Cursor has launched Cursor Start, a new subscription plan exclusively for developers in India, priced at ₹649 per month inclusive of tax, as the AI coding platform deepens its presence in one of its fastest-growing markets.

The plan includes access to Grok 4.5, Cursor’s flagship coding model, Composer, higher agent request limits than the Free tier, always-on cloud agents and UPI payments.

The company said its user base in India has tripled over the past year to more than three million developers, making the country its third-largest market globally.

It also said India has more power users than any other region, with developers generating more agent requests per user than anywhere else.

“For a long time, our users in India have asked us for two things: pricing that reflects the local market, and the ability to pay with UPI,” the company said.

Cursor Start sits between the company’s Free and Pro subscriptions. It includes Grok 4.5, Composer, higher agent request limits, always-on cloud agents, iOS support, and integrations with plugins, MCP servers, hooks and skills.

The subscription is billed in Indian rupees and supports payments via UPI, credit cards and debit cards.

“Cursor Start sits between our two other individual plans, Free and Pro,” said the company. Cursor said the Free plan is designed for first-time users, offering Composer access and a limited number of local agent requests each month without requiring payment.

The Pro plan targets heavier users, adding access to models from multiple AI providers alongside Cursor's own models, as well as features including Bugbot, Auto mode, Automations, the Cursor SDK and the ability to purchase additional usage beyond included limits. The Pro plan is priced at $20 per month.

According to the company, Start is intended for everyday development workloads, while Pro is aimed at developers requiring broader model access and advanced automation capabilities.

Cursor is also expanding its developer outreach in India. The company announced community events in Hyderabad on July 30 and Bengaluru on August 1, saying it plans to learn from Indian developers before considering similar localised plans in other markets.

Cognizant has expanded its strategic partnership with artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, becoming one of a select group of Global Premier Partners in the Claude Partner Network, as the Nasdaq-listed IT services company steps up efforts to commercialise generative AI across enterprise clients.

The expanded alliance will see Cognizant embed Anthropic’s Claude family of AI models into its proprietary engineering and IT operations platforms, while scaling a workforce certified on frontier AI models as enterprises move beyond proof-of-concept projects to production deployments.

According to the companies, the expanded partnership addresses the gap between model capability and companies’ ability to drive business results. Closing that gap extends beyond model capability. It takes the domain context, engineering depth and delivery scale to embed AI into the systems enterprises already run on.

The partnership builds on an agreement signed in late 2025 and comes as global IT services companies race to differentiate themselves through alliances with leading AI model providers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

“AI capability is rising faster than enterprises can absorb it, and that gap is the defining problem of this moment,” Ravi Kumar S, CEO, Cognizant, said in a statement. “Our role is to be the bridge. We bring the industry context, the engineering scale and the trust frameworks that use Claude to deliver production outcomes inside the most demanding enterprise environments.”

As part of the partnership, Cognizant will integrate Claude into platforms including Flowsource, Neuro AI Engineering and Neuro IT Ops under what it described as a model-agnostic AI strategy. The company said Flowsource now incorporates Claude Code into its software development workflow to automate coding and validation against engineering standards.

Cognizant also said it has already deployed Claude-powered solutions across several industries. These include an AI-based customer experience portal for a global manufacturer, an agentic contract intelligence platform for a biopharmaceutical company that reduced contract review time by up to 40%, and a risk navigation tool for insurers that cut manual research time from hours to about a minute, saving underwriters roughly eight hours a week.

The company said more than 30,000 employees have completed Claude training so far. Under its recently announced Frontier workforce model, Cognizant plans to prepare 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators as part of a broader certification pipeline covering 40,000 professionals. Over time, the company expects Claude training to extend across its workforce of more than 3,50,000 employees.

“Deepening our partnership with Cognizant will help more companies harness AI’s growing capability and deploy it in real, practical ways for their businesses. From manufacturing to the life sciences, Cognizant is bringing Claude into the everyday work of some of the world's most demanding industries—the kinds of contexts where AI can demonstrate its greatest value for humanity,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-Founder and President of Anthropic.

Mid-tier IT services firm Coforge reported a 63% year-on-year jump in consolidated net profit for the June quarter, driven by growth in its AI-led engineering business and the integration of its recently acquired US firm Encora.

Consolidated net profit for the quarter stood at ₹518.6 crore ($54 million), compared with ₹317.4 crore a year earlier.

However, on a sequential basis, the net profit dropped 15.3%, primarily due to multiple one-offs incurred by the company during the quarter. These include acquisition and integration costs of ₹61.3 crore related to Encora, ₹5 crore of legal costs related to a cyber litigation matter, and provisions against customer receivables of ₹10.8 crore. These were partly offset by forex gains of ₹22.1 crore, arising from the devaluation of the Bolivian currency.

These led to Coforge incurring net exceptional costs of ₹55 crore during the quarter.

Revenue from operations totalled ₹5,527.7 crore ($577 million), up 49% year-on-year in rupee terms and 33% in dollar terms.

EBITDA rose 74% year-on-year to ₹1,123.3 crore ($117 million), with EBITDA margin expanding 285 basis points to 20.3%.

Basic earnings per share rose 67.3% to ₹12.34. The board also declared an interim dividend of ₹4 per equity share and gave in-principle approval to set up an entity in China as part of the company's expansion plans,

Coforge said AI-led engineering, data, and cloud services together accounted for 86% of its revenue in the quarter. AI-led Engineering alone made up 50.4% of revenue by service line, up from 45.9% in the year-ago quarter.

“The confluence of our next twelve-month signed order book of $2.23 billion, an exceptionally strong large deal pipeline and differentiated capabilities with 86% of our revenues coming from AI-led engineering, data and cloud services has set us up to be the industry growth leader for the third year running,” Sudhir Singh, Chief Executive Officer and Executive Director, Coforge, said in a statement.

During the quarter, the company launched Coforge Nuuron, described as an AI operating system meant to help enterprises industrialise AI-driven outcomes across the business by orchestrating knowledge, decision intelligence, AI agents, and execution systems into a unified autonomous operating model.

It also unveiled the NEXA Agentic AI Platform, built for the insurance industry, and Aeronova.AI, an AI-enabled framework to help airlines transition from legacy PNR-based systems to order-led retailing.

Fresh order intake for the quarter stood at $691 million in total contract value, up from $648 million in the preceding quarter.

The executable order book for the next 12 months rose to $2.23 billion, up 27% sequentially.

The company signed four large deals during the quarter across North America, Europe, and Latin America.

Coforge said its acquisition of Encora, a digital engineering services firm, was now fully operationally integrated. Two months of Encora's contribution added $100.7 million to the topline following the deal's completion on April 23.

“With the Encora acquisition completely operationally integrated and with strong demand, record visibility, and a rapidly expanding pipeline of AI-led opportunities, FY27 is shaping up to be an exceptional performance year for the firm,” said Singh.

The company reported a next-12-month order book increase of 27% quarter-on-quarter, and said its top five clients contributed 18.0% of quarterly revenue while its top 10 clients contributed 26.1%.

Total headcount stood at 46,228 at the end of the quarter.

Coforge’s shares were up 9.48% on the NSE at 12:30 pm on July 28, trading at ₹1,672.7 apiece.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the company has never supported banning open-weight AI models, as Washington debates potential restrictions on Chinese open-weight models

In a blog post, Amodei said reports suggesting that some US officials were considering banning Chinese open-weight models had led to claims that Anthropic supported such measures to protect its commercial interests.

“Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” he wrote. “Open-weights models that don't have dangerous capabilities are a public good.”

The statement comes as more than 50 technology companies and organisations, including NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Dell Technologies and Hugging Face, signed an open letter opposing restrictions on open-weight AI models and arguing that they are important for innovation, competition and national security.

Instead of restricting open-weight models, Amodei outlined three policy measures that he believes would better address national security risks.

To begin with, he called for tighter controls on exports of advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment to China, along with stronger enforcement against smuggling. According to Amodei, China’s limited domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity means access to advanced US chips remains a key factor in training frontier AI models.

He also urged governments to target what he described as “industrial-scale distillation operations”. Distillation is a training technique that allows smaller models to learn from larger ones while requiring far less compute than training from scratch.

“Distillation is a much more compute-efficient process than training models from scratch,” Amodei wrote. “It allows China to build much better models than its number of chips would ordinarily enable.”

He argued that policies should focus on deterring state-backed distillation efforts rather than banning open-weight models. “A blanket ban on open-weight models is neither the correct remedy nor something we have called for,” he said.

Lastly, Amodei proposed mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable AI models, regardless of whether they are open or closed. He said testing should evaluate cyber, biological and alignment risks before deployment.

“The best way to address threat #2 is to just directly test models for cyber, biological, and alignment risks before release,” he wrote, adding that the approach should apply equally to open and closed models while exempting less capable models from startups and academia.

Amodei also addressed arguments made in the industry-backed open letter. While agreeing that open-weight models broaden access to AI and strengthen competition in some areas, he disputed claims that they inherently improve security.

“I don't agree with the letter’s assertions that open-weight models necessarily make it easier to develop safeguards or that broad access to capabilities necessarily helps defenders more than attackers,” he wrote. “It seems at least as likely to me that the opposite will be true.”

He warned that advances in biology could create an attacker advantage if capable AI models make it easier to develop dangerous pathogens while defensive measures continue to take years to deploy.

Summarising Anthropic’s position, Amodei said the company’s focus remains on “keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands, stopping industrial-scale distillation, and requiring safety testing of all sufficiently capable models, open and closed,” rather than banning open-weight AI models.

Wipro has expanded its partnership with data and artificial intelligence (AI) platform provider Databricks and launched a self-contained business practice to help enterprises modernise their data infrastructure and deploy AI applications at scale.

The new Databricks-focused practice will develop industry-specific AI solutions by combining Databricks' data and AI platform with Wipro's own AI offerings and delivery capabilities.

The initiative, according to a stock exchange filing, is intended to help customers move from fragmented data environments and experimental AI projects to enterprise-wide AI deployments.

As part of the collaboration, Wipro will integrate Databricks' capabilities in agentic AI, data modernisation, analytics, and application development with its Wipro Intelligence suite and agent-native delivery platform WEGA to modernise legacy systems and build AI-ready data architectures.

“Our long-standing collaboration with Databricks reflects a shared commitment to help enterprises move from AI experimentation to measurable value,” Kanwar Singh, Managing Partner - Technology Services, Wipro, said in a statement. “The business practice will bring together platform specialists, consulting expertise, and industry teams to co-create solutions that accelerate data transformation and enterprise-wide AI adoption.”

The company did not disclose the financial terms of the partnership.

The partnership will initially focus on developing AI-led offerings across wealth management, manufacturing planning, telecom sales and marketing, energy asset management, and finance transformation.

“This global practice with Wipro will enable enterprises to build trusted data foundations and deploy production-ready AI at scale, turning data intelligence into real, measurable business impact,” said Kori O’Brien, Senior Vice President, Partnerships, Databricks.

The announcement comes as Indian IT services firms deepen alliances with hyperscalers and AI platform providers to capture growing enterprise demand for agentic AI and data modernisation projects.
